## Editing this runbook

- **The Contents list above is generated, not hand-written.** After adding, renaming or reordering a `## ` section, run `npm run runbook:contents` to rebuild it from the headings in document order. That script is `.freebuff/build-contents.mjs`; the slug rule and the block it writes live in `.freebuff/runbook-contents.mjs`, which the test below imports so the two can never disagree.
- Do not edit a Contents bullet by hand. Each one duplicates a heading and restates it as an anchor, so a hand-edit that disagrees with the heading is a link that clicks to nowhere — and a broken index is worse than none, because it looks navigable. `src/test/runbook-contents.test.ts` asserts the committed block is exactly the generator's output and fails, telling you to run `npm run runbook:contents`, when the two diverge, so a stale list breaks the suite instead of surprising a reader.
- **The anchor is GitHub's heading rule**: lower-case the heading, drop ASCII punctuation (everything except `-` and `_`), and turn spaces into hyphens. So a slash, apostrophe, parenthesis, colon, semicolon or comma simply disappears: `Feed/notification dev behaviours` becomes `#feednotification-dev-behaviours`.
- The generator is idempotent: run when nothing changed, it reports "already up to date" and leaves the file byte-identical. It preserves the file's line endings, and will insert a Contents block below the title if the file somehow lost one.

## Reproduce artifacts

- From the main checkout, copy `.env.local` into this worktree as `.env.local`; do not commit or document secret values.
- Use the npm package manager and run `npm install --legacy-peer-deps` from the project root; the dependency tree currently has Vite/Cloudflare peer-version conflicts that require this flag.
- **Verify both with `npm run preview:preflight`** (`.freebuff/preview-preflight.mjs`) rather than by eye: it checks `node_modules`, every key `.env.local` must define (names only — it never prints a value), and whether any of those keys is set in the shell where it would shadow the file.

## Run the server

- Start the development server with `npm run dev` from the project root.
- Use the default port 3000 when available; if it is occupied, run `npm run dev -- --port <free-port>` and register the resulting loopback URL. **Find out whose server holds a busy port before treating it as merely busy**: on this machine port 3000 has been taken by a *different* checkout's app (a plain `next` server run from `C:\Workspace\Base88`, answering `200` on both loopback families), so a `reach` check saying something answers on the default port is not a statement that the something is this project — the check that turns that into a named failure is `port owner` (below), which is why you register on `preview:preflight`'s own `registerUrl`/`pid` rather than on a hand-rolled `curl`. `vinext dev` records the port it was given in `.vinext/dev/lock.json` (taking a stale entry over on the way), and the gate reads the port back **out of the lock** instead of assuming 3000, so `--port <n>` is only needed before a server has written one; after that a bare `npm run preview:preflight` names the running port and pid itself (observed with a lock on port 3001: `ready to register http://localhost:3001 (pid 20700)`, and the `--json` report carrying `port: 3001` with the same `registerUrl`).
- **Before registering a preview, run `npm run preview:preflight` and register only if it exits 0.** That single command is the gate for everything below: it re-checks the artifacts, then reads the dev lock, the pid in it, and the lock's `cwd`, and finally probes `http://localhost:<port>/` on both loopback families. It exits 0 only when a server is actually up (optionally `--port <n>` and `--timeout <ms>`). An **absent dev lock is not itself a failure**: before the first launch — or when a server was started some other way, or its lock was removed while it kept running — the preflight still exits 0 with a `WARN` on the dev-lock check as long as a server answers on the lock's default port (3000); the missing lock only stays `FAIL` when nothing answers, so the gate is usable both before and after the first launch. Pass `--json` to replace the formatted report with one JSON object on stdout — `{ projectRoot, port, gate ("pass"|"fail"), exitCode, registerUrl, pid, failures, warnings, checks: [{ name, status, detail, fix? }] }` — for CI or another tool to consume; the exit code is the same either way, and the human report remains the default. Pass **`--only=<check>`** (comma-separated; each token matches a check name case-insensitively as a substring, so `--only=reach` gates on every reachability check and `--only="dev server pid"` on that one) to narrow both the report and the gate to the named checks, so a caller can gate on a single concern. Checks that do not match are still evaluated but neither appear nor gate; a selector that matches no check fails loudly rather than passing on an empty gate (the JSON then carries an `error` field naming the checks that were available). The JSON gains an `only` array (`null` when unset) and withholds `registerUrl` unless reachability was actually among the gated checks, so a narrowed pass never advertises an unconfirmed server; the human pass line says the same. **Three checks cover what a probe cannot see, in states where the artifacts and the lock all still look right.** `port owner` covers *whose* server answered: something answering on the port is not a statement that the something is this checkout's, and a dev server in another checkout (or any other app holding the port) answers a probe exactly as happily as this one's — so the listener is identified from the process table (the owning pid first, then what that process is running — and the second read only when the pid alone cannot answer, so a healthy preview pays for the cheap half only) and held against the lock: the port has to belong to the pid the lock names, or to a process whose command line runs out of this checkout. Any other owner **fails, naming the pid and its command line**, with a fix that says not to register that URL; a pid whose command line could not be read fails as well, because a port nobody can vouch for is the one thing this gate exists to keep out; and a port with nothing listening is `INFO`, not a failure of its own, since the reach checks are the ones that speak there. This is the check that catches the trap on this machine: `:3000` held by another checkout's `next` server answers `200` on every probe, so before it existed the lock-and-pid pair was all that stood between that URL and a registered preview. Two notes on its shape. The process table is read **per platform** — `netstat -ano -p tcp`/`-p tcpv6` and `Win32_Process` on Windows, `lsof -t` (with `ss` as the Linux fallback for a host without `lsof`) and `/proc` or `ps` elsewhere — and where none of that can answer, the check reports that it did not look rather than passing on a port nobody vouched for. And its verdicts are driven in tests through **`PREFLIGHT_PORT_OWNER`** (a `{"pid":…,"commandLine":…}` record, or `unknown`), handed over the way `--tab-state` hands over the tabs, because a test cannot arrange a foreign listener on every machine; each platform's *own* read is pinned instead by a live case that starts a real foreign listener on whatever machine the suite is running — the same case on Windows, on Linux, and on macOS — and a host with neither `lsof` nor `ss` skips it rather than failing it, which is why the mutation table deliberately holds no anchor inside a platform read: an anchor only one platform's case could catch would survive on the other. `dev server health` says whether the pid in the lock is actually *serving*: a pid can survive `process.kill(pid, 0)` while answering nothing on its port (a wedged or mid-restart `vinext dev`), and that case names `taskkill /PID <pid> /F` as the fix rather than `npm run dev`, which the still-live lock would refuse — a *dead* pid stays the `dev server pid` check's stale lock, which the next launch takes over. It refuses that phrase for a port another process holds — the answer being served is not that process's — and points at `port owner` instead. `preview tab` covers the browser half, which no loopback probe can see: this script inspects the machine, not the tabs, so the caller hands its open tabs over with **`--tab-state=<json|file>`** (the JSON itself when it starts with `[` or `{`, otherwise a path; an array, or an object with a `tabs` array, of entries that are a URL string or carry `url` (or `appUrl`), so `--tab-state='[]'` says nothing is open). With it, a server that answers while **no open tab points at it** fails — the preview tab was closed, so the fix names re-opening it at the register URL — and the mirror case, a tab left open on a port nothing answers on, warns that the server died behind the tab; the loopback spellings (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`) count as one machine, so a tab is not missed over spelling, and a bad or unreadable tab list fails loudly. Without `--tab-state` the check reports that it was *not* checked, so gating on it is never a silent pass. Note the preflight's `--only` selects *checks*, while the CI runner's `--only` selects *stages*. Its own load-bearingness is swept by **`npm run mutation:preflight`**, which breaks each branch of the mid-session checks — the wedged lock, the port's owner and the tab — one at a time and requires this file's tests to fail (see the gate bullets below).
- **In CI, gate on `npm run ci`** (`.freebuff/ci.mjs`) rather than on the individual commands: it runs the whole verification pass — **typecheck** (`tsc --noEmit`), the **runbook Contents check** (`build-contents.mjs --check`, so a heading renamed without regenerating the list fails here rather than as a dead link), the **lint baseline** (`lint-baseline.mjs`, a whole-project ESLint run where a single finding — error or warning — fails the stage, its findings folded under a counted heading per file the way the drift stage folds its rows by watch family), the **vitest suite** (`vitest run`, read through vitest's JSON reporter so a failure names the failing tests rather than dumping the tree), the **preview preflight**, the **gate drift check**, and the three tree-editing checks — the **coverage-gate mutation check**, the **preflight mutation sweep**, and the **route-guard mutation sweep** (`npm run mutation:guards`) — cheapest first, so a type error surfaces before the suite and the three sweeps (which rewrite files as they run) go last, and the two smaller sweeps go before the route one. It stops at the first failing stage — the stages are cheapest-first precisely so a red typecheck does not wait for the minutes-long suite and sweeps behind it — and names the stages it did not reach rather than letting them look passed. A detected CI environment (`CI=true` — the convention nearly every system follows — or another marker such as `GITHUB_ACTIONS`) turns `--keep-going` on by itself, so a scheduled job reports **every** problem rather than only the first, while a local run stays fail-fast; a falsey `CI` (`""`, `"0"`, `"false"`) counts as local. The effective value is reported as `keepGoing` in the `--json` report (and mentioned once in the log when CI is what turned it on). How far to go after a failure has three answers, and at most one may be asked for: `--keep-going` runs the whole list, `--fail-fast` stops at the first, and **`--max-failures=<n>`** is the middle ground — it runs past a failure but stops once `n` stages have failed, so a job can report several distinct problems without paying for the minutes-long suite and sweep behind them. A non-positive or non-numeric value is refused, a capped run does **not** take the CI `--keep-going` default (it would defeat the cap), and `maxFailures` is reported in the `--json` report alongside `keepGoing`. `--from=<name>` is the resume path: it starts at that stage and runs the rest in canonical order, so once a failure low in the order is fixed you do not replay the cheap stages that already passed — and the stopped-early summary suggests the first stage it did not reach (`--from=<that stage>`), so the resume point is named rather than something to work out. An unknown `--from` is rejected rather than quietly widening to the whole job, and `--from` with `--only` is refused, because each already answers where the run starts and honouring one would silently run a different set than the other describes. It exits nonzero if any selected stage failed. On failure it prints a compact summary naming what broke — the `TSxxxx` error, the failing test, the failed check with its fix, or the surviving mutant by file and line — instead of the full report. Whether it passed or failed, a **one-line verdict** — `ci: verdict — N passed, N failed, N skipped, N unchanged, N reused, N excluded (N selected)` — **brackets** the run: it counts each selected stage by outcome (the `--skip` exclusions included) on the line that opens the log, projecting what the run is about to attempt (nothing has passed or failed yet, but change detection and the result cache already know which stages it will not run), and again on the line that closes it, so a long log has the counts at both ends rather than only at the end of a scroll. It is a projection, not a promise — a run that stops early turns stages the opener listed as `unchanged` or `reused` into `skipped` — and under `--json` both lines go to stderr with the rest of the progress, keeping stdout the report alone. Every stage that runs a gate script **declares** it (`script`, reported by `--explain-cache`), and that script and every module the script loads are behind the stage's own key, so a gate whose machinery changed cannot be answered from a recorded pass. The same policy covers the pin: before it opens its log, the run asks which pinned gate files are behind no key at all — counting both halves, a stage's own `inputs` and the `GLOBAL_FORCE` files that sit behind every key — and a file behind neither stops the run with the file named (and `uncovered` in the `--json` report) rather than being answered from a pass that never measured it; `KEY_EXEMPT_PINNED` is the one way such a file becomes a decision rather than a failure, and `npm run gates:status` prints the map that says which it is (`NO KEY` for the first, `EXEMPT` for the second, each gap naming the watch rule that pinned the file beside it and, when that rule's own family points at one, the stage that should have named the file *and* the file of that family already behind that stage's key, so the repair reads as a stage and a sibling to extend rather than a family to decode — and the refusal prints that stage's whole entry in the alarm's own stage table with the file appended to its `inputs` — `{ name: "runbook", label: "runbook contents", script: { env: "CI_RUNBOOK_SCRIPT", path: "./build-contents.mjs" }, inputs: [ … ] },` — a line to paste into `.freebuff/gate-drift.mjs`, where each stage is declared, rather than a stage to go find in the runner; it is the whole entry and not a fragment so that pasting it cannot drop the label a report calls the stage or the script the run spawns). One more refusal comes before the log for the same reason, and on the scripts rather than the pin: the run asks `node --check` about the script each stage it is *about to run* declares — the same `stage.script()` reading it takes when it spawns them, so a `CI_*_SCRIPT` stub stands in here exactly as it does there and a run narrowed by `--only`, by `--changed-only` or by a reused cache never refuses over a file it will not run — and a script node will not compile stops the run with the file, the line and the parser's own message named (`unparsable` in the `--json` report). Without it, one truncated write is reported as four unrelated failures: the lint stage a finding in a file it never linted, the gate that runs it a killed process with no JSON, the suite whose subject never loaded, and the drift alarm a pin that moved. The check runs before every stage and costs nothing on a fully warm cache, since a reused stage's script is one it will not spawn. The file that refusal was written for now holds its own tail by shape too: `src/test/preview-preflight.test.ts` asserts that the script still closes its report block and that both of its sentences are still in it, because a write cut on a *statement* boundary parses cleanly and takes the sentence a reader needs without a gate ever noticing — the one truncation the parse check above cannot see. That pin is itself held: `mutation:preflight`'s `report/register-sentence` case drops that arm's `else` whole — the same cut by another hand, and one that still parses — and requires this test to fail, so a relaxed assertion (a shortened count, a dropped sentence) is reported as a survivor rather than passing as a pin that no longer holds anything. The sweep has since proven it on the repaired source — the first full 28-mutation run the truncation allowed ends `Checked 28 mutation(s)` with every branch caught, and `report/register-sentence` runs last: `[28/28] caught report/register-sentence — caught by 1 of 27: closes the report block it opened, with both of its sentences still in it` — the one strike whose proof had to wait for the file it pins to be whole again, the tree restored byte-identical (`f45b2c93`) and no lock left behind. The same map is read a second way below the rows — grouped by the watch rule that pinned each file, with how many members of each family sit behind each stage's key (`family coverage`, families with a member behind no stage's key first, then the ones no stage but the pin's own `drift` re-key holds whole, which carry `a new member would be held by drift alone`) — so a family a stage only half holds is visible while the tree is green rather than only once one of its members falls out of every key, and a family a *widened* rule would leave behind the re-key alone is a family to name in a stage's `inputs` before that happens rather than after (the `exposed` field of the `--json` `families`) — and every row ends with the stage that should own the family, the same owner clause a red drift's family headings carry: the stage that *names* the most of its members with an input scoped to a place (a literal path, a directory glob, a watch rule) — counted ahead of one that only sweeps the family up with a whole-tree extension glob, so the lint stage's `mjs` sweep keeps a `.mjs` family only where nothing else names a member of it — then the one holding it whole, the one to extend with the member it already keys, or a flat `no stage keys it` when none does, resolved from the same rows (the `owner` field of each `--json` family), so a green tree says what to do about a half-held family rather than only that it is half held. **`npm run gates:status -- --watch=<file-or-rule>`** reads that same view once more with a *proposed stage input* in hand and answers the mark's question about a concrete edit — "is this file, named in a stage's `inputs`, enough?" — without writing anything. The candidate is a file path or a glob (matched the way a glob input is matched) or a watch rule in the `dir/pattern` shape the views print (resolved through the alarm's own scan, so the files it would watch are the files the pin would hold); the narrower path reading is tried first, and where the two overlap they name the same file. A family is `closes`d when some stage's `inputs` naming the candidate would leave that stage holding every member — reported with the stage that already holds part of the family (the extension the coverage refusal would name), or as `any stage naming it` when no stage holds a member of it today, which is a different instruction and is kept apart — and the families it cannot close stay on the report with how many of their members it does cover, so a proposal that fixes one family of three cannot read as a fix for all of them; a `verdict` line says how many of the marked families it closes. A spec that is neither a path the pin holds nor a rule that compiles is named for what it is (the alarm's own two refusals, surfaced) rather than reported as matching nothing, the pin and the stage list are only ever read, and `--watch` outside `--status` — or with no spec, or one the shell ate — is refused rather than silently ignored. The `--json` form carries the whole reading as a top-level `watch` beside `families`. When the **drift stage itself** fails, its summary says which of the pin's watch families moved — `4 gate file(s) no longer match the pin — 2 watch families moved: .freebuff/^coverage-.*\.mjs$ (2), .github/workflows/^.*\.ya?ml$ (1), 1 file(s) no watch rule names` — grouping the findings by the rule that names each path (the stage's `inputs` *are* those rules, so it is the stage describing itself), scariest first — a family with a member behind no stage's key, or one no stage but the pin's own `drift` re-key holds whole, leads whether one of its files moved or forty, the same exposure order `--status` prints, with the moved count as the tie-break — with a pinned path no rule names any more counted apart because that is the rule to re-check rather than the tree to re-pin; and the per-file rows keep their diffs while folding under a heading per family — the same rule, counted the same way as the clause above it — so a whole-tree re-pin reads as a few families rather than forty interchangeable rows, with the paths no rule names any more under a heading of their own, and each heading a detail that names no file (flagged `heading` in the `--json` `details` and skipped by the annotations, so every file still gets exactly one) which also carries the repair beside the grouping — the same owner clause the `--status` family rows carry above: the stage that holds the family whole, the stage to extend (with the file of the family it already keys) when one only part-holds it, or a flat `no stage keys it` when none does — the same two repairs the coverage refusal spells out for a lost file, said here for a family that is merely red, so a reader who follows the leading family is told what to do about it rather than only that it moved. The repair is on the **alarm's own report** too, and off the one declaration: the stage list a family's owner is read from now lives in `.freebuff/gate-drift.mjs` beside the watch rules (the runner builds its `STAGES` from it and imports the same matching and owner readings), so `npm run gates:drift` — the alarm run on its own, without CI — folds its findings under a heading per watch family the way the stage above folds its rows: `FAMILY  <rule> (<moved>)<owner clause>`, the same rule and the same words, with the per-file rows kept in the order they were collected so `changed`, `unpinned` and `gone` still read in that order *inside* a family, and a pinned path no watch rule names any more under a closing `UNNAMED  <n> file(s) no watch rule names` heading rather than drifting between families. The headings take the runner's own order — the families a new member would leave behind the re-key lead, then how much moved, then the rule's name — carried on the payload as `movedFamilies` beside the flat rows, so a consumer folding the alarm's own report puts the same family first instead of re-deriving an order it has no exposure reading for; `--json` still carries the same `family` and `owner` fields on every finding row, so the flat list is still there for a consumer that wants it. A check whose moved families include one that **no stage's key names** refuses as well as reports: re-pinning those records the new hash and leaves the family measured by nothing — the next loosening in it is reported as drift and never fails a gate that reads those files — so the ordinary advice is incomplete for exactly them, and a report that gave only that advice would be advising the hole. The refusal names the families that moved with no key, carries them as `refused` (the sentence as `refusal`, so a consumer reports what the alarm said rather than re-cutting it), and prints last — after the paragraph that says to re-pin — because it qualifies that advice rather than adding to it; the CI runner's drift stage puts the same sentence on its **summary**, the one string the log, the `--json` report, the run page and the nightly comment all carry. A moved family a stage *does* key (even by a whole-tree sweep) is an ordinary finding with its clause and no refusal, a rule whose last member is `gone` is the re-pin decision the check already asks for, and a pin that will not resolve has no family view to refuse from — the alarm says what it could read rather than inventing a hole. A stage that passes records a digest of everything it reads — the files its `inputs` globs name, plus the `GLOBAL_FORCE` build and config files — in the git-ignored `.ci/cache.json`, and a later run that finds the same digest does not run it again: it is reported as **reused**, named per stage, listed in the report's `reused` array and counted apart from `passed` rather than read as a pass this run. The key is content rather than a timestamp, so a bare `touch` invalidates nothing and any input change, a missing entry or `--no-cache` sends the stage back through a real run; only passes are cached, since a failure is what you are iterating on and so always re-runs with fresh evidence. A recorded pass is trusted for a week and then **expired** — a content digest cannot see a dependency that drifted outside a stage's globs — so the stage runs again and records afresh, with the stages it expired named both up front (`ci: re-running N stage(s) — recorded pass expired (cap 7d): …`) and on each stage's own line, so a run that looks like it ought to have reused one says why it did not and a stale entry cannot vouch for a tree indefinitely. `--cache-ttl=<duration>` (`30m`, `12h`, `7d`) moves that line; `--cache-ttl=0` removes the cap; and `--no-cache` neither reads nor writes the cache. The policy in force is reported as `cacheTtlMs` (`null` meaning no cap) and the re-run stages as the report's `expired` array. When a stage that looked reusable ran anyway, **`--explain-cache`** answers why without paying for the suite: it reports the decision the run is about to take for every selected stage — `reuse`, `run` (with the reason: no recorded pass, a digest that moved, the cache is off), `expired` or `unchanged` — with the files behind each key, each named beside the input that put it there, and how recently they were touched, then exits without running anything. When the files will not fit on the line the inputs are given with how many files each contributed, which is what makes the drift stage's line an answer rather than a roster: its inputs are the alarm's watch rules, so the reader sees which gate family a key is built from (`^coverage-.*\.mjs$ ×7`) instead of thirty-six file names. Secret-looking inputs — `.env*`, `*.pem`, credential files — become a `<redacted>` marker in both the human line and the JSON, one entry at a time rather than collapsed so the pairing survives, so the explanation can be pasted into a pull request or a log without publishing a name that was meant to stay out of the repo, while the honest count of files behind the key is kept. It reads the *same* decision record the run reads, so the explanation cannot describe behavior the runner would not take; `--json` gives it as an object with every file paired to the input that matched it (`matchedBy`) and the build and config files that re-key every stage resolved once as `globalForce` — the half of a key a stage's own `inputs` never name, counted on the header line too (`, N file(s) behind every key`), and each selected stage also carries the watch-rule families its key already holds a member of, each with the file that earned it — the sibling the coverage refusal names, reachable by naming a stage on a tree where nothing is uncovered — and `--dry-run` remains the shorter report of the selection alone (the two report-and-exit modes are kept apart rather than combined). `--only=<name>` (comma-separated, e.g. `--only=typecheck,test`) runs a subset, which matters because the suite and the sweep together are minutes long — an unknown name is rejected with the offending token rather than silently narrowing the gate, `--from` (above) is its resume counterpart and the two are kept apart, and `--dry-run` prints the stages that would run (the resumed tail included) and exits without running them; `--port`/`--timeout` forward to the preflight, `--file=` and `--no-fail-open` to the route sweep, and **`--limit=` to both sweep stages** — the only flag two of them read, so a slice taken by count is taken for whichever of the two the run selected rather than only the expensive one. `--json` replaces the human report with a single machine-readable object on stdout (progress moves to stderr) — `{ gate, exitCode, stages[], failed[], skipped[], stoppedEarly, keepGoing, maxFailures, unchanged[], excluded[], annotations[] }`, each stage carrying its name, pass/fail, summary, details and raw lines — so a CI system can read the result without parsing the log; the exit code is unchanged and a usage error is reported as JSON too. The report also carries an **`annotations`** array — one entry per failing (or warning) detail, `{ level, file?, line?, column?, title, message }`, in stage-then-detail order so the first failure leads — which is where a type error, a lint finding, a failed test or a surviving mutant gets the file and line to point at (`message` folds in the `fix` when the detail has one). **`--github-annotations`** renders that same array as GitHub Actions workflow commands on stdout — `::error file=…,line=…,col=…,title=…::…`, `::warning` for a warning-level finding, with `%`, CR, LF, `:` and `,` escaped — so the first failure lands inline on the diff instead of only in the log; it is mutually exclusive with `--json`, since both spell their output on stdout and either would corrupt the other. For the JSON gate stages it reads their `--json` contract rather than the rendered report, and it fails — rather than passes — when a gate produces no JSON at all, so a crashed gate is a loud CI failure instead of a silent green. Every stage's script is overridable through an env var — `CI_TYPECHECK_SCRIPT`, `CI_RUNBOOK_SCRIPT`, `CI_LINT_SCRIPT`, `CI_TEST_SCRIPT`, `CI_PREFLIGHT_SCRIPT`, `CI_DRIFT_SCRIPT`, `CI_MUTATION_COVERAGE_SCRIPT`, `CI_MUTATION_PREFLIGHT_SCRIPT`, `CI_MUTATION_SCRIPT` (an absolute path, or one relative to `.freebuff/`) — the seam `src/test/ci-runner.test.ts` uses to drive any stage against a stub (a pass, a failure naming its checks, tests or survivors, or no output at all) without running the real tool. That test also runs the **real** preflight (over an unused port) against the real runner and asserts the runner's summary is derived from the preflight's own `gate`/`checks[].status` fields — a rename on either side makes the printed counts disagree, so the two cannot drift apart silently. A mutation counterpart does the same for the sweep's `gate`/`checked`/`survivors[]`, but is **opt-in** (`CI_SHAPE_CONTRACT=1 npx vitest run src/test/ci-runner.test.ts`) because the sweep rewrites source as it runs and cannot share a tree with the rest of the suite without a route test observing a half-mutated guard; the always-on real sweep is the CI runner's `mutation` stage.

**The stage table is declared once, in `.freebuff/gate-drift.mjs`, and checked on every run**, so neither the count below nor a stage's own fields can be typed by hand: the table carries each stage's `label`, the gate `script` it runs with the override a test drives that script through, the `inputs` its cache key covers, and `editsTree` on the three checks whose pass rewrites the working tree — the runner builds its `STAGES` by mapping that table onto its own `run`s, so it cannot restate a label, a script, an input list or the order — the line between the markers is written by `npm run stages:write`, and a copy of the order that disagrees with the table — here, in the runner's own header, in the runner's tests, in the nightly job's selection, or in a list written in the table's own file — stops the run before its first stage. `npm run stages:check` names every disagreeing claim, and alongside them the claims an entry makes about the list itself (a stage with no label, one whose label another stage already carries, a declared script behind none of its own `inputs` or with no override variable, and an `editsTree` that is not one of the tail or that shares the lock `check` name another stage holds); `npm run stages` prints the order itself.

<!-- stage-order:begin -->
11 stage(s), in canonical order: `typecheck`, `runbook`, `lint`, `test`, `preflight`, `drift`, `mutation-example`, `mutation-fifth`, `mutation-coverage`, `mutation-preflight`, `mutation`.
<!-- stage-order:end -->
- **`npm run ci -- --changed-only` runs only the stages the working tree feeds, so a one-file change does not pay for the minutes-long sweep.** It reads the changed paths from the working-tree diff — `git diff --name-only <base>` (base from `--diff-base`, default `HEAD`) plus `git ls-files --others` — or from `CI_CHANGED_FILES` (newline-separated) when a CI system hands over the pull request's own file list. Each stage declares the globs it reads, and a stage no changed file matches is reported `SKIP … nothing it reads changed` (and named in the `--json` report's `unchanged` array) rather than failed, so a green job still says which stages did not run. The example it exists for: a change to `src/lib/foo.ts` runs `typecheck`, `lint` and `test`, and leaves the `mutation` sweep for when a `src/app/**/route.ts` or its neighbour `route.test.ts` moved. It is conservative by construction — an unreadable diff (an unborn `HEAD`, a ref that does not resolve), an **empty** change set, or any build/config file (`package.json`, the lockfile, `tsconfig*`, `vite.config.*`, `vitest.config.*`, `eslint.config.*`, `wrangler.toml`, `.freebuff/ci.mjs`, `.github/**`) falls back to running **every** stage, printing the reason — so it can only ever skip when it positively knows a change reads nothing a stage reads, never when a change could plausibly matter. It is opt-in and is *not* the full gate: leave it off in CI, or pass an explicit `--diff-base`, rather than let a clean checkout skip everything.
- **`npm run ci -- --skip=<stage>` leaves a stage out of the run, and `.github/workflows/nightly.yml` is where that is used.** The nightly job runs the whole gate on a schedule (`17 2 * * *`, plus `workflow_dispatch`), on a clean checkout, as `npm run --silent ci -- --json --skip=preflight` — the `--silent` keeps npm's own banner off stdout so the one JSON object is all that is captured — and publishes the result: `.freebuff/nightly-report.mjs` renders the report into the run's Markdown summary and GitHub annotations, and the raw JSON (with the runner's stderr log) is kept as a `nightly-ci-report` artifact so a regression can be diffed against the previous night's — and both halves of that publish path collapse any secret-looking file name (`.env*`, `*.pem`, a credentials file) to `<redacted>` before it is written, since the run page is read by people and the artifact is downloadable. The runner redacts a name as it records a result (so the uploaded JSON is safe by construction) and the renderer redacts again at the publish boundary (so it does not trust its input), both through the one definition in `.freebuff/redact.mjs`; only a name is withheld — the count, the line and everything else are kept. Because the runner detects `CI=true` there, it also keeps going past a failure by itself, so a night reports **every** broken stage rather than only the first — the regressions a local fail-fast run, or a `--changed-only` one, would never reach. `--skip` is **subtractive**: it removes the named stages from whatever `--only`/`--from` produced (and composes with both). It is for a stage the *host* cannot run rather than one the change did not touch — that is `--changed-only`'s job. A name that matches no stage is refused like a `--only` typo, an empty list is refused, and a `--skip` that would leave nothing to run is refused. The omitted stages are named on the run's first lines and carried in the report's `excluded` array, so a green run that skipped something never reads as a full pass. The one stage the nightly drops is the **preview preflight**: it gates registering a *local* preview and can only pass with a live dev server on loopback and a `.env.local` on disk, neither of which a hosted runner has — running it there would fail every night for an environment it was never meant to judge.
- **`vinext dev` refuses to start a second server from the same directory** (`Another vinext dev server is already running`) and bails rather than binding a new port. The lock it uses is **`.vinext/dev/lock.json`** — a JSON object `{ pid, port, hostname, appUrl, startedAt, cwd }`, written by `vinext` itself (not a hand-rolled pid file; the stray `.freebuff/devserver.pid` is left over from an older mechanism and nothing reads it). So check that pid before launching: if it is alive, the server is already up and should be reused (register it) instead of starting another; only `taskkill /PID <pid> /F` it when the pid is genuinely dead — a dead pid means a stale lock, which the next `npm run dev` takes over on its own. `preview:preflight` performs all of this and names the failing check — and it tells the two lock failures apart, because their fixes are different: a *dead* pid is the stale lock the next `npm run dev` takes over, while a *live* pid that answers nothing on the lock's port is a wedged server, which the next launch is refused by (`Another vinext dev server is already running`) and which the `dev server health` check therefore fixes with `taskkill /PID <pid> /F`.
- **The listener is on IPv6 loopback** (`[::1]:3000`), so health-check `http://localhost:3000` — probing `127.0.0.1:3000` reports the port closed even while it is serving. That is why the preflight probes `localhost`, `[::1]` and `127.0.0.1` separately, and why a refusing `127.0.0.1` is reported as an expected note rather than a failure.

## Database endpoint note

- `DATABASE_URL` uses the Supabase pooler host (`*.pooler.supabase.com`); `src/lib/db/index.ts` rewrites port 5432 to the transaction pooler 6543.
- Do NOT switch to the direct `db.<project>.supabase.co` endpoint on this machine: that host is IPv6-only (AAAA record) and the machine has no IPv6 connectivity — verified with DNS lookups and TCP probes (even `google.com:443` over IPv6 times out).
- IMPORTANT: make sure `DATABASE_URL` is NOT set in the shell/OS environment before starting the server. A stale user-level variable overrides `.env.local` and silently points the client at the wrong host (this caused the client to fall back to `localhost:5432` and fail with `ECONNREFUSED`). Start with a clean env: `Remove-Item Env:DATABASE_URL` (PowerShell).
- Connection pool sizing matters: Supavisor silently drops idle sockets, and with `max: 1` a single stuck connect blocks every other query. The client keeps a small pool (`max: 5`) with a short `idle_timeout` and bounded `max_lifetime` so traffic is never serialized behind one stuck socket.

## Demo data

- Seed (or re-seed) the demo dataset with `npm run db:seed`. It is idempotent: every row uses a fixed id and `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, so re-running never duplicates or overwrites anything, and it never touches real accounts. The script loads `.env.local` itself via `tsx --env-file-if-exists`.
- It needs `R2_*` storage credentials: 8 avatars and 16 post images are generated locally with sharp from SVG and uploaded once under the `seed/` prefix, and 4 sample videos (Big Buck Bunny, CC-BY 3.0) are mirrored into the bucket. Existing objects are detected with a HEAD request and skipped, so re-seeds are quick and re-runnable offline.
- Run it with a clean environment (`Remove-Item Env:DATABASE_URL`) for the same reason as the dev server — and note that inherited environment variables win over `--env-file`.
- The 8 demo members are content-only personas with no credentials; they cannot sign in. Sign in with a real account to see them in the feed.

## Live feed updates (Supabase Realtime)

- The feed subscribes to `public.posts` INSERTs instead of polling. For that to work the table must be in the Realtime publication, which is **not** on by default for tables created outside the dashboard:
  `alter publication supabase_realtime add table public.posts;`
  Without it the subscription still reaches `SUBSCRIBED` and simply never receives a row, so the feed silently looks healthy but never updates.
- Realtime carries only the raw `posts` row, so a pushed id is resolved through `GET /api/posts?ids=<uuid,...>` to get the author and media the card needs (max 25 ids per request).
- `posts` has **RLS disabled** and `anon`/`authenticated` keep default SELECT grants, which is what lets a browser subscribe with the public anon key. Consequences to know before changing it: enabling RLS requires a permissive SELECT policy for the subscriber role, or Realtime delivers nothing; and because the raw rows are broadcast, anything in `posts` (including `visibility = 'private'`) reaches any client holding the anon key. PostgREST already exposes the same rows to `anon` today, so Realtime adds no new exposure — but locking it down is a table-wide decision, not a feed-level one.
- The first query after an idle gap pays a Supavisor cold connect (measured 2-19 s for `/api/posts?ids=`; steady state is ~0.6 s). That dominates how fast a pushed post becomes a card, and it affects every API route equally — it is not the Realtime path.
- To verify by hand, publish as a demo member and watch for the pill, e.g. `node --env-file-if-exists=.env.local .freebuff/live-insert.mjs maya_designs "probe"` (`--clean` removes those probe rows again).
- Comment and reaction activity is **not** a `postgres_changes` subscription. Adding `comments` and `reactions` to the publication would broadcast every row of both tables — including `reactions.user_id`, i.e. who reacted to what — to any client holding the anon key. Instead the trigger in `drizzle/0003_feed_activity.sql` publishes `{post_id, absolute counts, added/removed comment id}` to the Realtime topic `feed:activity` (applied as the `feed_activity_broadcast` migration; every statement is idempotent, and drizzle has no snapshot for it, so do not regenerate it with `drizzle-kit`).
- A Supabase channel's **name is the broadcast topic**, so the feed subscribes to a channel literally called `feed:activity` and also binds the post row changes to it. `supabase.channel(topic)` returns the existing channel when the topic matches, so a second subscriber on the same topic shares it rather than opening a new one.
- The trigger wraps `realtime.send` in an exception block on purpose: the event describes a write that already committed, and a Realtime hiccup must not turn a successful comment into a failed one.
- Counts are computed in SQL in two places (`GET /api/posts` and `GET /api/posts/counts?ids=`). **Do not interpolate the outer column into those correlated subqueries with `${posts.id}`**: drizzle drops the table qualifier when a query has a single table, so it renders a bare `"id"`, which the subquery resolves to its *own* `comments.id` — the count then silently returns 0. Write `"posts"."id"`. The list endpoint only escapes this because its joins force full qualification.
- `GET /api/posts/counts?ids=` returns only live posts, so a requested id **missing** from a successful response means deleted. The feed uses that after a reconnect to remove posts deleted while the socket was down.
- Check what a verification run left behind with `... activity-probe.mjs stats` — read-only totals (posts, live, non-public, edited, media, follows, notifications) to compare against the baseline above.
- Verify comment/reaction activity with `node --env-file-if-exists=.env.local .freebuff/activity-probe.mjs <post|comment|react|unreact|comment-remove|post-remove|post-purge|counts|stats|cleanup> ...`. `cleanup` removes probe posts and their comments; note it does **not** remove reactions left on *seeded* posts, so clear those yourself after a reaction test. `post-purge` and `cleanup` also delete the probe posts' own R2 objects (see the storage-cleanup section); they still cannot clean up objects belonging to rows they do not delete.
## Notifications (nav badge)

- Rows are created by the database, not by the API: the `notify_engagement` trigger in `drizzle/0004_notifications_live.sql` (applied as the `notifications_live` migration) fires on `comments`, `reactions` and `follows` inserts, resolves the recipient, skips self-activity, dedupes re-reactions, and stores the finished wording in `notifications.message` so the pushed row and the API can never disagree. It is idempotent, and drizzle has no snapshot for it — do not regenerate it with `drizzle-kit`.
- Delivery is `postgres_changes` on `public.notifications`, which **must stay in the `supabase_realtime` publication**. It does not rely on a client-side filter: the table has RLS enabled with a `for select to authenticated using (user_id = auth.uid())` policy, and Realtime evaluates that policy as the subscriber. Verified — an event addressed to another user leaves the badge untouched, and an `anon` PostgREST read of the table returns `[]`.
- The alternative (a private broadcast topic per user) is not available here: it needs a policy on `realtime.messages`, which is owned by `supabase_realtime_admin` and cannot be modified by the migration role.
- `GET /api/notifications` returns the newest 50 rows plus the authoritative `unreadCount`; `POST` marks one or all read and returns the recomputed total. `created_at` is selected as text (`to_char(...)`) because postgres.js reads a `timestamp without time zone` back as local time; the provider normalises a pushed row's timestamp the same way (bare `2026-09-23 09:20:00` is treated as UTC).
- The provider subscribes to the channel `notifications:<userId>` and re-reads the API on every re-`SUBSCRIBED`, because Realtime never replays what was missed while the socket was down. It also resets its state whenever the signed-in user changes — the badge sits in the nav, outside any auth gate.
- Counting rule: the server total is authoritative and hydration sets it; a pushed insert adds 1; marking read subtracts 1 locally and is then corrected by the response's recomputed total. A burst of inserts between hydrations is therefore self-correcting on the next read or reconnect.
- Verify by hand with the notification commands added to `.freebuff/activity-probe.mjs`: `follow <username> <target>`, `unfollow`, `notify <username>`, `notify-add <username> <type> "<message>"`, `notify-clean <username> <minutes>`. `notify-clean` is scoped to one inbox and one time window on purpose. **`notify-add` exists because the trigger means a probe `follow` would seed a count too, but only by touching `follows`** — and a probe follow is the thing that is expensive to undo here (see the warning below). Seeding the row directly keeps the follow edges untouched, and one `notify-clean` puts the inbox back; it writes an unread row with no `source_user_id`, so it renders as a row that only marks read, which is fine for checking the badge. Remember to run the matching `unfollow`/`unreact`: `cleanup` only removes probe posts and `[activity-probe]` comments, not reactions or follows. **A probe `follow` printing `"id": null` means the edge already existed** (the insert is `on conflict do nothing`, which the unique index now actually enforces) — it does not mean the probe failed, and deleting that pair deletes a seeded row. **And never clean up probe follows with `delete ... where created_at <> min(created_at)`**: every seeded follow shares one `created_at`, but the database's `now()` is *earlier* than that stamp, so `min()` selects a probe row and the predicate matches the seeded ones instead — that deleted all 32 seeded edges once. Delete an explicit list of the pairs you created. To restore a seeded pair, insert it with the exact stamp `'2026-09-23 13:13:52.897371'::timestamp` **inlined in the SQL text**: sent as a parameter it is inferred as `timestamptz` and shifted by the UTC offset (the same hazard the timestamp section describes). Restored rows get new uuids, so the tiebreak order inside a list (`follows.id desc`) is not the original one.
- To prove the reconnect path, disconnect the socket from the page and reconnect it (a dynamic `import('/src/utils/supabase/client.ts')` returns the cached singleton, so `client.realtime.disconnect()` / `.connect()` reach the app's own channels). Expect no badge change while down, then one `GET /api/notifications` and a catch-up count after rejoin.

- The bell itself is a `DisclosureButton` with `controls="notification-panel"`, and the panel carries that `id`; both are written from the same `isOpen` boolean, so the trigger cannot end up saying `false` about a panel it just opened. Inside, an unread row's dot is a `StatusIndicator` labelled `Unread` — it was a bare `aria-hidden` circle, so the row's read state was drawn and never said. See the state-conventions section.

## Opening what a notification refers to

- A notification row stores `target_type`/`target_id`; a comment or reaction points at its post, a follow points at the user who followed (`source_user_id`). The bell renders those rows as links: `/feed?post=<id>` for a post, `/profile?user=<id>` for a follower. Rows with no destination stay buttons that only mark read.
- The feed reads `?post=`, pages forward for it (up to `MAX_FOCUS_PAGES = 5`, i.e. ~100 posts) and only fetches it by id — inserting it at its timestamp — when it is older than that. Paging first matters: cursor pages are strictly older, so a post reached that way can never be overtaken by a later page, whereas a hand-inserted one can and would slide out of view. It then scrolls the windowed list to that card, rings it for ~2.6s and replaces the URL with `/feed` so a reload does not jump again. A post that no longer exists gets a "no longer available" notice instead of a silent no-op.
- A deep-linked post is also *pinned* (`pinnedPostIdRef`), because a refresh replaces the list with page one; without the pin the post the reader was just taken to would vanish underneath them. The list is re-sorted newest-first after every fetch so an out-of-order insert cannot leave newer posts below an older one.
- The jump re-checks its position at 120/400/800/1400/2000/2600 ms — as long as the ring lasts, because an item above the target can be measured late (an image finishing loading grows its card) and push the target down. Reader input cancels the remaining checks. Measured on a post two pages deep: it lands at 69px under the sticky header (target 68) and stays there.
- Jumping does not depend on estimated heights: an item is absolutely positioned at exactly its layout offset, so scrolling to that offset lands on the card. What *does* move it afterwards is measurement, and the list compensates — including a **first** measurement (estimate → measured), which is why `applyHeight` now compares against `estimateHeight` when a key has no recorded height. Without that, a jump of many screens slid by ~200-700px as items above the fold were measured. `scrollToKey` additionally re-checks the position at 120/400/800ms and cancels on any wheel/touch/key, so a correction can never fight the reader.
- `/profile` accepts `?user=` (a follow notification) and `?username=` (the QR share link) and renders that member read-only: no composer, no Edit/Story/QR controls, real follower and following counts. Both feed and profile use `useSearchParams`, which is why each page's default export wraps its body in `Suspense`, as the search page already did.
- `/api/users/follow` takes an optional `following` boolean and **states the intent** rather than toggling; omitting it keeps the old toggle behaviour. A toggle would silently unfollow somebody when a client held a stale view, which is exactly what the search page did before. It returns the target's fresh follower total so the UI never has to guess ±1, and it is idempotent (201 only when something changed). It fires the follow notification trigger, like any other follow insert.
- `follows` has a unique index on `(follower_id, following_id)` (`drizzle/0005_follows_unique.sql`, applied as the `follows_unique` migration) plus per-column indexes. The route's read-then-write is not atomic, so the index is the backstop: the insert uses `onConflictDoNothing` and the unfollow deletes **every** matching row. Without it, two interleaved requests (two tabs, a retried request, or two Cloudflare isolates — the project also targets Workers) insert twice, and unfollow then removes only one row, leaving the button on "Follow" while the next load reads "Following" and the follower count inflated. The migration collapses any pre-existing duplicates onto the earliest row before creating the index. Verified: five concurrent `following: true` requests for one pair → one `201`, four `200`, and exactly one row.
- `FollowButton` writes to that endpoint for real, optimistically, and rolls back on failure (the error also lands in an sr-only live region, since a reverted button looks the same as a failed one). `ProfileHeader` renders it for non-owners along with a Message button.
- `Message` opens a dialog that sends the first message through `POST /api/messages`, which creates the conversation when there is not one and returns its id; the app then opens `/messages?c=<conversationId>` and the messages page selects that conversation. `?c=` needs `useSearchParams`, hence the Suspense boundary on that page too.
- The messages page now **persists** what you type: it POSTs with the conversation's other member as recipient (the API reuses the existing conversation) and swaps the optimistic bubble for the saved row. Before this the composer only sent over `useWebSocket`, whose socket never connects — the hook reads `data` off `useSession()`, which returns `session`, so no message was ever saved or delivered. The hook itself is untouched and still broken; nothing else in the app relies on it now.
- `GET /api/search?type=users` also returns `isFollowing`, so a result does not offer to follow somebody the viewer already follows. Same drizzle caution as elsewhere: the subquery interpolates `users.id` and only renders correctly because that query has joins.
- Verification data to remove after testing: the follow row(s) from the viewer, the notification they generate, and the conversation with its messages and members. Use `activity-probe.mjs` for all of it: `conversation <username>` lists the conversations that user is in with message counts, and `conversation-purge <username>` deletes them — **scoped to one user's conversations**, and `messages` and `conversation_members` both cascade from `conversations`, so that one delete is the whole cleanup. `stats` now also reports `conversations` and `messages`, so a verification run can prove it left nothing behind. Note the demo data already contains **one conversation with two messages between two members that the viewer is not part of** — it predates this runbook entry and was left as found; do not "tidy" it away.

## Live follower counts

- A profile's follower and following totals update over Realtime. The `follower_counts_broadcast` trigger (`drizzle/0006_follower_counts.sql`) fires on `follows` INSERT **and** DELETE and publishes `{follower_id, following_id, followers, following}` to the topic `profile:counts` as event `follower_counts`. `0007_follower_counts_event.sql` re-creates the same function adding `added` (`tg_op = 'INSERT'`), which is what lets an open member list know whether a row joined or left rather than inferring it from the totals; a client ignoring the extra key behaves exactly as before. Like the migrations before them, both are idempotent and have no drizzle snapshot — do not regenerate them with `drizzle-kit`.
- `0008_follows_feed_audience.sql` adds a **second** trigger on `follows` that publishes the follow edge to the feed's topic `feed:activity` as event `follows` (see the audiences section for why). **Applying a migration here is manual:** this database has no `drizzle.__drizzle_migrations` table, so `npm run db:migrate` would replay `0000`–`0002` from scratch. Run the file straight at `DATABASE_URL` — `.freebuff/apply-sql.mjs <file>`, which is how `0003`–`0008` were applied — and keep `drizzle/meta/_journal.json` in step (a new entry with the next `idx` and a `when` above the last) so a fresh database would apply it. Trigger migrations have no snapshot and must not be regenerated.
- Absolute totals, not deltas, for the same reason as the feed counts: a missed or duplicated event cannot make the number drift, and applying one twice is harmless. Measured commit → DOM: **15–29 ms** across a follow, an unfollow, a follower of the viewed member, and the member following somebody else.
- The profile page applies it to whichever side of the event it is showing — `following_id` matches → the follower count, `follower_id` matches → the following count — so viewing your own profile also ticks when you follow somebody from another tab. A follow between two other members changes nothing on screen (verified).
- `profile:counts` is deliberately a different topic from the feed's `feed:activity`: `client.channel(name)` returns the *existing* channel for a name, and each page removes only its own on unmount, so two pages sharing a topic can tear down each other's handlers. On `/feed` the joined channels are `feed:activity` and `notifications:<user>`; on a profile they are `notifications:<user>` and `profile:counts`.
- Realtime never replays events missed while the socket was down, so a re-`SUBSCRIBED` bumps `profileReloadKey` and re-reads `GET /api/users` instead of waiting for the next follow. The first subscribe needs no catch-up (the page just fetched). Verified: a follow committed while disconnected left the count untouched, and reconnecting produced exactly one `/api/users` request and the corrected total.
- The payload carries two uuids and two public totals and **no row of `follows`** (who follows whom is never broadcast). It is a public topic, so anyone with the publishable key can observe follow counts — which adds nothing today, because `follows` itself has RLS **disabled** with `anon` holding `SELECT` (and INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) through PostgREST. Reported, not changed; enabling RLS there would be a table-wide decision.
- Only the profile page subscribes, so a profile owner watching the feed or messages does not see the badge-less count move until they open their profile.

## Member lists behind the profile's stat tiles

- The three stat tiles are real controls. **Posts** switches to the posts tab (that tab *is* the posts list); **Followers** and **Following** open `MemberListDialog`. Each tile carries an `aria-label` naming the member and its number, because a bare "4" next to "Followers" is not a control name.
- `GET /api/users/follow?userId=&type=followers|following&limit=&cursor=` lists a member's followers or the members they follow, newest relationship first, keyset-paginated exactly like the feed (`encodeCursor`/`decodeCursor`, one extra row to decide `hasMore`). 400s on a malformed id, cursor or `type`; 404 on an unknown member.
- It joins `profiles` **LEFT** and coalesces the display name to the username. An inner join would drop a follower whose profile row is missing while every count still counted them — a list that quietly disagrees with the number above it, which is the same class of bug the comments list had. The row's `isFollowing` says whether the *viewer* follows that member, and the outer id in that subquery is written `"users"."id"` on purpose (drizzle drops the qualifier in a single-table query, which would make it compare a column against itself).
- A row's Follow button is `FollowButton` with `subjectName`, added for these lists: without it every button in the list announces a bare "Follow" and nothing says who it belongs to.
- **Live rows.** The `0007_follower_counts_event` migration re-creates the counts trigger with an `added` flag, so a client knows a row joined or left instead of inferring it from the totals. An addition fetches just that member from `GET /api/users/brief?ids=` and prepends the row; a removal drops it. Page one is *not* refetched, because that would throw away any pages the reader had loaded. Measured commit → DOM: count **21-36 ms**, row removal **24-40 ms**, row addition **570-1100 ms** (one round trip; `/api/users?id=` costs ~850-1400 ms because it also ensures the viewer's profile exists and counts followers, which is why the brief endpoint exists).
- The dialog shows a skeleton row while an addition is in flight (`pendingAdd`): the count moves before the row can, and "Showing 0 of 1" above "No followers yet" is a contradiction the reader would see for ~0.6 s.
- **Do not reach for `scrollIntoView` to reveal the posts panel.** The panel sits inside a Card with `overflow-hidden`, so the browser treats the Card as the scroll container and scrolls it internally — the page does not move. Scrolling the window explicitly works for one frame, but Radix then focuses the newly-selected tab and the browser scrolls *that* into view, so a smooth scroll is left short by the header height (three competing `window.scrollTo` calls measured). The scroll was dropped: by the time the tile is off-screen you cannot click it, so it bought nothing.

## Profile posts tab

- **The section switcher is not a tab set, and the markup says so now.** The six sections used to be Radix `TabsContent`s under a `Tabs` with no `TabsList` — the switcher is the header's own row of buttons plus the stat tiles — which gave every panel an `aria-labelledby` pointing at a trigger that was never rendered, and a `tabpanel` role with no tab to belong to. They are conditional sections now, keyed on the same `activeTab` state the switcher already set, and the switcher itself is unchanged. See the audit section for how it was found.
- The tab pages with `POSTS_PAGE_SIZE = 20` through `GET /api/posts?authorId=&limit=&cursor=` (opaque keyset cursor). **Load more** appends the next page, deduped by id, and its cursor is the only thing that advances. The tile reads `20+` while a page remains and the exact number once the last one is loaded — that is the point of the button.
- A failed page load keeps the list on screen and reports in the footer (`role="alert"`); the same button stays put, so it doubles as the retry. Footer shows `Showing N+ posts` (a polite live region) while more remain and disappears when everything is loaded.
- Verified by inserting 25 probe posts for one member: page one showed 20 with the tile at `20+`, and loading the rest produced 33 in strictly descending order with no duplicates, the button gone and the tile at `33`. Re-run the same way — `activity-probe.mjs post <username> ...` in a loop, then `cleanup`, which removes them by their `[activity-probe]` prefix.
- The profile's composer is wired and publishes: `handleProfilePost` renders the card optimistically, swaps it for the saved row, and on failure removes it, shows `role="alert"` and hands the text back (`PostComposer` clears itself the moment it calls `onSubmit`).
- **Never store a `blob:` URL on a post.** The card preview is `URL.createObjectURL(file)`, and `POST /api/posts` persists whatever URL it is handed, so a blob URL becomes a dead image for everyone else and for the author on reload. Both the profile and the feed go through `src/lib/publish-post.ts`, which stores the file first and passes the resulting public URL. The feed used to persist the blob URL raw.
- **Uploads go through `POST /api/posts/media` (multipart), not the presigned route.** A browser PUT to the media bucket is refused: R2 returns no `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, so the preflight fails (`403 Preflight`, then `ERR_FAILED`) and the file never leaves the page. `/api/uploads` still returns presigned URLs for anything outside a browser; the browser path is the server-side route, as `avatar` and `cover` already were. `publishPost`'s upload step is the only consumer to change if the bucket later gets a CORS policy.
- The composer must not collapse itself on submit. `PostComposer` clears its text and attachment but stays expanded, and collapses on blur only when it is empty *and* focus moved to another control (`relatedTarget !== null`, so opening the file dialog never hides the toolbar). Collapsing on submit left the toolbar — including the Post button — unreachable, because the textarea keeps focus and an already-focused element fires no further `focus` event.

## Deleting a post removes its files from the bucket

- `DELETE /api/posts?id=` is the app's only post-removal path and it soft-deletes (`deleted_at`). Nothing restores a deleted post, so the same request now removes the post's objects from R2: it reads the post's `post_media` URLs (after the update — a soft delete leaves the rows, which is what lets them be read then; a hard delete would have to read them **first**), maps each back to its key and deletes it. Verified: a post with a stored photo + an external URL → object `200` before, `404` after, `200` response, `Deleted 1 stored object(s)` in the log, and no attempt on the external URL.
- **A stored media URL is only ever deleted if it starts with `R2_PUBLIC_URL`.** `post_media.url` is whatever `POST /api/posts` was handed, and seeded demo posts point at arbitrary external hosts; `keyFromPublicUrl` in `src/lib/r2.ts` returns `null` for anything not ours, and `deleteStoredObjects` skips those. Never delete by reconstructing a key from a filename.
- The cleanup is best-effort and never fails the request: `deleteStoredObjects` swallows per-object errors, logs `Failed to delete stored object "<key>"` and leaves the rest as latent garbage. Deleting an absent key succeeds, so a repeat feels correct — a second `DELETE` of the same post still answers `200` and logs the same count. Ownership is still enforced by the update, so deleting somebody else's post is a `404` and touches no object (verified against a seeded post: `404`, its video still `200`).
- **Raw SQL deletes bypass this entirely** — `delete from posts` in a probe or psql cascades `post_media` and leaves every object in the bucket, which is how the bucket accumulated orphans. That is why `.freebuff/activity-probe.mjs` `post-purge`/`cleanup` now read the URLs before deleting and remove the objects themselves. Any future hard-delete route or trigger has to do the same; a database trigger cannot reach R2.

## Deleting a post from its card

- The three-dot button on a card is two different controls depending on ownership: the reader's **own** posts get `PostOptionsMenu` (a dropdown holding "Delete post", which then opens a confirmation dialog — deleting cannot be undone, and the card leaves as soon as the request does), and everybody else's keeps `ReportPostDialog`. Both render a trigger with the same accessible name, so a locator on `aria-label="More post options"` matches every card; tell them apart by `aria-haspopup="menu"` (own post) versus `aria-haspopup="dialog"` (report).
- `PostCard` only offers delete when the page hands it an `onDelete`, so the decision sits where the viewer is known: the feed passes it when `post.author.id === viewerId`, the profile only when `isOwnProfile`. A member profile reached through `?user=`/`?username=` therefore shows the reporter on every card and has no composer (verified: 8 cards, all `aria-haspopup="dialog"`).
- Removal is optimistic: the card goes *before* the request is sent and is put back, re-sorted by its own timestamp, if the request fails, with the failure in the ordinary banner (`role="alert"`, dismissed by a button labelled "Dismiss error"). Verified by patching the page's `fetch` to reject the DELETE: the card vanished, came back, the banner read "We couldn't delete that post. It's still here.", the dialog had closed, and the server still had the post (and its R2 object).
- A successful delete is applied **twice** — once optimistically, once by the Realtime `postgres_changes` UPDATE the feed already listens to, which removes any card whose row gained `deleted_at` (that is also how a post deleted in another tab disappears here). The second removal is a no-op. The API answers `200` for an already-deleted post, so a repeat cannot fail a client that retried.
- The profile's posts tile and the "Showing N posts" footer both read the loaded list's own length, so they follow a deletion without a second count; while a page remains the tile keeps its `+` and stays a floor ("19+" after deleting one of twenty). The Photos/Videos grids are deliberately not patched — switching to those tabs re-runs their fetch, so the grid is current by the time it can be seen.

## Editing a post from its card

- The same menu now carries **Edit post** above **Delete post** and opens `PostEditDialog`: the post's text in a textarea plus the audience picker, labelled "Who can see this". Media is out of scope — `PUT /api/posts` accepts `content`/`visibility`/`hashtags` and an attachment is its own stored object, so the dialog only offers what the route can already do and the card's `hasMedia` prop tells it whether clearing the text is allowed.
- **The audience control is shared, not copied.** `<PostAudienceSelect>` and its `audienceOptions` live in `src/components/social/post-audience-select.tsx`; the composer renders the same component (with `compact`, which drops the label on narrow screens where its toolbar has no room), and `PostEditDialog` renders it too. The audiences themselves, their names and their rule are not that file's business — see the audiences section.
- **Choosing an audience no longer needs text in the box first.** The composer collapses an empty box when focus leaves it, and the picker's menu is portalled outside `composerRef`, so focus moving onto an option read as the author leaving: the composer closed and took the menu with it, and the audience could not be set until something had been typed. The decision is now `shouldCollapseComposer`, exported from the composer and tested in `post-composer.test.ts` — collapse only when focus went to a control *outside* the composer, no popup of the composer's own is open, and nothing is written. The picker reports its menu opening and closing (`onOpenChange`); the open case is held in a ref, because the blur arrives before any re-render, and the close case looks again on the next frame, putting focus back in the textarea first: a mouse selection hands focus to nobody, and a composer that was just given an audience must not close over the choice. Verified live: an empty composer opens the menu and stays open; choosing "Only me" leaves it open showing the choice, twice in a row; focus moving to another control still collapses an empty composer (so the rule still does its job); and posting still leaves the toolbar and the chosen audience in place.
- Saving is optimistic in both pages (`updatePost` on the feed, `handleProfileUpdate` on the profile), the same shape as delete: patch text, audience and a fresh `edited_at`, then on failure put all three back from the copy taken before the request. Failure reports in the page's own error banner ("We couldn't save your changes. Your post is unchanged.") and the dialog closes on success **and** on failure — the form does not linger over a rollback.
- A text-only post may not be emptied: **Save changes** stays disabled while the trimmed text is empty unless the card has media (`hasMedia={Boolean(image)}`), which would otherwise leave a card with nothing in it that its author could no longer reach to fix. An empty text on a media post is legitimate and renders as the attachment alone.
- `posts.edited_at` is the only record that a post changed, and it is a marker, not a timestamp: `GET /api/posts` returns it, the card shows `· Edited` beside the time (with `title="This post was edited after it was published"`), and the feed's Realtime UPDATE handler copies `edited_at` across — set *or* cleared, so a row that was never edited cannot inherit the mark. Never use it for ordering; nothing sorts by it.
- An edit reaches every other viewer on its own: the feed already patches `content`/`visibility` from `postgres_changes` UPDATE events, so the author's optimistic patch and the broadcast land on the same values. Verified live: text + audience (`Only me`) edited on the feed, card patched in place with `· Edited`, `PUT /api/posts → 200`, `edited_at` written, marker still there after a reload; then with `fetch` patched to reject the PUT, the text reverted, no `· Edited` appeared on a post that had never been edited, and the banner read the message above while the row stayed untouched.

## Post audiences are enforced when posts are read

- `posts.visibility` is an audience, not a display label. One predicate decides who may read a row — `visiblePostsCondition(viewerId)` in `src/lib/db/post-visibility.ts`: `public` for everyone, the author always sees their own, and a `followers` post only for a member with a `follows` edge to the author. `private` is author-only. Any query that returns posts must include it, or a post marked private is served to whoever asks.
- **`src/lib/post-audiences.ts` is the only list of audiences.** `postAudiences` declares them (in picker order), `audienceLabel` names them where a member reads them, `audienceRule` says who each admits, and `isPostAudience`/`toPostAudience`/`canReadPost` work off those three. Everything else derives from it: `visibilityEnum` in `schema.ts` is built from `postAudiences`, so the database cannot hold an audience the rule does not describe; the picker's `audienceOptions` and the composer's menu are built from the list plus the shared labels; the post card's pill and the picker's icons come from one `<AudienceIcon>` map; `publish-post.ts` and the API's `POST /api/posts` narrowing use the same type and helper. The module imports neither drizzle nor React, so both sides can import it. It replaces five separate copies of the same three names — the enum, the picker's options, the pill's labels, `PostAudienceValue` in `publish-post.ts`, and the literal array the route validated against — which is how a picker could offer an audience the predicate did not enforce.
- **Adding an audience is one line, and it is deliberately not quiet.** Appending to `postAudiences` produced five compile errors, one per decision it forces: `audienceRule` (who does it admit?), `audienceLabel` (what is it called?), the picker's `audienceDescription`, `audienceIcons`, and the SQL renderer that indexes the rule. Three tests failed too. The DB-enum test did *not* fail, and should not: the column is derived from the list, so that pair cannot diverge at all.
- **The rule is one table, and both its renderings are derived from it.** `audienceRule` records only *what* each audience admits beyond the author — `public` anyone, `followers` a reader with a follow edge, `private` nobody. `visiblePostsCondition` renders that table to SQL for the queries; `canReadPost(viewerId, post, viewerFollowsAuthor)` evaluates the same table in process, and is what the integration suite's fake endpoint answers from. Neither restates the audience set, so the fake cannot drift from what the server returns. The keys are the `PostAudience` type from `postAudiences`, so an audience added to the list fails the build (`TS1360`) *and* a test until somebody decides who it admits. How a follow edge is looked up — the shape of the `exists` subquery — stays in the renderer, since nothing else can express it.
- Rendering from the table puts the authorship check first (`"author_id" = $1 or "visibility" = 'public' or (…followers…)`); the previous hand-written predicate had `public` first. The text is otherwise byte-identical and the bindings are unchanged (`[viewer, viewer]`), so the 6 `visiblePostsCondition` tests passed untouched — that, not the refactor's intent, is the evidence the predicate still selects the same rows. Audiences are inlined as literals (from the enum, never user data) rather than bound, so the predicate still reads in an `EXPLAIN`.
- **A `followers` post is gated on following its *subject*, and the subject of a Page's post is the Page.** `audienceRule.followers` says only that a follow edge is required; which edge is a property of the post, and `canReadPost` decides it: a post published by a member is readable by their followers, and one published as a Page by that Page's followers. The two are not interchangeable in either direction — a member who follows the *admin* of a Page cannot read that Page's followers-only posts, and following the Page does not admit the member's own — which is why the SQL renders *two* arms, and why the author arm carries `page_id is null`: without that guard it is merely less specific than the Page arm rather than inapplicable, and every follower of the admin would be let into their Page's followers-only posts. The Page arm needs no guard, because `pf.page_id = null` matches nothing. A Page's `public` post is public and its `private` one is the admin who pressed publish, exactly as the audience list says. The `private` case is worth naming because it is the one place a Page's post is not the Page's: "Only me" on a Page means the person who wrote it.
- **Both renderings moved together, and that is the whole design.** `canReadPost(viewerId, post, viewerFollows)` now takes `{ author: boolean, page: boolean }` — both edges, because the caller has to read the post to know which one to look up, and one round trip answers both — and `visiblePostsCondition` renders the same two arms. The integration fake reports both edges from its world and still answers by *calling* `canReadPost`, so it cannot drift from the server. `audienceRule` itself is untouched: only the *subject* concept was added to it, in a doc comment, because *which* edge belongs to the renderers.
- **The live check that matters is the one a single session cannot make.** Every member with a session here is the admin who published the Page's post, and authorship masks the arm — so the rule was executed against the real development database, inside a transaction that was rolled back, with the app's own rendered predicate: `northwind_studio`'s demo post set to `followers` and read by a second seeded member (`theo_demo`) gave **author → readable, no edge → not readable, follows the admin only → not readable, follows the Page → readable**. The middle pair is the point: the wrong edge was proven not to open it, which is also the evidence that the `page_id` correlation is not the `pf.page_id = pf.page_id` self-comparison it would become if the qualifier were dropped. (The first attempt at that check failed with `invalid reference to FROM-clause entry for table "posts"`, because the wrapper query aliased `posts p` — an accidental demonstration that these references really are qualified, which is now pinned by a test rather than by a habit.)
- It is applied by `GET /api/posts` (the feed, the profile's posts — the same endpoint with `authorId=` — and a Page's posts, `?pageId=`), by the `?ids=` lookup, by `GET /api/posts/counts`, and by the post branch of `GET /api/search`.
