Verified live: another member's post set `private` disappeared from both the feed listing and a by-id lookup; a `followers` post by a member the viewer follows stayed while the same post by a member they do not follow did not; an author's own post set `private` still came back to them; the profile listing went 8→7 when one of that member's posts was made private; and a post's text stopped being searchable the moment it was private.
- The predicate is written with drizzle table objects, not literal column names. Drizzle *does* drop qualifiers in a single-table query — which is the trap the counts route warns about with a bare `"id"` — but **measured, it does so in the select list and not in `where`**, and this predicate is only ever a `where`. That difference is load-bearing rather than incidental now that a second subquery joins the predicate: `page_follows` has a `page_id` of its own, so an unqualified `${posts.pageId}` inside `pf.page_id = "page_id"` would compare the subquery's column to itself and admit *every* reader to *every* Page's followers-only post. It is pinned against the query builder — single-table **and** joined — in `post-visibility.test.ts`, which asserts `pf.page_id = "posts"."page_id"` and, explicitly, that `pf.page_id = "page_id"` does not appear. The predicate must never be moved into a select field; that position is where the qualifier does go missing.
- **The feed drops a card whose audience narrows underneath it.** The Realtime UPDATE handler patches `visibility` as before, and when the value *changes* on a post that is not the reader's own it re-checks visibility through `GET /api/posts?ids=` — the same predicate the feed was built from — and removes the card if it comes back empty. Whether `followers` includes this reader is a follow edge the client does not hold, so it asks rather than guessing. Only a change is re-checked, so an ordinary content edit costs no extra request. Verified: with the feed open, setting a mounted other-author post to `private` in the database removed its card within a beat, while the same change to the reader's own post left it in place.
- A narrow is also caught **without** realtime: `counts` excludes the post, and the feed treats a missing id on the reconnect reconcile as removed, exactly like a deletion.
- **Unfollowing takes a member's `followers` cards off the feed at once**, including another tab or device. Removing a follower is a DELETE on `follows`, which the feed cannot see: `postgres_changes` carries only the primary key of a deleted row, and the post itself never changes. So `drizzle/0008_follows_feed_audience.sql` (applied as the `follows_feed_audience` migration) adds a trigger on `follows` that publishes `{follower_id, following_id, added}` to the **feed's own topic** `feed:activity` as event `follows`, and the feed subscribes to it alongside `counts`. The topic is shared on purpose — a channel's name *is* the topic, and the page already owns one, so no second channel is opened. The payload is the same pair of ids `profile:counts` already publishes, and no post row or audience is included.
- The feed handles an unfollow itself, with no round trip: only `followers` cards by that member **as themselves** can be affected (`public` stays public, a `private` one could not have been on screen), so they are dropped as the event arrives; a card whose `visibility` is unknown is left to `GET /api/posts?ids=`. A `followers` card that belongs to a **Page** goes to the API instead of the drop list: the edge that admits a reader to it is the one to the Page, so losing the edge to its author settles nothing about it — an admin can run a Page whose followers do not follow the admin at all. The same unfollow therefore produces `drop: [their own post]` and `recheck: [their Page's post]`, which is the shape `followLossEffect` is tested for. Measured commit→DOM ≈ the unfollow request's own latency (the removal lands with the response), against ~3.3s when it was left to an API re-check. Verified: a `followers` post by a member the viewer followed dropped the moment the viewer unfollowed, while a `public` post by the same member stayed.
- **Following a member brings their `followers` posts in without a reload**, the other half of the same edge. Those posts were filtered out of every page already fetched, so `revealAuthorPosts` re-reads that member's recent posts (`GET /api/posts?authorId=&limit=20` — the API now returns them) and merges the ones the list lacks, sorted by date, where a page would have put them. Older posts need nothing: they are visible from then on, so ordinary paging reaches them. The merge dedupes against the list itself, so a page fetched afterwards cannot double them up. Measured: card present ~730 ms after the follow response; verified in one live flow — a `followers` post by an unfollowed member was absent, appeared when the viewer followed them, and vanished again when the viewer unfollowed, with no reload.
- Revealed posts are inserted, not held behind the "N new posts" pill: that pill and its scroll-to-top are for posts that have just *arrived*, and an older post would land at the top, out of order. The cost is that a revealed post newer than the reader's position shifts the cards below it down by one.
- The insertion is **announced**: a `role="status" aria-live="polite"` line under the composer reads `Following <name> added N post(s) to your feed.` so the list growing is explained rather than puzzling. It is measured against the ids the list already held, so a follow that adds nothing says nothing, and it clears itself after `REVEAL_NOTICE_MS` (8s) or on the dismiss button — both verified live, along with the count and name in the copy. It is deliberately not shown when the post was already on screen: in that case no new card arrived, which the back-to-back unfollow/follow case produces (the removal and the reveal race, and the older card simply stays).
- The status is a **link**: clicking it jumps to the first revealed card (the newest of them, `fresh[0]` — the API orders newest first) and rings it, which matters because a revealed post can land below the fold. It reuses the notification jump wholesale — `setFocusTarget` drives the same `scrollToKey` + `feed-highlight` path, and `clearFocusParam` is a no-op when there is no `?post=`. Clicking also dismisses the status, which has done its job. Verified: a revealed card sitting at `top: 942` in a 723px viewport scrolled to `top: 70` and carried `.feed-highlight` within 50 ms, and the ring cleared itself after `FOCUS_HIGHLIGHT_MS`. Note the ring only lasts ~2.6s, so a check that goes through a couple of tool round trips will miss it — drive it inside one `preview_evaluate`.
- Both of the feed's transient statuses — this one and the notification-"post opened" notice — are one component, `src/components/shared/inline-notice.tsx`. It owns the polite live region, the spacing and the dismiss button; each caller supplies only its message (a string, or a control that carries one as the reveal status does). Anything that has to *interrupt* belongs in the page's own `role="alert"` banner instead. Adding a third status means adding a `<InlineNotice>`, not another copy of the markup.
- **Alt+J** does the same from the keyboard, and the status shows it on a `<kbd>` chip (hidden below `sm`, where there is no room). The listener is attached only while `revealNotice` is set, so the shortcut exists exactly as long as there is something to jump to, and it is inert otherwise. `Alt` rather than a bare letter: a character-key shortcut must be remappable or scoped to focus to satisfy WCAG 2.1.4, and the feed's composer is a textarea. The handler matches `event.code === "KeyJ"` with `altKey` and rejects the other modifiers — `event.key` is wrong here because Option+J reports `"∆"` on macOS. The button carries `aria-keyshortcuts="Alt+J"` too. Verified: a real `Alt+j` press moved the list from `scrollY 0 / top 942` to `scrollY 807 / top 70` and dismissed the status; a synthetic `KeyboardEvent` did the same and put `.feed-highlight` on the right card within 134 ms; with the status gone the same press changed nothing.
- `.freebuff/visibility-probe.mjs` drives the above: `show <postId>`, `set <postId> <visibility>`, `content <postId> <text>`, `uid <username>`, `following <username>`, `candidates <viewerUsername>` (live posts with a `follows` flag), and `state` (live/total, non-public, edited, `follows`). Always `unset DATABASE_URL` first and restore every row you touched — the seeded database has **zero** non-public posts, so `state`'s `non_public` reading is how you know it is clean.

## Group membership moves a group's posts on and off the feed

- **A `group` post is readable exactly while the reader is a member of the group it was published into** — the same "an audience, not a label" rule as `followers` (see the audiences section), gated on a `group_members` row instead of a `follows` edge (`canReadPost` and `visiblePostsCondition`). Leaving that group writes to a different table than the post, so the post row itself never changes and the feed's own `postgres_changes` stream knows nothing about it; a DELETE on `group_members` carries only the deleted row's primary key, so the feed could not even tell *whose* membership went. `drizzle/0013_group_members_feed_audience.sql` is that signal, told exactly as `0008_follows_feed_audience.sql` tells the follow one.
- **The trigger** (`group_members_feed_audience`, `after insert or delete on public.group_members for each row`) is `security definer … set search_path = public`; it reads `old.*` on DELETE and `new.*` otherwise, null-guards, and publishes `{user_id, group_id, added: tg_op = 'INSERT'}` to the **feed's own topic** `feed:activity` as event `group_members` via `realtime.send`. The send is wrapped in `exception when others then null`, because the membership has already committed and a Realtime hiccup must never fail it — a missed announcement costs one stale card until the next reconnect reconciles against the API. The topic is shared with `counts` and `follows` on purpose: a channel's name *is* the topic, and the feed already owns one. `src/lib/db/schema.ts` declares neither the function nor the trigger, so this file is their only home — **do not regenerate it with `drizzle-kit`**. Every statement is idempotent, so re-applying is a no-op (the `drop trigger if exists` prints one harmless `NOTICE … does not exist, skipping` the first time).
- **Applying it is manual.** This database has no `drizzle.__drizzle_migrations` table, so `npm run db:migrate` would replay `0000`–`0002` from scratch. Run the file straight at the pooler: `unset DATABASE_URL` first, then `node --env-file-if-exists=.env.local .freebuff/apply-sql.mjs drizzle/0013_group_members_feed_audience.sql` — that tool rewrites the host to the transaction pooler port `6543` and sets `ssl: require` (`.freebuff/apply-migration.mjs` does **not** set SSL). Keep `drizzle/meta/_journal.json` in step: idx `13`, tag `0013_group_members_feed_audience`, `when 1790440000000`, so a fresh database would apply it. **The enum value is a separate, older file:** `0012_good_corsair.sql` is `ALTER TYPE "public"."visibility" ADD VALUE 'group'`, which is therefore **not** idempotent (a second run errors) — it was applied once with the same tool, and it is the prerequisite `posts.visibility = 'group'` depends on.
- **After applying, the catalogue is the check:** the `visibility` enum holds `['public','followers','private','group']`; `pg_trigger` shows both `follows_feed_audience` and `group_members_feed_audience` with `tgenabled = 'O'`; the new definition is `AFTER INSERT OR DELETE ON public.group_members FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION group_members_feed_audience_broadcast()`, and the function body contains `realtime.send` with `'group_members'` and `'feed:activity'`.
- **The client path is one subscription and one handler.** The feed's channel (topic `feed:activity`) gained `.on("broadcast", { event: "group_members" }, …)` beside the `follows` one, calling `applyGroupChange` in `src/app/(main)/feed/page.tsx`. It ignores a payload that is not about the reader — `payload.user_id !== viewerIdRef.current` — because the row it came from is somebody's, and another member's membership says nothing about this feed; it ignores a payload with no `group_id` or no boolean `added`, since guessing a direction would either hide readable posts or show unreadable ones. On `added` it calls `revealGroupPosts(groupId)`; on removal it calls `groupLossEffect(postsRef.current, groupId)`.
- **`groupLossEffect` drops outright, because the membership is what showed the cards.** `src/lib/feed-audience.ts` gained `groupLossEffect(posts, groupId)`, returning the shared shape now named `AudienceLossEffect` (`{drop, recheck}`; `FollowLossEffect` is an alias of it): for each card whose `post.group?.id === groupId` — the same membership test the author edge uses — a `group` post goes in `drop`, anything the client cannot settle goes in `recheck`, and optimistic cards are skipped exactly as they are for a follow loss. `drop` feeds `removePost` directly with no round trip; `recheck` feeds `revalidateVisiblePosts` (`GET /api/posts?ids=`, the predicate the feed was built from). The client never guesses an audience it does not hold.
- **`revealGroupPosts` is the mirror of `revealAuthorPosts`.** The reveal was made generic — `revealPosts(url, notice)` fetches, filters against `knownIdsRef`, `mergeRevealedPosts` by date, and sets the `role="status"` notice for `REVEAL_NOTICE_MS`; the two callers differ only in the URL and the wording. Joining fetches `GET /api/posts?groupId=<id>&limit=<REVEALED_POST_LIMIT>`, and the notice reads **"Joining <group name> added N post(s) to your feed."** (`groupRevealNoticeMessage`, the sibling of "Following <name> added N post(s)"). Older posts need nothing: they are readable from then on, so ordinary paging reaches them.
- **Verified live, through the real route and the real Realtime, in an open feed** (the same recipe as the unfollow check above; unset `DATABASE_URL` and use the admin SQL path for the setup and cleanup). A throwaway group ("Realtime Leave Verify") was created with a demo member as a second admin, the viewer added as a member, and one `visibility = 'group'` post inserted. A reload showed it at the top, credited "in Realtime Leave Verify" with the **Group members** pill.
  - **Leave:** `POST /api/groups/members` `{groupId}` → `200 {member: false}`, and the network log showed **only that POST** — no `/api/posts`, no navigation — yet the card left the screen. Measured `leaveResponseMs` **3052**, `responseToCardGoneMs` **0** (the broadcast beat the HTTP response), `totalMs` **3052**, `stillOnScreen` **false**. Cards by other authors were untouched.
  - **Join:** a re-POST → `201 {member: true}`; the only extra request was the reveal's own `GET /api/posts?groupId=<id>&limit=20`. The card returned `responseToCardBackMs` **472** with `joinResponseMs` **1063**, and the status read **"Joining Realtime Leave Verify added 1 post to your feed."** No console errors in either direction.
  - **Cleanup** (delete the probe post and the group by SQL) restored the seeded baseline — 2 groups ("Design & Product Makers", "Indie Builders"), **6** `group_members` rows, **0** group posts — verified `{deletedPosts: 1, groups: 2, groupPosts: 0, memberships: 6, groupRowsLeft: 0, postRowsLeft: 0}`. The card also vanished from the still-open feed the moment the post row was hard-deleted, by the ordinary posts DELETE path.
- **Tests:** `src/lib/feed-audience.test.ts` pins `groupLossEffect` and `groupRevealNoticeMessage` as units (a matching card drops; another group's card and a group-less card are left alone; a public card naming the group is kept; an unsettled group card is rechecked; in/out/plain are separated; pending is skipped), and `src/lib/feed-audience.integration.test.ts` drives the flows through those same real functions against the fake `GET /api/posts` — its world gained memberships (`joinGroup`/`leaveGroup`/`groupsFor`) and the fake now answers `?groupId=`, while both call the shared audience rule rather than restating it. The two files run green together at **64 tests** (28 + 36), and no other test file changes; `npx tsc --noEmit` reports nothing new in the files this touched. Read any suite total as a property of the checkout at that moment — the tree is shared.

## Posts in a group (what publishing into a group means)

- **A group post's audience is the group, not a choice.** `GroupComposer` (`src/components/groups/group-composer.tsx`) renders on `/groups/[id]` for a member and sends `{content, groupId}` with **no `visibility` at all**. `POST /api/posts` checks the membership server-side — a `group_members` row, or `403 Only a member of this group can post in it`; an unknown group is `404` — and then pins the stored audience: `visibility: groupForPost ? "group" : selectedVisibility`. Any member may post (a lower bar than a Page's admin — a group is where members talk to each other), and the post is attributed to the **member** (`author_id`), not the group. `DELETE`/`PUT` keep comparing against that `author_id`, so the member still owns the row.
- **The body can be wrong and it is refused rather than honoured.** A body naming **both** a Page and a group is `400 A post is published as a Page or in a group, not both` (one post, one subject); a `visibility: "group"` with **no** group is `400 A post is only visible to group members inside a group` — `group` is a real audience, so the validator lets it through, but without a group the rule admits nobody, and storing it would make a post its author cannot share; and `groupId` must be a uuid (`400 Invalid group id`).
- **The composer says the audience instead of offering it.** It renders the label "Post in <Group>", a sentence — a `<Users/>` glyph beside **"Members of <Group> can see this"** — and no picker. The reason is written into `composerAudiences` in `src/lib/post-audiences.ts`: `group` is deliberately **not** in the picker's list, because the audience is a fact about where the post is being published rather than something a member chooses *about* it; offering it beside Public and Private would let somebody pick "Group members" for a post that has no group and is then readable by nobody but its author. A surface that can honour an audience is a surface that may offer it. `group-view.test.tsx` asserts both halves — the sentence is present **and** the string `Post audience` is absent.
- **Editing cannot widen a group post.** `PostEditDialog` swaps its picker for the written line **"Everyone in <Group>"** when `groupName` is set, and its save sends `visibility: groupName ? "group" : audience`; `PUT /api/posts` independently pins `visibility: existing.groupId ? "group" : requestedVisibility`. So neither the dialog nor the route will let a group post become public, and it takes two files to agree about that rather than one.
- **The `group` audience itself is one row in the shared list.** `audienceLabel.group` is **"Group members"** and `audienceIcons.group` is `UserRoundCheck` — a deliberately different symbol from `followers`' `Users`, so a post in a group and a post for your followers are told apart at a glance. `audienceRule.group` sets `requiresGroupMembership`, which `groupMembershipClause(viewerId)` in `src/lib/db/post-visibility.ts` renders as `exists (select 1 from group_members gm where gm.group_id = "posts"."group_id" and gm.user_id = $viewer)`. A `group` post whose `group_id` is null matches nobody (`gm.group_id = null` is never true) and stays with its author, which is the fail-closed answer. The usual qualifier caution applies: the outer column is referenced through drizzle's `posts` table object, and `post-visibility.test.ts` renders the predicate through the query builder to keep it that way.
- **That arm is how a group's posts reach the feed at all.** The feed asks `GET /api/posts` with no group and gets every post the reader may see — which is exactly the union of the groups they belong to, the members they follow, and everything public. A group's **own** page asks `?groupId=`, which the route validates as a uuid and adds to its conditions; the membership check is deliberately **not** repeated there, because the audience rule already admits a group post to its members and to nobody else — so a non-member asking for a group's posts is answered with none of them rather than with a 403 the client would have to interpret. The endpoint `leftJoin`s `groups` and returns `group: {id, name}` on a group post and `null` on every other post.
- **The peer's identity on the card is two marks, and the pill is one of them.** The feed passes `groupName={post.group?.name}` into `PostCard` (`src/components/social/post-card.tsx`), whose header then renders **`in <group name>`** beside `@username` — a group speaks in the voice of the member who wrote it, so there is no Page-style identity swap — and whose audience pill renders `<AudienceIcon/> Group members` from the same `audienceLabel` the picker and menu use, with `title="Audience: Group members"`. Because the card is the member's, the author's delete/edit menu is offered exactly as for any other post; only the editor's audience control is gone (above).
- **A non-member gets a door, not an empty room.** On `/groups/[id]` a stranger's whole page is the group's identity plus **"Join <Group> to see its posts"** and a Join control; the posts are **not fetched at all** (the view test asserts `/api/posts?groupId=` is never called), so nothing is drawn with a lock over it and no "No posts yet" implies the group is empty. Joining calls the membership route and *then* reads the list; leaving empties it again. A **private** group answers `403` to a non-member, which this page renders the same as a `404` — "Group not found … it may only be visible to its members" — a door and a wall are the same answer from outside.
- **Creating a group is a dialog on `/groups`.** `POST /api/groups` writes the group and the creator's `group_members` row with `role: "admin"` in one request (a group whose creator is not a member is a group nobody can post in); `visibility` is validated against the group's own three values (`public`/`followers`/`private` — note this is a *group* visibility, not the post enum). The directory lists only public groups and the ones the reader already belongs to. The seeded baseline is **2** groups ("Design & Product Makers", "Indie Builders") with **6** `group_members` rows and **0** group posts, which is the state to compare a verification run against.
- **Tests:** `src/app/(main)/groups/[id]/group-view.test.tsx` (**6**, jsdom) pins the view's own decisions — a member is offered the composer and told the audience as a fact (and no picker), a published post goes out as exactly `{content, groupId}` with no visibility, the list is credited to the member and labelled with the group, a stranger is given the way in and never asks for the posts, joining then reads them exactly once, and a `403` renders as not-found. The rule is pinned in `src/lib/post-audiences.test.ts` (22) and its SQL in `post-visibility.test.ts`; the route's pinning of the audience is in `src/app/api/posts/route.test.ts` (13) — the group create test asserts `{pageId: null, groupId, visibility: "group"}` and the edit test asserts the audience stays `group` when the body asks for `public`. The three files run green together at **41 tests** (6 + 22 + 13).
- **Verified live in the same pass as the membership eviction above:** the `visibility = 'group'` probe post rendered in the open feed at the top, credited **"in Realtime Leave Verify"** with the **Group members** pill, and was readable only while the viewer was a member — leaving took it off, joining brought it back. The group's own page is the other end of it: a member sees the composer and the list, a non-member sees only the Join notice.

## Auditing for the portal-vs-focus class

- The composer's bug — a parent deciding something from DOM containment while its own menu renders in a portal — was worth looking for elsewhere. It is not elsewhere. Searched and found nothing: no `relatedTarget`, `activeElement` or `onBlur` outside `post-composer.tsx`; no `focusin`/`focusout` listeners; no document-level `mousedown`/`click` outside-click handler; no `.contains(`/`.closest(` containment check except the composer's; no Radix `onInteractOutside`/`onCloseAutoFocus`/`onPointerDownOutside` override anywhere. The only document-level `keydown` listener is the feed's Alt+J reveal shortcut, which touches no focus state.
- Menus and dialogs are portalled by their shared wrappers — `ui/dropdown-menu.tsx` (`DropdownMenuPrimitive.Portal`), `ui/select.tsx`, `ui/dialog.tsx` — and dismissed by Radix's dismissable layer, which treats its own portal as part of itself. Nothing hand-rolls a modal either: no `pointer-events`, `inert` or `overflow` manipulation outside Radix.
- Exercised live, each opened and then used through its portalled content; none closed, hid or unmounted itself: the nav account menu (Profile / Settings / Cover Studio / Sign out), a card's own menu (Edit post / Delete post), the delete confirmation (focus lands on **Cancel**), the edit dialog (focus lands in the textarea), the settings visibility `Select` (focus lands in the listbox) and the report dialog on another member's card (focus lands on the first reason). The direct analogue of the composer bug — a menu opened from *inside* a dialog — is clean too: with the edit dialog open, opening the audience picker leaves the dialog open and puts focus in the menu.
- **Drive these with real clicks, never synthetic events.** Dispatching `PointerEvent`s by hand takes a different path through Radix: the edit dialog then opened with focus still on the card's menu button — outside the modal, inside the `aria-hidden` region — a stray `Enter` reopened the menu *over* the dialog, and `Tab` walked the page behind it. All of that was an artifact of how it was driven; with a real click focus goes to the textarea and the trap holds. It reads exactly like a genuine defect, so it is the easiest false report to make here. Verify with `preview_click` (a locator scoped to `#post-<uuid>`) and a real `preview_press`.
- Radix menus and selects are **modal by default**: while one is open the body gets `overflow: hidden` and the page behind gets `pointer-events: none`. That is why a card cannot scroll out from under its own open menu — the state-driven unmount (realtime removal, optimistic delete) is the only way, and is intended — and why any focus bug in this class is keyboard-only.
- `src/components/ui/tooltip.tsx` was a stub — all four exports rendered their children with no Radix behind them, and nothing imported the module, so `TooltipContent`'s text would have appeared as ordinary page text. It is now a real wrapper over `@radix-ui/react-tooltip`, which was already a dependency and already installed; see the tests section for what pins it. **A tooltip needs a `TooltipProvider` above it** — Radix throws `` `Tooltip` must be used within `TooltipProvider` `` without one, so a forgotten provider is loud rather than silent.
- **The provider is wired once, in `src/app/layout.tsx`**, around the nav, the page and the footer, which is what lets any component below it use a tooltip with no ceremony. The first consumer is the post card's action row: the icon-only **React / Comment / Share / Bookmark** buttons show their purpose on hover. The "Sticker" button already has a visible label, and the three-dot menu opens a menu, which is its own explanation, so neither is tooltipped. Each hint is the *same string* as that button's accessible name, from one variable per button (`reactionLabel`, `commentLabel`, `shareLabel`, `bookmarkLabel`) — a tooltip and a screen reader cannot say different things, and the saved bookmark's hint follows its label to "Remove bookmark". That pair also forced a wording fix: the reaction's accessible name used to be `"Remove reaction" + " post"`, which reads badly aloud and now reads badly on screen too, so it is "Remove reaction".
- **The pairing is a component now: `src/components/ui/icon-button.tsx`.** It takes one `label` and renders a `Button` whose `aria-label` *and* whose tooltip are that string, with `aria-label` omitted from its props so a second name cannot be passed in. The card's four action buttons use it — the hand-rolled `Tooltip`/`TooltipTrigger`/`TooltipContent` around each one collapsed into a single element — and their labels stay as per-button variables only because two of them change with state. Use it for any control whose meaning is not written on it; keep a plain `Button` with an `aria-label` for one that already has a visible label or a neighbour that explains it (the send button beside the comment box), and give a menu trigger no hint at all, because the menu explains itself the moment it opens. Its test file pins the name, the attached tooltip, the hint-inside-the-name rule, the link shape and props pass-through, and — now that a DOM environment exists — **the hint string itself**: it mounts the control, focuses it, and asserts the tooltip's rendered text against the accessible name, which used to be a property of the component's shape rather than of any output. See the tests section.
- **The hint and the name are allowed to differ, in one direction only: `detail`.** A second prop appends wording the name carries and the hint does not (`name = detail ? \`${label}, ${detail}\` : label`; the tooltip still shows `label` alone). It exists for a control whose *state* belongs in the accessible name but not on screen — the visible badge already says the number — and it is deliberately constrained instead of being a free-form `name` prop: because the hint is the prefix of the name by construction, WCAG 2.5.3 ("Label in Name": the accessible name must contain the visible label) cannot be broken by whoever calls it. If a control needs a name that does *not* start with its hint, that is not this prop, that is a control whose hint is wrong.
- **Every labelled control in the app was audited against that rule.** Converted as well: the nav's **Search** and **notification bell**. The bell is the case `detail` was added for: it hints the short `Notifications` while its name reads `Notifications, N unread`. The count has to stay in the *name* because the badge that shows it is `aria-hidden` — otherwise a screen reader hears only "3" — but it does not belong in the *hint*, because the badge already puts the number in front of anyone who can see the button, and repeating it makes the tooltip say what the page says. Verified live both ways: with one unread row seeded, the trigger's `aria-label` was `Notifications, 1 unread` and the open tooltip's text was exactly `Notifications`; with the inbox back at zero, both read `Notifications`, and the panel still toggled `aria-expanded` false→true→false. Deliberately left alone, each for a reason rather than by oversight: the **comment send** button (its input explains it), the **cover video's mute and play** controls (universal glyphs, and they are bespoke circular overlays — `IconButton` renders a `Button` whose variants would fight that styling), the **QR panel's Close** (it has visible text), the **Dismiss** buttons on the three inline notices (an × is already unambiguous), and every **menu or dialog trigger** (the three-dot menus, the audience picker, the report dialog) — the layer explains itself.
- **An icon control that navigates gets `href` and renders a `Link`, not a `<button>` with a route `push`.** A button that navigates cannot be middle-clicked or opened in a new tab, keeps no address for a screen reader to announce, and sits in the tab order as something that will act on the page rather than replace it. `Button` is `asChild`-capable and still cannot be borrowed for this: its slot would be handed to the glyph *inside* the control instead of to a link around it, so the link branch borrows only `buttonVariants` styling. Its props are then the anchor's — the caller wrote an `href`, so that is what its props are for — which the component expresses with one cast. Nothing here fetches; the link is the whole behaviour.
- The nav's **Search** is that link (`href="/search"`, hint and name `Search`), and it was the app's only control with **no behaviour at all** before this — a placeholder that already carried a hint, so it looked more functional than it was. Verified live: it renders as an `<a href="/search">`, focusing it opens the "Search" tooltip, and a real click lands on the search page.
- Verified live by focusing each button (Radix opens a tooltip on focus, which is the only one of its two triggers a tool can drive here): all four read back their label, including "Remove bookmark" while bookmarked, and the tooltip sits above its button in the app's dark navy. Note a programmatic `focus()` was *not* enough in the preview browser — `document.hasFocus()` is false there, so the focusin never fires; dispatch `new FocusEvent("focusin", { bubbles: true })` on the trigger instead, then wait a moment.

## Search

- The nav's Search control used to be the app's **only dead control** (see the tooltip section); `/search` and `GET /api/search` already worked, and `src/components/shared/search-bar.tsx` already built `/search?q=…` — **nothing imported it**. So the feature was wired everywhere except at the two ends: no way in from the nav, and no way to type a query on the page whose empty states say "use the search bar above". Both ends are now connected.
- **`src/lib/search-query.ts` is the one place that decides what a query is and where a search goes**: `normalizeSearchQuery` (trim, `""` for missing/blank) and `searchHref` (the address, or `null` when there is nothing to search for). Both ends read it — the form and the page — because each trimming for itself gives two bugs that are invisible until someone hits them: `?q=%20` read as a query searches for a space, and the API wraps the term in `%…%`, so a space **matches everything**; and a form that navigates from a blank box replaces the page with an empty search. `searchHref` returns `null` rather than `/search` so the caller has to decide what a blank box means instead of navigating by default.
- The search page's **`All` tab shows the people results when there is a query** (under a `People` heading, the same list the `People` tab renders), because people is the one kind of result this page searches and an `All` tab that said "Start searching" to somebody who just searched read as broken. With no query it keeps the "Start searching" empty state. **The `Posts` / `Groups` / `Jobs` / `Marketplace` tabs are still placeholders**: they render "No posts match your search query" without ever searching posts, even though the API can (`?type=posts`, `?type=groups`, …). That copy is a lie, not a gap, and it is the next thing to fix here — the API side already exists and the audience rule is already applied to the post branch.
- Verified live end to end: focusing the nav control opened the `Search` tooltip; a real click landed on `/search` with the input rendered and focused-prefill empty; typing `theo` and pressing Enter went to `/search?q=theo`, the heading read `Results for "theo"`, the input kept `theo`, and the `All` tab listed `@theowumicrosoft` and `@theo_demo`; `?q=%20%20` read as no query (heading `Search`, no `Results for`, the input empty, `All` showing "Start searching"); and submitting three spaces from the input did **not** navigate.

## The nav fold: Groups, Pages and Messages live under Social

- **Social is one destination with four surfaces, and the navigation now says so.** The header used to offer Feed, Groups, Pages and Messages as peers — four items beside Marketplace and Jobs — and Cover Studio was a page of its own. Now `mainNavItems` is **three** items (Social, Marketplace, Jobs) and `socialNavItems` is four (Feed, Groups, Pages, Messages). `/groups`, `/pages`, `/messages` and `/cover-studio` are deliberately **gone from the header**; the last is the profile's `?tab=cover` tab now, reached from the account menu, and `main-nav.test.tsx` asserts none of those four `href`s appears.
- **Two lists, one active rule, and `matches` is why one item can stand for a module.** `src/lib/nav-items.ts` holds `mainNavItems`, `socialNavItems` and `isNavItemActive(pathname, item)`. Each item carries an `href` — where a click goes — and a separate `matches` list, the path prefixes it *stands for*. Social has no page of its own: its `href` is `/feed` (the door) and its `matches` are `["/feed", "/groups", "/pages", "/messages"]`, which is exactly why the header stays lit while the reader is in Groups, Pages or Messages. Keeping the two apart is the point of the field.
- **The active test is boundary-matched, not a bare `startsWith`.** `isNavItemActive` trims a trailing slash and then requires `path === prefix || path.startsWith(prefix + "/")`, so `/groups` is not lit by `/groups-old` and a module prefix is not lit by a route that merely begins with its letters. `main-nav.test.tsx` pins that from `/feed` **exactly one** item carries `aria-current="page"`, and that from `/groups` the lit one is `href="/feed"` — the reader inside a folded surface is told which module they are in rather than shown a blank header.
- **The three renderings read the same two lists.** The desktop header, the mobile panel and the phone's bottom bar (`bottom-nav.tsx`) all map `mainNavItems`, so the bottom bar cannot offer a destination the header does not — the divergence the single list exists to prevent. `bottom-nav.tsx` says the consequence out loud: Groups, Pages and Messages are **not missing** from the phone bar, they are inside Social, and the strip under the header is how a small screen reaches them.
- **The strip is `SocialNav`, and it decides for itself where it belongs.** `src/components/layout/social-nav.tsx` renders the four `socialNavItems` as a sticky `nav aria-label="Social"` of links with `min-h-11` targets that scroll rather than wrap on a narrow screen. It returns `null` unless `socialNavItems.some((item) => isNavItemActive(pathname, item))`, so it appears on `/feed`, `/groups`, `/groups/abc`, `/pages`, `/pages/new`, `/pages/<username>` and `/messages` — and nowhere else (Marketplace, Jobs, profile, settings and search render no strip). It is mounted **once**, in `src/app/(main)/layout.tsx`, rather than per page: a page that forgot to render it would be a page with no way back, and the layout expresses "the four surfaces and the Pages sub-routes, and nothing else" in one place.
- **The strip carries the same "you are here" as the header, and the two agree by construction.** Each tab gets `aria-current="page"` only while it is active, so exactly one of the four is marked; and a Page's own address (`/pages/<username>`) lights the **Pages** tab rather than nothing. The addresses are the ones the surfaces already had, so the fold was no redirect — a bookmark, a deep link to a conversation and a Page's URL all still work.
- **Two different things on the feed page are called "Social", and they are not the same thing.** The feed draws its own uppercase `Social` eyebrow over its heading and an `aria-label="Social shortcuts"` rail of page shortcuts — furniture, not navigation. The strip is the named navigation landmark; `social-nav.test.tsx` tells them apart by the exact string `aria-label="Social"`.
- **Tests:** `src/components/layout/social-nav.test.tsx` (**5**, jsdom) pins the strip's own behaviour — every surface offered on every Social path (including `/groups/abc` and `/pages/new`), exactly one `aria-current="page"` and the right one, a Page's address lighting the Pages tab, the landmark's name, and **nothing** rendered on Marketplace, Jobs, profile, settings or search. `src/components/layout/main-nav.test.tsx` (**8**) pins the fold from the header's side: exactly the three modules with none of the four that moved, one current item, and the Social item lit from `/groups`. Together they are **13 tests**, green. The rendered-a11y audit adds the strip as a surface — `the Social strip, which is the only way between the four surfaces`, opened on `/feed` because off Social it renders nothing and auditing emptiness would pass for the wrong reason; see the audit section.

## The Cover Studio is a profile tab now, not a page

- **What changed and why.** `/cover-studio` was a destination in the main navigation beside Marketplace and Jobs, which made a member's own cover look like a module of the app. It is a **section of the profile** now — the last step of setting up a profile — so the header's own tab bar carries it: `tabs` in `src/components/profile/profile-header.tsx` gains `{ id: "cover", label: "Cover studio" }`, placed **ahead of `More`**, which stays the catch-all at the end of the row. `ProfileTabId` is derived from that array (`(typeof tabs)[number]["id"]`), so the id cannot drift from what the tab bar draws.
- **Owner-only, and enforced twice on purpose.** The tab bar filters it out of a stranger's profile — `.filter((tab) => tab.id !== "cover" || isOwner)` — and the page renders the section only under `{activeTab === "cover" && isOwnProfile && <CoverStudio />}`. That is not belt-and-braces for its own sake: the studio writes *the signed-in member's* cover, so on somebody else's profile it would be a door into the wrong room.
- **The address opens the section, exactly once.** `?tab=cover` is read by the profile page (`requestedTab = searchParams.get("tab")`), and an effect sets `activeTab` to `"cover"` only when `requestedTab === "cover" && isOwnProfile`. It is deliberately **read once, on mount** (guarded by `appliedTabRef`): a member who arrives at the studio and then taps Posts means it, and leaving `?tab=cover` in the address bar is no reason to put them back a moment later. The read lives in an effect rather than a `useState` initial value because on a client navigation the parameters are not there during the first render. On somebody else's profile the parameter is **ignored**, rather than opening a section the tab bar does not offer.
- **The old address forwards instead of 404ing.** `src/app/(main)/cover-studio/page.tsx` is now a one-liner: `redirect("/profile?tab=cover")`. The link was in the header, in the feed's sidebar and inside the cover dialog, and a bookmark is not a thing to break because the layout changed; naming the tab in the URL means the redirect says exactly where it meant to go. So a bookmarked `/cover-studio` renders the studio section — which is the state the third test renders.
- **The account-menu shortcut deep-links to it.** `main-nav.tsx`'s account menu carries `<Link href="/profile?tab=cover">Cover studio</Link>` — a shortcut to the tab rather than a page of its own, as its own comment says. Since `/cover-studio` is deliberately gone from `mainNavItems` (see the nav-fold section above), this menu item is the one deliberate route to the studio that is not the profile's tab bar itself.
- **How it announces itself.** The tab bar is `nav aria-label="Profile sections"` and marks the active tab with `aria-current="page"`, so once the studio is open its tab is the current section rather than a separate destination — the same marker the main nav and the Social strip use (see the state-conventions section).
- **Tests:** `src/app/(main)/profile/cover-tab.test.tsx` (**3**, jsdom) pins the two things that are the tab's own — clicking **Cover studio** on your own profile opens it (the studio's own `LinkMe+ Cover Studio` copy appears and the tab gains `aria-current="page"`), the `?tab=cover` address opens it, and a stranger's profile neither offers the tab nor opens the studio from the parameter while Posts and the other sections remain. `src/lib/nav-items.test.ts` (**10**) holds the list-level half, `/cover-studio` may not come back as a main-nav destination. The two files run green together at **13 tests**.

## Auditing for state that is only drawn on screen

The sibling of the tooltip audit, and the same failure in a different costume: a control that *looks* like it is telling you something and tells a screen reader nothing. The whole app was searched for it — every `variant={x ? … : …}` ternary, every conditionally coloured element, and every `onClick` on an element that is not a control. What the sweep settled on, as the app's conventions:

- **"You are here" is `aria-current`.** The desktop nav, the mobile nav panel and the **bottom nav** all tinted the current item and said nothing; all three now carry `aria-current="page"`, which is what `profile-header.tsx` had already been doing for its tabs. Verified live at 1100px and at 420px: exactly one *visible* nav link carries it at each width (both navs are in the DOM at all times, so the hidden one is display-none and out of the accessibility tree — the count of *visible* markers, not of markers, is the thing to check).
- **A single-select row of chips is `aria-pressed`, and it is a component: `src/components/shared/filter-chip.tsx`.** The chosen chip was the filled one — a signal made entirely of colour, which is also the shape WCAG's "use of colour" rule warns about. `FilterChip` takes `selected` and sets the variant *and* `aria-pressed` from it, so a chip cannot be drawn as chosen while announcing that it is not. It is used by **marketplace categories, jobs types, groups categories, and cover studio's template categories, background modes and speeds** — six rows, all of which also got `role="group"` and an `aria-label` on the row. That label is not decoration: **an `aria-label` on a plain `div` is ignored**, so the rows had no names at all before the role was added. Chips are `type="button"` — several rows sit in page markup where a bare `<Button>` would be a submit button.
- **A menu where exactly one option is chosen is a radio group, not a list with a tick.** The audience picker's items drew a `Check` beside the current audience and `role="menuitem"` with no state, so the one fact the menu exists to show was invisible to anyone not looking at it. `ui/dropdown-menu.tsx` now exports `DropdownMenuRadioGroup`/`DropdownMenuRadioItem` (Radix's `role="menuitemradio"` + `aria-checked`), and the picker uses them. **The guard matters more than it looks:** Radix reports `undefined` when the already-chosen item is chosen again — a menu may have no selection, a post's audience may not. Without the guard, re-picking the current audience set the audience to `undefined`, which the picker's `?? audienceOptions[0]` fallback renders as **Public**, i.e. a post silently becomes public. The guard is `isPostAudience` from the shared list rather than a local `!== undefined`, so the same door cannot admit an audience that no longer exists. Verified live by choosing "Only me", re-opening the menu and choosing "Only me" again: the name stayed `Post audience: Only me`.
- **A control that navigates or selects is a control.** The conversation rows on `/messages` were `<div onClick>` — not focusable, not in the tab order, activatable only with a mouse — and their selected state was a background colour. They are `<button type="button">` with `aria-current` now. Verified live by creating a conversation through the app (profile → Message → Send): one `Tab` from the search box lands on the row, which reports `aria-current="true"` and an `sr-only` status. Their unread badge also gained `sr-only` " unread", because a bare `2` in a badge is not a sentence.
- **State drawn as a colour or a glyph gets words.** `OnlineStatus` was a green dot or a grey dot and nothing else — the colour *was* the message, and green-vs-grey is the pair a reader with a red-green deficiency is most likely to lose. The status text is now always rendered (`sr-only` when the caller did not ask for it) and the dot is `aria-hidden`. Two things fell out of making it audible: `formatLastSeen` returned the literal `"Unknown"`, which read aloud as **"Last seen Unknown"**, so it now returns `null` and the component says **"Offline"** when there is nothing to say (the hook answers *when*, the component chooses the words). The admin report rows were the same defect on a status rather than a control — a colour plus an icon, no text — and now carry `sr-only` "Status: pending". The landing preview's slide dots mark the current slide `aria-current`; its strip had an `aria-label` on a plain `div`, which is the ignored-label trap above. That preview then had the same defect one level down: its card swaps the post's text in place every three seconds, which a screen reader cannot hear at all, so a polite `sr-only` `role="status"` now names where the preview moved to — `Slide 2 of 3: Marcus Rivera`, the position and who is showing rather than the whole post again, mounted from the start because a live region only announces changes made after it exists, and it falls silent on its own when the carousel is paused. The preview also opens **paused** when the system asks for reduced motion, instead of rotating at someone who has asked for stillness — the preference picks the *opening* state and then yields, so pressing play still moves it, which is why it is read when the preview mounts rather than inside the interval (a check there could only ever refuse the viewer), and a viewer who turns the preference on mid-visit stops the carousel where it stands. The sign-in page's live visual had the identical defect one file over — the same guard inside its cycle's interval, so the card sat still under a button that claimed it was playing and pressing it changed nothing at all — and now reads the preference the same way, opening paused with a working play control. Its scene strip had the ignored-label trap too (the same `aria-label` on a plain `div`, and a chosen scene told apart by colour alone), and its cycle had the landing preview's timer defect on the same 4.2s interval — picking a scene left the old cadence standing, so a scene could be replaced a moment after it was chosen. Both are now the landing strip's shape: `role="group"` with the label, `aria-current` on the scene showing, and a pick the standing cadence cannot override. The policy itself lives in one place — `src/hooks/use-ambient-playback.ts`, which both mount — because a rule copied into two components is a rule the two can disagree about later; each keeps only what is actually its own, its cadence and its content, and one mutation to the hook fails the reduced-motion tests of all three files at once. The two strips those carousels pick through — `role="group"` with the label, `aria-current` on the item showing, and a pick the cadence cannot override — are one component now, `src/components/shared/scene-strip.tsx`, with the showing index beside it in `src/hooks/use-carousel-rotation.ts`. Each caller keeps what is genuinely its own: the words the strip speaks (the group's label and each dot's accessible name), the two class recipes that make one strip a progress bar on the landing card and the other a row of scene dots on the sign-in glass, and its own cadence (3s against 4.2s, with the preview's style cycle riding the same beat). The strip draws three states — selected, seen, upcoming — because one that only knew "current or not" could not draw the landing preview's dimmed trail behind the current dot. Both consumers' own suites are what prove it: removing `aria-current` or the `onSelect` wiring from the shared component alone turns all three files red, and no consumer test needed changing to keep the 8 + 6 it already had. What a pick *means* moved in the same direction: it stops the rotation. The first answer to that defect was a re-arm counter — `select` bumped it beside setting the index, the surface's interval listed it as a dependency, and the timer was torn down and rebuilt from the pick; it had to be a counter rather than the index because the click that changes no state, on the dot already current, is exactly the case the index cannot carry. **Stopping replaced it, and the counter is gone.** A pick is the viewer taking control, so the rotation stops where they put it — the same thing pressing pause does, because that is what it is — and the play control beside the dots is how it starts again; nothing races the choice because nothing else is running. That rule needs both halves of the carousel's state, so it lives in `src/hooks/use-ambient-carousel.ts`, which is the motion policy and the position above joined by it, and both surfaces consume that instead of wiring the two up themselves. The click that changes nothing is still the load-bearing case, and the motion is now the evidence it landed — which is exactly what the counter was standing in for. The beat's own step deliberately stops nothing: the interval calling it *is* the rotation, and a timer is not a person — and now that the interval lives inside the hook, that walk is not handed back at all, since the interval is its only caller left, so a surface has nothing left to hang a timer on. A mutation that removes the stop fails 8 tests across all three files, one that makes `advance` stop as well fails the two "advances on its own" cases, and the strip's own re-arm cases were rewritten rather than deleted — one of them is now the arrow-key version of the same rule. The play/pause control above each strip had the same shape of duplication and is one component now too — `src/components/shared/ambient-playback-button.tsx`, which takes `playing`, the setter `useAmbientPlayback` hands back, and the noun the name is built from, so **the verb is derived from the state** rather than written twice: the glyph is the same either way, which is why a control still reading "Play" while the thing is already playing is a button that appears to do nothing — and the one thing a viewer with reduced motion has to press, since pressing play is the only way past a preference that opens these carousels stopped. Its glyph is `aria-hidden`, so a reader hears the words and not the `Ⅱ` character as well, and the flip itself (`setPlaying((value) => !value)`) lives in the component rather than being repeated at each call site. It is deliberately not `IconButton`, whose own doc excludes exactly this case — a player control drawn onto the surface it controls — and the two skins stay with the callers (32px on the landing card with a brand-blue focus ring, 28px on the sign-in glass with a white one). And the sign-in visual now says *where* its cycle moved to, which was the last of the four defects this shape had: it carried no live region at all, so its in-place copy swap was as silent as the landing preview's once was. It has the same `role="status"`/`aria-live="polite"` `sr-only` line — `Scene 2 of 3: Find your people.`, the position and the title, not the subtitle and the whole scene again — mounted from the start, because a live region announces only changes made after it exists, and outside the card, so the change is spoken without being drawn and without adding anything to what is read in order. It falls silent on its own while the cycle is paused, since a paused cycle changes nothing, and its test file grew to the landing preview's eight. Both strips then name their dots the same way — by what the dot switches **to**, never by where it sits: the landing preview already said `Show Sarah Chen's preview` while the sign-in visual said `Show scene 2`, which is a number a reader learns nothing from, so its dots now say `Show “Find your people.”` and the rule is written on `SceneStrip`'s own `labelFor` prop so the next caller inherits it rather than rediscovering it. Those quotes are typographic deliberately: a straight `"` inside an accessible name breaks any selector built from that name, `ui.byName` and a Playwright name locator included — which is a trap worth one departure from the file's usual quotes. And the strip is one keyboard control now rather than three tab stops: exactly one dot is in the tab order and it is the one showing, Left and Right walk the selection from there and wrap, Home and End jump to the ends, and each keystroke picks the scene the way a click does (including the stopping: `select` is the pick, whichever input reached it) — carrying the tab stop and the focus with it, because a keystroke that changed the scene and left the focus behind would strand a keyboard user on a dot that is no longer theirs. The arrows move from the dot the key was *pressed on* rather than from the item showing, since those two come apart the moment the carousel advances under a focused dot. Every key the strip does not answer is left alone, which is what keeps Tab — the one key it must never swallow — moving the focus on, and a mutation that swallows it fails the strip's suite. The dots also gained a focus ring in each caller's own colour (`focus-visible:ring-brand-blue` on the card, `:ring-white` on the glass), because the browser's default outline around a 4–6px pill is barely an indicator. It stays `role="group"` marked with `aria-current` rather than becoming a tablist or a radiogroup: those are the roles whose arrow keys a reader is *told* to expect, and adopting one is a decision about what these dots are — tabs need panels, radios are chosen rather than shown — so the group is given the keyboard behaviour of a single control and says so in `SceneStrip`'s own doc. The clock was the last hand-rolled piece of the pair, and it is the shared hook's now too. Both surfaces wrote the same effect — bail out while paused, open an interval, clear it on teardown, list `[playing, advance]` so a pause rebuilt it — and the only thing that ever differed was the number in the middle, 3s against 4.2s, which made the cadence look like something each surface decided when it was the one part of the rule with no rule *in* it; the teardown that has to be right, or a pause leaves two intervals running, was the part written twice. `useAmbientCarousel` now takes the beat as `cadenceMs` and owns the interval, so a surface states its content and its cadence and nothing about how a timer is taken down. The one surface with a second thing on the same beat — the landing preview's style cycle beside the slide — reads `beats`, the count of beats the clock has moved on, and derives its style from it (`beats % styles.length`). A count rather than an `onTick` callback, because a callback is the same shape of leak the returned `advance` was: it lets a surface run anything at all on the beat, and the inline arrow a caller naturally passes has to be held by reference or it tears the interval down and resets the cadence mid-beat, where a value has nothing to stabilise and can only be read — anything a callback could have done, an effect on `beats` still can. It also makes the two cycles honest about being independent: three slides against thirty styles, so the style wraps at thirty while the slide wraps at three, both on the one beat but not each other, which is why the style is the beat's own count wrapped and not a copy of the slide. The evidence is what the mutations cost: dropping the teardown fails three of the hook's tests (the beat keeps counting while stopped, so a pick no longer holds), ignoring the caller's cadence fails five, and dropping the beat count fails the hook's beat cases plus the landing preview's — which was the one part of the cadence no consumer test could see advance until this step read the drawn "Style NN / NN" line, held it across a pause, and walked it through its full thirty, wrapping where the three slides have wrapped many times over. That consumer suite is **11** and the sign-in visual's **9**, and the sign-in cadence is now pinned to the millisecond instead of only in multiples of its own beat, which is what let a wrong beat there pass until now. And the seam is a convention guard now rather than a note in a doc comment, from both of its ends: `src/test/beat-seams.test.ts`, whose two detectors sit in `src/test/convention-guards.ts` beside the mount, settle, body-clear, stylesheet and runbook ones, so the same meta-test that proves each of those still fires proves these do too. Against the **hooks** — every `src/hooks/use-*.ts`, read through `readHookSources` in `@/test/source-scan` — it fails on a per-beat callback option, on a declared function *referenced from the hook's own clock step* (the limb a rename cannot dodge, since the step is where the removed `onTick` was called from), and on the clock-owning hook handing the walk back (`advance` again) — while the position-only hook's returned `advance` stays legal, because it owns no timer. Against the **surfaces** — every component, through `readComponentSources` — it fails on the mirror image: a component that mounts the carousel family and opens a repeating clock of its own, which is the `[playing, advance]` interval both surfaces used to write by hand. That limb looks for the *clock* rather than a callback on purpose: a surface never calls its beat a beat, so the hook-side vocabulary would not see it. The boundary is stated rather than implied — the clock *is* allowed in `src/hooks`, and the guard test pins that the owner fires the same detector, so a later session that widens the application set has to answer for it there — and a component that animates without mounting the carousel (the typing indicator's interval, a canvas's frame loop) is left alone by both fixtures and a real-tree control — and, past the static control, by a real component with the refused clock *written back into it*: the typing indicator's file patched with a surface-held interval stays silent, since the gate is the carousel it does not mount, and the same clock is reported the moment the carousel is named on it, so the silence is the gate rather than a detector that stopped seeing intervals anywhere. Both detectors also state what they do *not* read (a callback typed through an alias, an API returned as a variable) rather than reading as stronger than they are.
- **A disclosure announces whether it is open.** The mobile menu button was a hamburger that became an × and had **no accessible name at all** — it announced "button" and nothing more. It is now an `IconButton` labelled `Open menu`/`Close menu` with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`, and the panel below it has that id. Verified live at 420px: `aria-expanded` false → true, the name flips, and the panel contains the current page marked `aria-current`.
- **Deliberately left alone, each for a reason.** The follow button, the group Join/Leave button, the post card's reaction and bookmark buttons and the cover video's mute/play buttons already *change their own text or name* with state ("Following", "Leave group", "Remove bookmark", "Unmute cover video"), so the state is in the name and `aria-pressed` would be a second, redundant way of saying it. (The one pressed control that *does* pair them, `follow-button.tsx`, used to spell the pairing out by hand; it and every chip now go through `ToggleButton` — see the state-conventions section.) The typing indicator is not a control: its state is already words, and making it a live region would announce arrivals and departures in a chat, which is noisier than useful. The notification panel's backdrop `div` stays a `div`; it is a duplicate of the panel's own close control. **`MediaGallery` is gone**, and so are its two siblings — see the media section below.

## State conventions are components, not habits

The sweep above fixed four kinds of drawn-only state by hand, which is not the same as making them unwritable. Each convention now lives in a component that derives the attribute from the same boolean that draws it:

- **`src/components/ui/toggle-button.tsx` — a fill and `aria-pressed` from one boolean.** `pressed` picks the `variant` *and* sets `aria-pressed`; `variant`, `type` and `aria-pressed` are all omitted from the props so a caller has nothing to remember. `FilterChip` is this component with a chip row's name for the same boolean (`selected`), and **`FollowButton` now goes through it too** — the two hand-written copies of the pairing are one. Forcing `type="button"` also fixed something real: `FollowButton` had no `type` at all, so inside a form it was a submit button.
- **`src/components/ui/disclosure-button.tsx` — `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` from one boolean.** The mobile menu button and the notification bell both use it: `open` and the panel's `id` are passed once and the component writes both attributes. The bell's panel gained `id="notification-panel"`. The panel mounts only while it is open, so the reference dangles while closed — which is what the app already did by hand for `mobile-nav`, and `aria-expanded` is the attribute assistive technology actually reads.
- **`src/components/ui/status-indicator.tsx` — a mark that cannot exist without its words.** `label` is required, the mark is always `aria-hidden`, and the sentence is in the markup whether or not the caller drew it (`sr-only` when not). `OnlineStatus` is a thin wrapper over it now, and the component gained a second user with a real defect attached: **the notification row's unread dot was a blue `aria-hidden` circle that said nowhere that the row was unread.** It goes through the same component now, so that state has words. It renders a `<span>` where `OnlineStatus` used to render a `<div>`, which is also a validity fix — a `div` inside a `<button>` is not allowed, and the conversation rows are buttons.
- **`ToggleButton` also owns *which surface* a control is on** (`surface="light" | "dark"`), after the cover studio's dark panels turned out to be the reason its chips were invisible. A surface rather than the two variants, because a caller that could name the off-look could destroy the on-look: see the cover-studio bullet in the audit section for the measurement (`tailwind-merge` lets a caller's `bg-*` replace the variant's fill). The pressed state stays `default` on both surfaces, so the fill keeps meaning "chosen" wherever the control is.
- **What cannot be derived, and is therefore checked instead.** A `role="group"`'s name: six rows got theirs by hand, and the audience picker's Radix radio group had none at all (now `Post audience`). No component knows what a group is for, so the audit fails an *unnamed* group rather than manufacturing a name.
- **The cover studio: a dark-surface toggle, and a page whose panels had no background.** The chips were one symptom of a page-wide fault, so the fix is two coordinated parts. **One: the panels get the surface their contents assume.** The page is a dark studio (`bg-[#0a0f1a]` on the wrapper) and its five right-hand `Card`s were left on `Card`'s white; they now use one constant, `PANEL = "border-white/10 bg-[#0f172a]"`, which the preview card already spelled out inline. Measured before/after: the panel backdrop went `rgb(255,255,255)` → `rgb(15,23,42)`, and a contrast sweep over all 556 elements on the page went from five invisibly-white texts to none (the four remaining low-contrast items are the blue-on-blue step badges — see below). **Two: the chip's off-look is chosen by the component, not the call site.** `ToggleButton` gained `surface?: "light" | "dark"`, which picks the outlined look — `outline` or the new `onDark` variant (`border-white/20 bg-white/5 text-white`) — while the *pressed* look stays `default` on both. That split is not cosmetic: `cn` runs through `tailwind-merge`, so a caller's `bg-*` **replaces** the variant's fill (measured: `twMerge("bg-brand-blue", "bg-white/5")` is `"bg-white/5"`), which means the house recipe on that page — `border-white/20 bg-white/5 text-white` — would have stripped the selected chip's blue and left it drawn as unchosen while announcing `aria-pressed="true"`. The caller now says only where the control *is*. The three dropzones and the export button moved to `variant="onDark"` for the same reason: they were already inline-copying that recipe, and two of them had no text colour at all, relying on the white card to keep them dark.
- **Verified live.** On `/cover-studio` all three chip rows report backdrop `rgb(15,23,42)`, unfilled chips `oklab(1 0 0 / 0.05)` with `rgb(255,255,255)` text and real labels ("Color", "Video", "Normal"), and the filled chip `rgb(37,99,235)` — the selected fill untouched, which was the constraint. A real click moved the pressed chip and left the others unfilled. Screenshots of both halves of the page confirm the headings, labels, inputs, dropzones and sidebar cards are all legible. `/marketplace` is unchanged (`surface` defaults to `light`): white pill, `rgb(2,8,23)` text, blue filled chip.
- **What is *not* fixed, and is now slightly worse: the four step badges.** `bg-brand-blue/20` with `text-brand-blue` numerals was about 3.5:1 on the old white card and is about 2.9:1 on the dark one — legible, but below AA and the one place this change reduced contrast. It is left alone because it is a design choice about those badges (one word, `text-white`, fixes it) rather than a fault, and because it is pre-existing: it never met AA on either surface.
- **The `@layer` bug that made every `border-<colour>` class inert, found here and fixed in its own pass.** `globals.css` had `* { border-color: hsl(var(--border)) }` **outside any `@layer`**, and unlayered CSS beats everything inside `@layer utilities` — so `border-white/20`, `border-surface-border`, `border-navy-700`, `border-brand-blue` and the rest all computed to that one slate, on every page. The rule now sits in `@layer base` (see the CSS comment for the full reasoning). Before/after, class by class — the counts are elements on the live page, and *every* element carrying a border colour class was slate-200 before:

  | page | border classes, before → after |
  | --- | --- |
  | `/feed` | 27 elements: `surface-border` 19 ×`rgb(226,232,240)` → `rgb(215,227,242)`; `surface-border/90` 5 → 90%; `brand-purple/20` 1 → 20%; `navy-700` 1 → `rgb(39,47,78)`; `input` 1 unchanged |
  | `/settings` | 27: `surface-border` 11 → `#d7e3f2`; `white` 1 → `rgb(255,255,255)`; `brand-blue/15` 1 → 15%; `input` 13 unchanged |
  | `/cover-studio` | 61: `white/10` 36 → 10%; `white/20` 19 → 20%; `brand-blue` 1 → real blue; `brand-blue/20` 1; `surface-border` 3 |
  | `/profile` | 20: `surface-border` 12, `surface-border/90` 3, `white/70` 2, `input` 2 unchanged, `navy-700` 1 |
  | `/login` | 13: `white/15` 2, `white/10` 1, `white/25` 1, `surface-border` 4, `input` 4 unchanged, `navy-700` 1 |
  | `/register` | 13: `white/15`, `white/10`, `brand-purple/15`, `surface-border` 4, `input` 5 unchanged, `navy-700` |
  | `/marketplace` `/jobs` `/groups` `/messages` `/admin` `/search` | 16 / 17 / 11 / 7 / 16 / 9, all `surface-border` → `#d7e3f2` plus the `input` and footer `navy-700` pairs |

  **Element counts are identical before and after on every page**, which is the check that nothing gained or lost a class. The regression risk was the other direction — elements that *rely* on the default — so that was measured too: on `/marketplace`, two elements with a border width and no colour class still compute `rgb(226,232,240)`, because a rule in `base` is still a default. What the fix leaves: nothing at all relies on it being unlayered.
- **No test can see the computed cascade — but one can now see the thing that broke it.** jsdom computes no CSS, so nothing here can assert what colour an element ends up; the cover-studio `PANEL` sits in the same gap and is likewise only verified by measurement. What *is* assertable is the source shape that caused it, in **`src/test/globals-layer.test.ts`** (10 tests since the theme pass; 5 for the layer half). It parses `globals.css` itself and fails if any rule **outside a layer** sets `color`, `background-color`, `border-color`, `border-*-color` or `--tw-ring-color` from a selector containing a class. That is the invariant both bugs in this file violated, stated once: an unlayered rule outranks every layer, so such a rule cannot *compete* with Tailwind, it overrides it. Three further assertions keep it honest — that the parse found a real stylesheet (`> 40` rules, a `base` layer, and a `@theme` block with more than 30 declarations), so it cannot pass by parsing nothing; that **every semantic token is declared in a `@theme` block as `--color-<name>: hsl(var(--<name>))`**, so deleting one fails; and that **none of those class names is hand-written**, which is what makes the deletion of the twenty rules a covered change rather than a silent one. The last two are what replaced the old "the twenty tokens are still inside a layer" assertion — that check existed to stop the first assertion passing on a file with no token definitions at all, and it would now fail on a file that is *correct*.
- **The twenty hand-written token rules are gone, and the way they went is the point.** They were `globals.css`'s own definitions of `text-muted-foreground`, `bg-accent`, `border-input`, `ring-ring` and sixteen siblings — written by hand because the tokens live in `:root` as HSL component triplets rather than in `@theme`, so **Tailwind generated nothing at all for those names** (measured, not assumed: of the 792 rule-groups in the generated `utilities` layer, not one was named any of them). They were therefore never competing with a real utility; they *were* the only definition of those classes. And because each covered only the bare name, every variant and opacity form the app writes was inert — the fault the next bullet measures. An intermediate pass moved them into `@layer utilities`, which fixed the *precedence* half (bare, `.border-input` at (0,1,0) outranked a layered `.focus:border-brand-blue` at (0,2,0) for no reason but the layer) and left the real one: an incomplete family. Both halves are now fixed at the root — the tokens are declared once, in `@theme inline`, and Tailwind writes the rules. `globals.css` no longer contains any `@layer utilities` block at all.
- **The before/after, done offline over the whole stylesheet and then measured live on every page.** The comparison is between two compiles of the same source by the same plugin: `node .freebuff/css-diff/build-before-after.mjs` writes `before.css.txt` (the twenty hand-written rules put back, no `@theme inline`) and `after.css.txt` (the file as it stands), both through `@tailwindcss/postcss` with `from` set to the real `src/app/globals.css` so content detection is identical in both runs. `node .freebuff/css-diff/rule-diff.mjs <before> <after>` then reports, rule by rule: **22 added, 0 removed, 0 changed.** Nothing that existed before was removed or altered — the change is purely additive, which is *why* no element that already had styling could move. `cascade-diff.mjs` says the same thing the hard way: `node .freebuff/css-diff/cascade-diff.mjs <before.css> <after.css>` computes, for every pair of rules that can match one element and set one property, which wins (layer, then specificity, then source order), and reports **118 co-matching rival pairs, the same rule wins in all 118 — 0 winner changes.** The rivals are bare element selectors (`*`, `body`, `hr`, `a`, `button`, `input`, `select`, `optgroup`, `textarea`, `table`). A third check states the claim as coverage rather than as a diff: of the **22 distinct token-family classes the app's source writes**, the production sheet has **22/22** and the pre-change sheet had **10/22** (`node .freebuff/css-diff/family-coverage.mjs <sheet>…`). (An earlier version of this bullet reported "102 of 118" and caught a double-escaping slip in the reconstruction at the same time: the hand-written `focus-visible:ring-ring` selector has to be written with one backslash, or the differ reports a rule removed that never existed.)
- **What was inert, and what each one now measures.** Every spelling the app writes that is not the bare name had **no rule in the built stylesheet** — `hover:bg-accent` and `hover:text-accent-foreground` (every `ghost` and `outline` button: 29 elements on `/feed`, 26 on `/profile`, 5 on `/`), `focus:bg-accent` / `focus:text-accent-foreground` (every dropdown and select item, so keyboard focus inside a menu drew nothing), `bg-secondary/80`, `bg-destructive/90`, `hover:bg-destructive/10`, `hover:text-destructive`, `focus:text-destructive`, `placeholder:text-muted-foreground`, `focus:ring-ring`, `data-[state=open]:bg-accent`, `data-[state=open]:text-muted-foreground`, `data-[state=active]:text-foreground`, and `data-[state=unchecked]:bg-input` — **the switch's off track, which had no background at all**. `bg-border` (the scroll-area thumb and the separator) was inert and is not even a variant. Nothing could catch this from source, and nothing did: the base name of `hover:bg-accent` *was* declared, so a source-level check passed. Measured on the live page, before → after — `placeholder:text-muted-foreground` `oklab(0.137053 -0.00715154 -0.0352408 / 0.5)`, which is the browser's own default placeholder colour and therefore proof there was no rule, → `rgb(100, 116, 139)`; `bg-border` `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)` → `rgb(226, 232, 240)` on `/settings`, `/login` and `/register`; `data-[state=active]:text-foreground` on `/admin`'s four tabs and `/search`'s six, `rgb(100, 116, 139)` for *all* of them → `rgb(2, 8, 23)` for the active one and unchanged for the rest; and on a detached probe element, `focus:bg-accent` `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)` → `rgb(241, 245, 249)`, `focus:ring-ring` `""` → `hsl(221.2 83.2% 53.3%)`, the switch's off track `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)` → `rgb(226, 232, 240)`. Hover needs a real pointer and gets one: `preview_click` leaves the mouse on the element, and a genuinely hovered `hover:bg-accent` reads `rgb(241, 245, 249)` while `hover:bg-destructive/10` reads `oklab(0.636792 0.187796 0.0888786 / 0.1)` — the opacity modifier really does compile, to a 10% `color-mix` inside the `@supports` block Tailwind emits after its opaque fallback. The Radix select on `/settings` opened with a real click shows the whole point: its focused item carries `focus:bg-accent focus:text-accent-foreground` and computes `rgb(241, 245, 249)` with `rgb(15, 23, 42)` text, where the two unfocused items are still `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0)`.
- **The live pass, and the fingerprint that made it a check rather than an impression.** Both states were measured over **14 pages** (`/`, `/feed`, `/marketplace`, `/jobs`, `/groups`, `/messages`, `/profile`, `/settings`, `/cover-studio`, `/admin`, `/search`, `/login`, `/register`, `/help`), by reverting the real stylesheet to `before-globals.css.txt`, sweeping, restoring it, and sweeping again. Per page the fingerprint returns a count of elements carrying any token-family class, the same count restricted to elements whose classes *all* had a rule before, a rolling hash of those elements' eight colour properties, and — for the elements that carry a class which had no rule — the resolved value of the property that class sets. **On all 14 pages the two counts and the hash are identical** (e.g. `/feed` 61/31/`1534360084`, `/settings` 59/40/`1559652343`, `/profile` 67/40/`-530578439`), and the only field that differs is a marker for which stylesheet is loaded. That is the regression question answered element by element: everything that had styling still has exactly the same styling. The script is `.freebuff/css-diff/fingerprint.js`; it is stashed in `sessionStorage` and run with `eval(sessionStorage.getItem("fp"))`, because a full navigation wipes `window` and pasting 2.5 KB of snippet into 28 page loads is how a sweep stops being run.
- **Two traps in driving that from the browser, both worth knowing.** `:focus` does **not** match unless `document.hasFocus()` is true: a probe element was `document.activeElement` (the focus call worked) and still `matches(":focus") === false` with `--tw-ring-color` empty, which reads exactly like a missing rule and is not one.
