A single real `preview_click` on the page's `h1` fixes it, and then the same probe reports `matchesFocus: true`. Anything that measures focus, `focus-visible` or a `focus:` utility needs that click first, or it will "prove" a rule is absent. And `preview_click` is the only way to get a real `:hover` — a synthetic `mouseover` does not create one — which is why the hover evidence is a click on an injected probe rather than an event dispatch.
- **Tailwind scans every file it is not told to ignore, so a build artifact left in the repo becomes an input to the next build.** Writing `before.css` and `after.css` into `.freebuff/css-diff/` made the *next* run's output grow — `.flex-shrink` and `.border-collapse` appeared as rules "removed" in the diff, extracted from the previous compile's own selectors — and it grew again on every run, a feedback loop that also produced a `.bg-accent\/50` rule nothing in the app asks for. Renaming them `.css.txt` **did not help: the extension is not consulted.** The fix is to stop relying on detection at all — `build-before-after.mjs` now compiles with `source(none)` and one explicit `@source "../../src"`, which is deterministic and cannot drift. Worth remembering for any future generated file: the real dev server and build scan `.freebuff` too.
- **A side effect worth recording rather than discovering later: the test's own token list is scanned.** `DESIGN_TOKENS` in `globals-layer.test.ts` names the tokens — `"accent-foreground"` among them — and Tailwind reads that string out of the test file as a *class* candidate, so the production sheet contains `.accent-foreground { accent-color: hsl(var(--foreground)) }`, a rule nothing in the app uses. It is one unused declaration and it is harmless, but it is the reason the rule-diff shows an addition the app did not ask for, and it is named here so it is not mistaken for one.
- **`@theme inline`, and three variables the app never reads.** The block uses `inline` rather than plain `@theme` because the values reference other custom properties (`hsl(var(--accent))`); `inline` substitutes the value into each utility instead of emitting a `--color-accent` that would itself point at another variable. It does not inline all nineteen, though — measured, `--color-accent`, `--color-input` and `--color-ring` are still emitted into `:root`, and the other sixteen are not. Nothing references any of the three (`grep` for `var(--color-<name>)` in the built sheet: zero hits), every utility is inlined, and a probe that isolates a single utility reproduces none of it, so the trigger is somewhere in the full source set rather than in any one class. Recorded as a measurement, not explained: it is cosmetic today and it would only matter to someone who wanted to retheme by overriding `--color-*` at runtime.
- **The one unlayered rule with a colour left, and what it costs — measured, because this one is visible.** `:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid var(--color-brand-blue) }` still sits outside any layer, so the same precedence applies to it, and `focus-visible:outline-none` (layered, and higher on specificity at (0,2,0)) cannot win. Verified on `/settings` after a real click gave the page focus, so `el.matches(":focus-visible")` was true and `document.hasFocus()` was true: an `<Input>` whose class list contains `focus-visible:outline-none` computes `outline-style: solid` with `outline-color: rgb(37,99,235)` — the global rule's brand blue, and nothing else in the class list offers an outline. **23 controls on that page alone carry the class**, so the ask is common and uniformly ignored. It is deliberately left as-is: moving that rule into `base` would remove the outline from every control that asks for ring-only treatment, which is an accessibility stance rather than a layering fix, and changing it is a decision to make on purpose. The new invariant excludes it by construction — no class in the selector, and `outline` is not in the property set the test checks.
- **Verified live, both disclosures and the chips.** On `/feed` the bell reports `aria-expanded="false"` with `aria-controls="notification-panel"` and no panel in the page; a real click flips it to `"true"` **and** the panel appears with both header controls named. At 420px the menu button reports `Open menu` → click → `Close menu`, `aria-expanded="true"`, the panel present, exactly one `aria-current="page"` inside it, and the bell correctly back to `"false"`. On `/marketplace` the row is one named group whose filled chip is `aria-pressed="true"` and the other eight are `"false"`, all `type="button"`.
- **The cover studio's invisible chips, fixed — and the diagnosis in the previous version of this bullet was wrong.** It said the page was dark and the chips wanted an on-dark variant. The page's *cards*, in fact, were white: five `Card`s carried `border-white/10` and every bit of content styling for a dark surface, but never a background, so they fell back to `Card`'s own white. Every heading, label, chip, input and dropzone on the right half of that page was written in `text-white` and drawn on white — 18 white texts, 15 `border-white/20`, 11 `bg-white/5`, and not one light-surface class anywhere in the region. See the state-conventions section for the two-part fix and the measurements.
- **A hyphenated prop cannot be refused by the type system.** `Omit<ButtonProps, "aria-pressed">` reads like enforcement and is not: TypeScript skips the excess-property check for JSX attribute names containing a hyphen, so `<ToggleButton aria-pressed={false}>` compiles. Verified by writing it, not assumed. The enforcement there is the spread order — `{...props}` first, the derived attribute after — plus a test that pushes a contradicting value through a cast. For `variant` and `type`, which have no hyphen, a `@ts-expect-error` does bite, and `tsc` guards it.

## Dark mode and a user-selectable accent

- **The mechanism, measured before it was relied on.** Every colour in this app reaches the screen through a `var(--color-*)` custom property, and that is a fact about the *build output*, not an intention: `dist/client/_next/static/css/layout.*.css` contains `.text-navy-800{color:var(--color-navy-800)}`, `.bg-surface-light-blue{background-color:var(--color-surface-light-blue)}`, `.text-white{color:var(--color-white)}`, `.border-surface-border{border-color:var(--color-surface-border)}` and, for the semantic tokens, `.bg-card{background-color:hsl(var(--card))}` / `.text-muted-foreground{color:hsl(var(--muted-foreground))}`; the palette itself is emitted into `:root` (`--color-navy-800:#1a2034`, `--color-white:#fff`). So a theme is a set of custom properties to override, and it needs no component to be touched. **The one thing that does not follow is an *opacity modifier on a palette colour*:** `.bg-white\/95{background-color:#fffffff2}` is a build-time hex, whereas the same modifier on a semantic token compiles to `color-mix(in oklab, hsl(var(--card)) 95%, transparent)` and therefore flips. That single distinction decided where the re-points went.
- **`globals.css` gained a `.dark` block and five `:root[data-accent=…]` blocks.** `.dark` is unlayered and sits *after* `:root`, so it beats the same-specificity `:root` on order and beats the palette variables Tailwind emits in `@layer theme` regardless of specificity (the same unlayered-beats-any-layer fact the `@layer base` border default exists to fix, working for us here). It overrides two families deliberately: **the nineteen semantic triplets** the light theme already sets (`--background` … `--ring`, the canonical shadcn dark values), so `bg-card`, `text-muted-foreground`, `border-border` and `focus:ring-ring` follow; and **the app palette that predates them** — `--color-surface-light-blue` `#080d17`, `--color-surface-white`, `--color-surface-border`, and the `navy` *text* ramp `--color-navy-600/700/800` flipped to light with `--color-navy-50/100` as dark hover surfaces — because the app writes `bg-surface-light-blue`, `text-navy-800` and `border-surface-border` directly and those classes resolve through exactly those names. It also overrides the callout shades (`red-50/200/600/700/800`, `emerald-…`, `amber-…`, `slate-50/700`) so a red-50 alert is a red-*tinted dark* box rather than a light one with dark text.
- **`--color-white` is the one name that must not be overridden, and saying why is the whole design.** `text-white` is the on-colour for a filled button and for text on the permanently dark panels, so white has to stay white in both themes. Solid white *surfaces* were re-pointed to `bg-card` (light: `--card` is `0 0% 100%` = the same white, so nothing moved) and translucent white *glass on a themed page* to `bg-card/<n>` — which is why the nav's `bg-white/95` became `bg-card/95` and now flips at all, where a palette opacity would have stayed `#fffffff2`. **Four `bg-white` were deliberately kept**: the switch thumb (it is read against `bg-input`/`bg-brand-blue`, and a card-coloured thumb would sit on a card-coloured track), the auth shell's `L+` mark, the landing hero's CTA on the permanently dark ink panel (with `text-ink-800`, since the *text* ramp flips), and the authenticator QR wrapper — a scanner reads the code against its white quiet zone, not against the app's palette.
- **The `navy` ramp is dual-purpose, so the panels got their own names.** `navy-800` was the app's heading colour (66 `text-navy-800`) *and* its dark-panel background (6 `bg-navy-800`: footer, landing hero, auth shell, tooltip, two video wells). Flipping it for the text would have turned those panels light, so a twin ramp was added to `@theme` and nothing overrides it: `--color-ink-100/600/700/800` at the same shades, and the eight panel usages moved to `bg-ink-800`, `border-ink-700` (the footer's inner rule), `from-ink-800 via-ink-600` (the cover-preview gradient) and `text-ink-100`. Light mode is byte-identical because the values are identical. The smaller conflicts were resolved the same way: `text-navy-500` (two places, body copy on a themed surface) became `text-muted-foreground`, and `text-navy-200/300/400` were left alone — they are only ever on the ink panels, and `navy-200` must stay light there.
- **Two traps in doing that with a script, both hit and both worth the line.** The `s/bg-white(?![−\w\/])/bg-card/g` pass correctly left `bg-white/90` (the lookahead excludes `/`) but **also hit `hover:bg-white`**, which is a *different* intent — a pill that must stay white because it sits over a user photo (the profile cover's two controls, the marketplace save button over a product image). Those are back to `hover:bg-white`, and the mismatch was found by scanning hover states rather than by reading the diff. And `text-navy-800` → `text-ink-800` on the profile-cover buttons was the *only* such change there: a global pass on that file would have taken the cover-preview gradient's own text with it.
- **The theme mechanism is three small pieces, split because two of them run in different languages.** `src/lib/theme.ts` holds the data and the pure helpers — `THEMES`, `ACCENTS`, `resolveTheme(choice, prefersDark)`, the storage keys, and `THEME_INIT_SCRIPT`. `src/components/providers/theme-provider.tsx` is a client context (`theme`, `resolvedTheme`, `accent`, both setters) that reads `localStorage`, follows the media query while the choice is `system`, and writes `.dark` + `data-accent` + `color-scheme` onto `<html>`; storage is best-effort in one place, because `localStorage` *throws* on access in some real browsing modes and a renderer may not define it at all (the test environment does not), and neither is a reason the page cannot have a theme. `layout.tsx` mounts the provider outermost and, in `<head>`, runs `THEME_INIT_SCRIPT` — a blocking inline script, because an effect runs *after* the server's light HTML has painted and that is the white flash this removes. `<html>` carries `suppressHydrationWarning`, since the script deliberately adds the attributes React last rendered without.
- **The accent is the brand ramp under a different name.** Each `:root[data-accent="…"]` block writes `--primary`, `--ring` and the three `--color-brand-blue*` steps, so `bg-brand-blue` buttons, `text-brand-blue` links, the unlayered `:focus-visible` outline and `focus:ring-ring` all follow from five variables. `:root[data-accent=…]` is (0,2,0) against `.dark`'s (0,1,0), so the accent wins in either theme — which is the point: choosing an accent chooses the brand colour, and it must not be undone by dark mode. `blue` is restated in a block rather than left to `:root` so the default is a declared choice the guard test can see.
- **Verified live on the real server, not asserted from the source.** With the theme set through the actual control: clicking **Light** on `/settings` removed the class, wrote `linkme-theme=light` and moved `body` to `rgb(243,247,252)`; clicking **Emerald** wrote `linkme-accent`, set `data-accent=emerald` and moved `--color-brand-blue` to `#059669`, `--primary` to `160.1 84.1% 39.4%` and the nav's mark to `rgb(5,150,105)`. Navigating to `/login` with `dark` + `violet` stored shows the pre-paint path working: `<html class="dark" data-accent="violet">` with `--color-brand-blue` already `#7c3aed`, the inline script present in `<head>`, `color-scheme: dark`, and `body` dark — before the provider has done anything. Screenshots were taken of `/` (both themes), `/login` and `/settings` in dark + emerald, and `/feed`.
- **The contrast sweep, and the false positive that taught the method.** A script walks every text-bearing element, composites the translucent backgrounds up its ancestor chain and computes a WCAG ratio; it found **exactly one** low-contrast item on every page checked (`/`, `/login`, `/settings`, `/feed`, `/profile`, `/marketplace`, `/cover-studio`, `/groups`, `/about`): the footer's `text-brand-purple` "+" on `bg-ink-800` at 2.83:1, which is pre-existing (the footer was already dark in light mode) and not a regression. The first version of that scan reported a *white* pill as dark-on-dark: `getComputedStyle` returns `oklab(0.999994 0 0 / 0.9)` for a `color-mix` background and the scan's `rgba()` regex silently skipped it, so it walked past the pill to a dark ancestor. Fixed by converting every colour through a 1×1 canvas (`ctx.fillStyle = c; getImageData`), which handles `oklab` exactly. Worth keeping: **a colour-computing scan that only parses `rgb()`/`rgba()` will report `color-mix` backgrounds wrongly, and `color-mix` is what every opacity modifier on a semantic token compiles to.**
- **The one page defect the sweep then found for real.** The feed's "Create something memorable" card used `bg-gradient-to-br from-white to-brand-purple/5` — a *palette* gradient stop, so it stayed `rgb(255,255,255)` in dark mode and its `text-foreground` (`rgb(248,250,252)`) became invisible. It is `from-card` now; light mode is unchanged because `--card` is white there. It was the only `from-`/`via-`/`to-white` left after the re-points.
- **Baselines after this pass:** `npm test -- --run` = **192 passed / 20 files**, `npx tsc --noEmit` = **51 errors** (unchanged), `npm run build` clean. The five new tests live in the theme-block describe of `globals-layer.test.ts`: `.dark` overrides every semantic token; it is unlayered and after `:root` (so it *actually* wins, which is the failure a layering mistake would hide); every app `--color-*` it names is declared in `@theme` (the typo guard — Tailwind's own palette families are allowed through, and that exclusion is what the first run of this test caught); every accent in `ACCENTS` has a block writing `--color-brand-blue`/`--primary`/`--ring`; and the pre-paint script names the same class, attribute and storage keys the provider does. The first version of the typo guard failed on 24 correct lines, because "declared in `@theme`" is not true of Tailwind's built-in palette — the guard had to learn that `.dark` overriding `red-50` is intentional.
- **One change to the audit harness was needed, and it is the honest kind.** `rendered-a11y.test.tsx` renders each surface inside `<TooltipProvider>`; the settings page now reads the theme, so the wrapper gained `ThemeProvider` — mirroring the real layout, where it is outermost. The provider had two latent environment assumptions that the audit found by failing: `window.localStorage` is *undefined* in this jsdom config, and `matchMedia` is stubbed by `setup.ts` but not guaranteed by a browser, so both reads are now guarded and both writes are best-effort. Nothing about the audit's assertions changed.
- **What is *not* claimed.** jsdom computes no CSS, so none of this is covered by a rendered test — the dark values, the accent blocks and the re-points are verified by the build output, the live measurements above and the screenshots. And it is a *theme*, not a redesign: the marketing pages' decorative gradients (`from-cyan-400`, `to-indigo-600` and friends) and the four step badges on `/cover-studio` are unchanged in dark mode, because they are design choices rather than palette tokens, and the `.dark` callout overrides are limited to the shades a callout actually wears (deliberately *not* `gray-600`, which is also the icon inside the white save-listing pill that stays white in both themes).

## The accent follows the account; the theme follows the device

- **What is synced, and what deliberately is not.** The accent is stored on the member's profile, so choosing Violet travels to the next machine they sign in on. The light/dark choice stays in the browser. That split is the design, not a limitation: the accent is identity ("this is my colour") and the theme is context ("it is dark in this room"), so the same person plausibly wants dark on a phone at night and light at a desk — and syncing the theme would take that away. It also keeps the pre-paint script honest, see the flash note below.
- **Storage: `profiles.appearance`, a JSONB object, not a column per preference.** Next to `contactPreferences` and for the same reason — a second preference is then a code change rather than a migration. Typed as `{ accent?: Accent }` with a **type-only** import of the accent union from `@/lib/theme`, so the allowed values are the ones the picker offers and the two cannot drift. (`postAudiences` → `visibilityEnum` in the same file is the same idea, imported as a value because the enum is built from it at runtime.) Read and written by **`GET`/`PUT /api/preferences`** (`src/app/api/preferences/route.ts`), a separate endpoint from `PUT /api/users` on purpose: that one writes the fields a reader sees on a public profile, and this writes a private display choice — and it is small enough to call from every page, where `/api/users` answers with three counts and a follow check beside the profile.
- **No client-supplied previous state, and that is a fix rather than an accident.** `PUT /api/users` merges `contactPreferences` by trusting a `currentContactPreferences` object sent by the caller, which is a lost update waiting to happen. Here the merge is one statement in the database: `coalesce(appearance, '{}'::jsonb) || '{"accent": …}'::jsonb`. Two devices cannot clobber each other's keys and nothing outside has to be believed. The accent is validated with `isAccent` — the same function the picker's list comes from — so `PUT {"accent":"chartreuse"}` answers **400 `Unknown accent`** (measured live).
- **The precedence rule is one function, because it is one decision.** `appearanceSync(local, remote)` in `src/lib/theme.ts` returns `adopt` / `publish` / `none`: **the account wins** whenever it has a value, and the device *publishes* its own only when the account has none. "Account wins" is what makes the accent travel; "publish when empty" is what seeds the account from the first device that had a local choice, and what keeps an accent chosen before signing in. Both inputs are `unknown`, because one comes out of `localStorage` and the other out of a response body, and a malformed remote value is *dropped rather than applied* — then the device's own is published to replace it, never the reverse, or an accent renamed on the server would both paint nothing and erase a working choice.
- **Signing out gives the accent up, and that is not tidiness.** Without it the next person to sign in on the same browser would find no account value, take the `publish` branch, and write the previous member's colour onto *their* profile. `ThemeSync` clears the stored accent back to the default when the session goes from a user to none — the same reasoning the notification provider uses for clearing its inbox, and stated in the same place.
- **One component does the reconciling, and it renders nothing.** `src/components/providers/theme-sync.tsx` is mounted in the layout between `AuthProvider` and the rest, because it is the only place both facts can be read: the theme context (inside `ThemeProvider`) and the session (inside `AuthProvider`). It does not watch the accent for edits — the picker writes its own changes — because watching would make *adopting* a value echo back a write of the value it just adopted, and a pull/push loop is exactly the bug that shape produces.
- **The device copy is still a cache, and the flash question is answered honestly.** The pre-paint script reads `localStorage`, so on a machine that has seen the account before there is no flash at all — the account's value was cached the first time it was adopted. On a genuinely new machine the first paint uses the default and the accent corrects a moment later, because the value can only arrive over the network. The alternative would be to render it into the HTML server-side, which means reading the session in the root layout and giving up static rendering for every page in the app; that was rejected as far more expensive than a one-frame correction on a device that has never been used. Written down so the next person does not rediscover it as a bug.
- **`drizzle-kit migrate` cannot be used on this project, and finding that out was the sharpest edge in this pass.** The schema was provisioned with `drizzle-kit push`, so **`drizzle.__drizzle_migrations` exists and holds 0 rows while the whole schema is already there.** `migrate` therefore starts at `0000`, whose `CREATE TABLE "users"` fails against a database that has one, and — each file being applied in a transaction — nothing is recorded and nothing changes. Verified after the attempt: still 0 rows, and no `profiles.appearance`. It also means **the generated migration was not applicable as written**: `drizzle-kit generate` compared the schema against a *snapshot* that had drifted, and proposed adding `profiles.work`, `profiles.education`, `profiles.website` and `notifications.message` alongside `appearance` — all four of which the running app already reads and writes, so the first statement would have failed with `column "message" of relation "notifications" already exists` and taken `appearance` down with it. The fix is that every statement is `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS`, which makes the file correct against both the current database and a fresh one (measured: three `NOTICE … already exists, skipping` and five `ok`s, no error), and which brings the snapshot back in line — `drizzle-kit generate` now reports **"No schema changes, nothing to migrate"**, so the drift does not reappear. Because `migrate` is unusable, the statements were applied by a small tool, **`.freebuff/apply-migration.mjs <file>`**, which strips comments, splits on drizzle's `--> statement-breakpoint`, and runs each statement in order — and which records *nothing*, so if the project is ever baselined that is the thing to remember. **Baselining is the real fix and is left undone on purpose**: it means writing migration history (`sha256` hashes and timestamps) into their database for migrations that were never run by drizzle, which is a claim about their schema's provenance and not a side effect to take quietly.
- **Verified live, in the running app and in the database.** With the session the preview browser already had: `GET /api/preferences` → 200 `{"appearance":{"accent":"blue"}}` (the *publish* path — the account was empty and the device's value was sent up), `PUT {"accent":"chartreuse"}` → **400 `Unknown accent`**, clicking Violet in the picker → `data-accent=violet`, `--color-brand-blue: #7c3aed`, `linkme-accent=violet`, and the row became `{"accent":"violet"}`. **Then the new-machine case, which is the whole feature:** `localStorage.removeItem("linkme-accent")`, navigate to `/feed`, and the page came back `data-accent=violet` with the nav's mark computed `rgb(124,58,237)` and the value re-cached in `localStorage`. The reset for sign-out is the one path not exercised in the browser — signing out ends the session the preview browser is using and there is no way back in — so it is covered by the test below instead, and said so rather than implied.
- **A `localStorage` shim, and the warning that taught it to define rather than test.** This jsdom has no `localStorage`, and the absence is not quiet: the lookup falls through to Node's experimental getter and prints `localStorage is not available because --localstorage-file was not provided` into the one output read closely. `setup.ts` now installs an in-memory store. The first version of that shim was written as `if (!window.localStorage)`, which is itself the read that prints the warning — this environment makes `window` and `globalThis` the same object, so the check produced the warning it existed to remove. It defines the property unconditionally now, and the note is in the code.
- **The tests, and the mutations that prove they bite.** `src/lib/theme.test.ts` (9) pins the rules: what `system` resolves to, that the near-misses (`"Dark"`, `"dark "`, `7`, `["dark"]`, `{ id: "rose" }`) are rejected by both guards, that storage access is inert without a browser (the SSR path), and the whole `appearanceSync` grid including the malformed-remote case. `src/components/providers/theme-sync.test.tsx` (4, jsdom) is the wiring: the account's accent is applied *and* cached, the device's is published when the account is empty, signing out drops it, and a **503 leaves the device's choice alone** (not adopted, not published — we do not know whether the account holds something worth keeping). The session is the only stub; the real `ThemeProvider` is mounted and the accent is read back out of its context, so the assertion is about the value that would reach `<html>`. **Two mutations, both caught and both reverted with `md5sum` verified:** making the device win instead of the account fails 3 tests (the rule test and both wiring tests that depend on adoption), and removing the sign-out reset fails **exactly 1** — the sign-out test — with the other three still green, so the guard is specific rather than incidental.
- **No API-route test, and why.** There is no test database here, and the route's first refusal is `requireAuth`, so a unit test would assert 401 and nothing else worth having. What the route is instead is small and its one real rule — that the accent is validated against the *picker's* list rather than a copy — is structural: it calls the same `isAccent` the picker's `ACCENTS` are checked by, so adding an accent is a one-line change in one place. The 400 and the merge are pinned by the live calls above.

## The theme, switchable from the nav's account menu

- **Dark mode used to be reachable only through `/settings` → Appearance**, and the account menu — the control a reader already reaches for to change something about their own account — is where the theme belongs. The menu now carries a **Theme** radio group between two separators, above Sign out.
- **Three `menuitemradio`s, not three buttons, and the group is named.** `DropdownMenuRadioGroup`/`DropdownMenuRadioItem` (the exports the audience picker already uses) give each option `role="menuitemradio"` with `aria-checked`, so the chosen theme is *said* rather than only ticked — the same pairing the settings card gets from its own radio group. Radix renders the group as a bare `role="group"` with no name of its own, so it carries `aria-label="Theme"`, which is what keeps the audit's "a group of options must have a name" rule satisfied (the rule that made the audience picker carry `Post audience` too) — and its items' `aria-checked` is what satisfies the other half, now that the rule reaches a menu's `menuitemradio`s at all (see the audit section).
- **The choice is expressed three ways, deliberately, and the third was added after looking at a screenshot.** `aria-checked` is for anyone listening; the `Check` tick is the same fact for anyone looking, and the first version left it out because the semantics alone seemed sufficient — the open menu then *announced* the current theme and did not *show* it, which is the defect this repo keeps finding (state drawn and never said) wearing its mirror image. Both derive from the same `theme` that drives the group's `value`, so the tick and the announcement cannot disagree. The tick and each `Sun`/`Moon`/`Monitor` glyph are `aria-hidden="true"`: a mark beside a label is decoration, not a name.
- **It is its own component, and that is load-bearing rather than tidiness.** `src/components/layout/theme-menu-items.tsx` calls `useTheme`, which throws without a `ThemeProvider`, and it is rendered inside the menu's *content* — which Radix mounts only while the menu is open. So the hook is never called in a render of `MainNav` that has no menu on screen. `main-nav.test.tsx` renders the nav to static markup with **no provider at all**, and it stays green because of that; calling `useTheme` in `MainNav` itself would have broken it, and would have re-rendered the whole nav — notifications, search, avatar — on every theme change for nothing.
- **The icons moved to `src/lib/theme-icons.ts`, and the module split is why.** `THEME_ICONS` (`light`/`dark`/`system` → `Sun`/`Moon`/`Monitor`, written `satisfies Record<ThemeChoice, …>` so a new theme fails the build) is now shared by the settings picker and the menu items, which had begun to hold a copy each. It is deliberately **not** in `theme.ts`: that module is imported by `src/lib/db/schema.ts` and by a JSON API route, and a `lucide-react` import there would drag React into both. `theme.ts` is data and pure helpers; the icon map is a view concern, so it is a peer of the components.
- **Radix closes the menu when an item is selected**, which is the conventional thing for a menu to do and gives immediate feedback: the page behind changes as the menu goes. The alternative — keeping it open so the three can be compared — costs a second dismissal at the end, which is the click this change exists to save.
- **Verified live on `/feed`.** The trigger is the 32×32 avatar button (`header button[aria-haspopup="menu"]`, named by its `<img alt="Theo Wu">`). **A real pointer could not open it in this environment** — `preview_click` reports "That element has no visible area to click" for it, and hand-dispatched `PointerEvent`/`MouseEvent`s (with `ctrlKey`, `button` and the rest set) do **not** take Radix's path either — while **focus plus a real `preview_press Enter` does**. With it open: `menuOpen: true`, `aria-expanded: "true"`, group name `Theme`, items `Light`/`Dark`/`System` with the stored choice checked, and the other items (`Profile`, `Settings`, `Cover Studio`, `Sign out`) unchanged. A screenshot confirmed the tick then draws the choice. This is the same caveat the audit section records for synthetic events: **a synthetic event takes a different path through Radix, and reading it as a defect is the easiest false report to make here.**
- **The test mounts the menu `forceMount`ed rather than opening it.** `src/components/layout/theme-menu-items.test.tsx` (4, jsdom) renders a controlled `DropdownMenu open` with `forceMount` content, the real `ThemeProvider`, and a probe that reads the resolved theme — because jsdom cannot produce the `pointerdown` Radix opens a menu on, so the *gesture* is checked in the browser and the *contents and effect* are checked here. It pins: the item labels are exactly `THEMES.map(t => t.label)` in the app's own order (so a renamed theme has to answer here); the group's name is `"Theme"`; **exactly one** item is `aria-checked="true"` and it is `Dark`; every item carries a non-null `aria-checked` (the shape that cannot be half-applied); **exactly one** item contains the tick (`svg.lucide-check`) and it is `Dark`; and that clicking `Dark` switches the probe to `dark:dark` and persists `THEME_STORAGE_KEY`, `Light` switches back, and `System` resolves to `system:light` (the `matchMedia` stub reports light) with `system` stored. `localStorage.clear()` runs around every test.
- **Three mutations, each reverted with `md5sum` verified.** Dropping `aria-label="Theme"` fails **exactly 1** test; making `onValueChange` a no-op fails **2** (the switch/persist test and the System one); and replacing the tick's condition with `false` fails **exactly 1** — the tick assertion, `expected [] to deeply equal [ 'Dark' ]`. The last one took three attempts to run **as a valid mutation**: the first two used `perl` to splice a bare `null` into the JSX, which React renders as the literal *text* `"null"`, so the failures read `expected [ 'Lightnull', 'Darknull', … ]` — a broken subject rather than a caught bug, which is exactly the difference a mutation check exists to keep straight. The mutation is now written so the subject stays valid (a TypeScript-clean `false`) and the assertion that fails is the one that reads the tick.
- **Baselines after this pass:** `npm test -- --run` = **209 passed / 23 files**, `npx tsc --noEmit` = **51 errors** (unchanged), `npm run build` clean. The four new tests are the file above; the jsdom files are now six.

## The theme, reachable on a phone

- **The account menu is the desktop answer, and on a phone there is no menu to reach.** The panel that opens from the nav's hamburger held links and Sign out and nothing else, so dark mode — which had just been brought one click closer on a desktop — was still `/settings → Appearance` away on a phone. The panel now carries the same three choices in the open, between the links and Sign out.
- **The picker is one component now, and that is the point rather than the tidiness.** `src/components/shared/theme-choice-group.tsx` (`ThemeChoiceGroup`) is a labelled `role="radiogroup"` of three `role="radio"` buttons with `aria-checked` on each, the label and glyphs drawn from `THEMES` and `THEME_ICONS`. `appearance-settings.tsx` was holding that markup inline and now renders the component, because the settings card and the mobile panel **are in the document at the same time on a phone** — the same reason `theme-icons.ts` exists, one level up. It is deliberately *not* used by the nav's account menu: a set of options inside a menu has to be `menuitemradio`s to sit in one at all, which is what `theme-menu-items.tsx` renders.
- **The group's label id is generated, and the live check is what says why.** The first version of the settings group carried a written `id="theme-label"`; with two of these on screen at once, the second group would have been named by the *first* one's heading. It uses `useId` instead. Measured on `/settings` with the mobile panel open: **two** theme groups, label ids `_r_9_` and `_r_4_`, distinct, both resolving to a node reading `Theme`.
- **The panel stays open on a choice, which is the opposite of what the account menu does — deliberately.** A menu is expected to close on selection; the panel is drawn from the same tokens as the page, so the change *is* the feedback, and closing it would hide the only feedback there is. Measured live from the panel: **Light** → `linkme-theme=light`, `.dark` off, `color-scheme: light`, the header's background computed `oklab(0.999994 … / 0.95)`; **Dark** → class back, stored `dark`; **both with the panel still in the page**, and `System` restoring `system` afterwards.
- **Verified live at 420px on `/feed`.** The panel opens from `Open menu` (the disclosure is a plain button, so `preview_click` reaches it — unlike the avatar trigger, see the account-menu section). Inside: the group is named `Theme`, the options are `Light`/`Dark`/`System` in the app's order, the checked one is the stored one, every option carries a non-null `aria-checked`, each tile measures **68px** tall (the tap target the settings card's `min-h-11` was for), and the six nav links and Sign out are unchanged. A screenshot is what the layout was judged from, and the settings page at the same width renders identically to before the refactor — same three tiles, same sentence underneath, accent row below.
- **The panel is opened the way a reader opens it, and that is only possible because it is not a menu.** `src/components/layout/mobile-nav-theme.test.tsx` (3, jsdom) mounts the real `MainNav` inside the real `ThemeProvider` and clicks the disclosure the nav already had — a plain `<button onClick>`, so jsdom's `element.click()` is enough, where Radix's `pointerdown` menus need the browser. It asserts: the options are exactly `THEMES.map(t => t.label)` in order; the group is named by **resolving** its `aria-labelledby` to the text `Theme` rather than restating the word; **exactly one** option is `aria-checked="true"` and it is the stored one, with every option carrying a non-null `aria-checked`; and that choosing Dark moves a probe to `dark:dark`, persists `THEME_STORAGE_KEY`, and **leaves the panel up**. Three modules are stubbed to get the nav to render (pathname, session, bell) and none is under test.
- **The audit gained a surface, and it is the only way the panel's controls get judged at all.** `the nav, with the mobile panel opened` in `src/test/rendered-a11y.test.tsx` opens the panel and audits it — without it, everything inside a panel that is mounted only while open is invisible to every other case (which is exactly how the notification panel's two nameless buttons survived earlier passes). The file is now **17 tests over 16 surfaces**.
- **Three mutations, each reverted with `md5sum` verified.** Removing `<ThemeChoiceGroup />` from the panel fails **exactly the 3** new tests — and leaves the audit green, which is the honest limit of a name audit: it can say a control is unnamed, not that a control is missing. Replacing `aria-checked={selected}` with a TypeScript-clean `false` fails **exactly 1**, the checked-one test (the switch test still passes, because it drives the click rather than the attribute — the two assertions cover different failure modes). And taking the word `Sign out` out of the panel's own button fails **exactly 1**: the new audit case, reported by name — `1 control(s) with no accessible name: button <button class="flex items-center gap-3 …">`. That last mutation is the argument for adding the surface.
- **Baselines after this pass:** `npm test -- --run` = **213 passed / 24 files**, `npx tsc --noEmit` = **51 errors** (unchanged), `npm run build` complete. Three of the four new tests are the file above and the fourth is the audit surface; the jsdom files are now seven.

## The accessible-name audit

The check that would have caught the nameless mobile menu button — an icon-only `<Button>` in the nav with no `aria-label` and no text, which announced "button" and nothing else and **survived a careful, deliberate sweep of every `aria-label` in the app, because a sweep of `aria-label`s cannot see a control that has none.** So the question is asked directly, by a run rather than by an eye: *is there any control a reader can reach but not name?* Three files, and the split between them is the point:

- **`src/test/a11y.ts`** is the name computation: `accessibleName(element)`, `unnamedControls(root)`, `describeUnnamed(offenders)`, `isRendered(element)`. It is the subset of accname that decides whether a control has *any* name, in the spec's order — `aria-labelledby` → `aria-label` → what the control is (an image's `alt`, a submit input's `value`, a field's `<label>`, a field's `placeholder`) → the readable text inside it (skipping `aria-hidden` descendants, counting an `<img alt>`) → `title`. Two rules in there are deliberate rather than incidental. Name-from-content is **not** applied to `input`/`textarea`/`select`: what is written inside those is their *value*, not their name, so an unlabelled `<select>` is genuinely nameless (`<select><option>Public</option></select>` is reported; every select in this app carries its own name). And a `placeholder` *does* count for a field, which is the spec's own last resort — the composer's box is named "What's on your mind?" by its placeholder and nothing else, and a real browser announces exactly that, so calling it nameless would report the app for how it is written rather than for something wrong with it. The container rule learned its lesson twice: `AUTHOR_NAMED_ROLES` — the roles that never take a name from what is written inside them — had `group` from the chip-row pass and gained `tablist` when a nameless one was first tested, because until then the tabs' own labels counted as the list's name.
- **`src/test/rendered-a11y.test.tsx`** (renamed from `accessible-names.test.tsx` when the second question moved in) is the audit proper — **17 surfaces**, each judged twice in one render. Names: the nav three times (with its account menu, with its notification panel and with its mobile panel opened), the bottom nav, the marketing page, marketplace, jobs, communities, search, admin, cover studio, messages, settings twice (closed, and with its select opened), feed, a profile, and the composer **opened** (the toolbar is where the icon-only controls live, so the audit focuses the textarea first and judges the second state). States, via `stateViolations`: the same 17, because the panels' controls, the bell's own disclosure and the select's options are only judgeable while the thing that holds them is open — which is why the nav has three surfaces rather than one (the account menu, the notification panel, and the mobile panel) and why the settings page has two (closed, and with its select opened). Each mounts through `src/test/render.tsx` and asks `unnamedControls(document.body)` — **the document, not the container**, because Radix portals menus, tooltips and dialogs onto `document.body`, and a control in a portal is exactly the one an eye-level check misses. Adding a surface is one `audit(<Page />)` call; a surface with a second state worth judging takes an `interact` callback.
- **The second question, and the eight rules it checks.** Having named a control, does it say what it is *doing*? `stateViolations(root)` in `src/test/a11y.ts` is the other half, run in the same pass so no surface is rendered twice: **(1) a group of options must have a name**, `role="group"` and `role="radiogroup"` both — which required teaching `accessibleName` that containers are author-named, since otherwise the group silently borrowed its chips' own labels as its name; **(2) a named group of options must state which one is chosen** (any of `aria-pressed` / `aria-checked` / `aria-selected` / `aria-current` on any member is enough — the first three always emit their value, `aria-current` is only correct on the chosen one); **(3) a control that owns a region must report a state for it**, and must not claim `aria-expanded` when the region is not in the page; **(4) and the region it names must exist**, unless the control reports itself collapsed — a reference to nothing is a defect whether or not the control is expanded, and the two names say which claim failed (`absent-region` for "I am open" over a region that is not there, `dangling-region` for an id nothing renders); **(5) and the names it points at must exist too** — the same reference defect one step further in, and the one nothing else can see, because a broken `aria-labelledby` does not leave a control nameless: the name computation falls through to `aria-label` and then to the element's own contents, so the first question is answered while the reference quietly does nothing; **(6) and a description must both exist *and* be attachable** — the reference check with a *worse* failure mode (a broken `aria-labelledby` at least falls through to the element's own contents, but `aria-describedby` is the only spelling for a hint, so a reference to an id nothing renders means the hint is simply never read and nothing on the page looks wrong to say so), and then the near-side check: the hint must be hung on something that can carry one, since a described bare `<div>` has the `generic` role, which does not support a description at all, so the target can exist in full and still reach nobody; and **(7) every id those three references resolve against must be unique** — a duplicate id is the one failure that breaks all three at once, since `getElementById` hands back the first claimant and every other element is silently unreachable, and it is the failure a hardcoded id produces the moment a component is mounted twice (which is why the pickers here generate theirs with `useId`). and **(8) a label's `for` (React's `htmlFor`) must resolve too** — it names a *field* the same way the rules above name regions and descriptions, so a `<label for>` whose id is not in the page is attached to nothing: the nameless field in its most plausible disguise, with the words rendered right beside the control they were never wired to. (The same loop asks a second question, reported as `unlabelable-target`: the id *did* resolve, and what it names is not something a label can attach to — a `<div>`, or a `role="textbox"` div, or a hidden field. A label wired to any of those is not a name either, and it is the failure a correct `for` hides. It is deliberately not enumerated as a ninth rule above, because it is the far side of the same walk of `label[for]`; what is still owed it is a mutation, and it has none yet.) Rules 6's second half, 7 and 8 are the three the last passes added; all are checked in the same `stateViolations` pass, so no surface is rendered again. Rule 3 is deliberately not specific about *which* attribute: the first version demanded `aria-expanded` and flagged Radix's four admin tabs, which correctly say `aria-selected`. The remaining drawn-only shape — a status that is only a colour — is **not** checkable from the DOM (a decorative bullet and a presence indicator are the same three spans), so it is prevented by construction in `StatusIndicator` instead, and the audit says so in its own doc comment rather than pretending to cover it.
- **The group rules were wrong about their own subject in three ways, and all three were closed together.** They looked for `role="group"` only, so a `radiogroup` — the one shape with a spec'd meaning behind "one of these is chosen", and what the theme and accent pickers are — was the one form the audit could not see; they counted options as `<button>`s, so a group of `role="radio"` spans or Radix's `menuitemradio`s read as *a group with no options* and passed **silently**, which is the worst way for a rule to be wrong; and even once a group was found, `aria-selected` was not among the attributes a choice could be stated with, so **Radix's real tablists looked silent while saying exactly the right thing on every trigger**. The third was found by the audit itself the first time it ran with the other two in, and it is the one worth keeping: `/search` and `/admin` both reported `[silent-choice]` — `a group of 6 options` and `a group of 4 options` — for tabs whose every trigger carries `aria-selected`, because the rule's own vocabulary was short an attribute. So the state half is asked of `[role="group"], [role="radiogroup"], [role="listbox"], [role="tablist"]`, their options are `button, [role="radio"], [role="menuitemradio"], [role="option"], [role="tab"]`, and the choice may be spelled `aria-pressed` / `aria-checked` / `aria-selected` / `aria-current`. **The name half is asked of every one of those containers except the `listbox`** — `tablist` joined the named set in a later pass, see the bullet below — and the listbox is the deliberate exception: it is Radix's `Select` popup, and the combobox trigger that owns it carries the name (the settings page's trigger is named through `htmlFor="visibility"`, and the popup is that control's face). Radix renders it unnamed, and asking it for a name would report the app for a decision its component library made. Measured rather than assumed: the app's only listbox is unnamed and reads as fine to both rules, which is exactly why the rule does not ask.
- **The two tablists are named now, and getting there needed a fix in the name computation itself.** `TabsList` carried no name on either page — and the rule could not have caught it, because `accessibleName` did not know that `tablist` is author-named, so the container **borrowed the tabs' own labels**: "All People Posts Groups Jobs Marketplace" read as a name and an unnamed tablist passed. That is the identical trap the marketplace's chip rows fell into, wearing the opposite mask (there a written label was ignored because a plain `div` takes no name; here there was no label and the contents supplied one). `tablist` is in `AUTHOR_NAMED_ROLES` now, the name half is asked of every choice container but the listbox, and the two real ones carry a name of their own — **`Result type`** (six tabs) and **`Admin sections`** (four). The older contract case that a tab may state itself with `aria-selected` also had to gain a name, so that it keeps settling one rule rather than two. **Confirmed live:** `/search?q=maya` renders `role="tablist" aria-label="Result type"` with exactly one `aria-selected="true"`, `/admin` renders `aria-label="Admin sections"`, and clicking a tab still moves the selection — all four panels are in the page, the selected tab's `aria-controls` matches the one that is not `hidden`, and the other three are hidden. Mutation: deleting the search page's `aria-label` fails **exactly 1** surface, `search, with a result`, with `[unnamed-group] a group of options has no name, so nothing says what is being chosen between` and the real `<div role="tablist">` echoed back. Reverted, `md5sum` verified.
- **Confirmed against a deliberately silent one of each, on the real components rather than on hand-made markup.** *The radiogroup:* deleting `aria-checked={selected}` from `ThemeChoiceGroup` fails **exactly the two surfaces that render it** (`settings` and `the nav, with the mobile panel opened`) with `[silent-choice] a group of 3 options says nothing about which one is chosen`, where the same mutation before the widening failed **nothing in the audit at all**; deleting the group's `aria-labelledby` fails the same two with `[unnamed-group]`. *The tablist:* suppressing `aria-selected` on Radix's tab triggers (`tabs.tsx` — the attribute Radix writes itself, cancelled with an explicit `undefined` after the spread) fails **exactly the two surfaces that render a tablist**, `search, with a result` (`a group of 6 options`) and `the admin dashboard` (`a group of 4`), each also reporting the tabs' own `[silent-region]` violations, since the same attribute is what says a tab owns its panel. *The listbox:* suppressing it on the select's options the same way fails **exactly one** — the new surface below — with `[silent-choice] a group of 3 options says nothing about which one is chosen` and the real `<div role="listbox">` echoed back. All reverted, `md5sum` verified. **Ten cases** were added to `a11y.test.ts` across the three widenings (a silent `radiogroup`, a `radiogroup` whose options are not buttons, a named-and-stated one, a nameless one, a menu's `menuitemradio` group, a silent `tablist` and a silent `listbox`, the stated version of each, and a named listbox whose options are still silent — which is what pins that a name is not an answer to the state question). The widened rule is **green across all 17 surfaces**, and that is itself the finding: every choice group the app renders names itself and says what is chosen — including the nav's theme menu, whose claim to satisfy rule (2) was, until this, only as good as the rule's blindness, since it is a `role="group"` of `menuitemradio`s, a shape the old rule skipped twice over.
- **The app's only listbox needed a surface of its own before it could be judged at all.** `the settings page, with the profile-visibility select opened` mounts the settings page and opens the select with a real key on `#visibility` — Radix opens it on a pointer **or** a key, and jsdom can drive the key and not the pointer, the same gap that makes the avatar menu's trigger a browser-only check with the difference that here the key path exists. The test **states that the listbox is in the document** before the audit judges, so it cannot pass by judging a page that has no listbox in it — the failure mode a popover-mounting test is most likely to have. `src/test/render.tsx` gained `press(element, key)` for it: focus, then a bubbling `keydown` inside `act`, so the component's own handler is what runs.
- **The reference rule needed one exemption, and the exemption is the whole design.** A control that reports itself **collapsed** is allowed to point at a region that is not in the page, because nothing mounts a closed popover's region — that is what every disclosure here does and what Radix's menus, selects and tooltips do. So the rule is keyed on `aria-expanded="false"` rather than on absence alone, and it is the control's own report that explains the absence; the state half of rule 3 is what makes that report mandatory in the first place. The other half of the judgement is that a *hidden* region counts as existing: Radix renders every tab panel and hides the ones that are not on, so an unselected tab's reference resolves, and only "I am expanded" has to be true of something on screen.
- **It found nothing in the app, and that is a result rather than a non-event.** All 17 surfaces are green with the rule in, so no control here names a region that is not there — while a dozen or so `aria-controls` legitimately dangle in exactly the exempted way: the mobile menu button and the notification bell closed, the settings select shut, the account menu unopened. **Confirmed it bites:** rewriting the real `TabsTrigger`'s `aria-controls` to an id nothing renders fails **exactly the two surfaces with a tablist** — `search, with a result` (6 violations, one per tab) and `the admin dashboard` (4) — each reading `[dangling-region] names #missing-panel, which is not in the page`. Reverted, `md5sum` verified. Two contract cases came with it: a tab naming a region nothing renders, and a tab whose panel is in the page but `hidden` — Radix's real markup, which must stay silent or the rule would report the app for how tabs work. Before this, a panel deleted or renamed out from under its tab was invisible to the whole suite.
- **The name half of the same idea found a real defect, on the profile page.** `dangling-label` asks whether every `aria-labelledby` resolves, and there the answer was **no, six times over**: the page's six sections were Radix `TabsContent`s under a `Tabs` that rendered **no `TabsList`** — the switcher is the header's own row of buttons and the stat tiles, both outside that tree — so Radix named every panel after a trigger that was never rendered. Measured live before the fix: six `role="tabpanel"`s, **zero** `role="tab"`s, and every `aria-labelledby` pointing at an id that does not exist, so what a reader got was six sections announced as tab panels with no name and no tabs to move between. **The fix is in the page rather than in the rule**: with no tablist there are no panels — these are sections, and the active one is simply rendered (`{activeTab === "posts" && …}`), which also stops six heavy sections being mounted and `hidden` at once. The `Tabs`/`TabsContent` import is gone from that file. Verified live after: zero tabpanels, zero unresolved `aria-labelledby` anywhere on the page, switching still works (Posts → About unmounts the composer and shows Intro/Details), no console errors, and a screenshot is unchanged — the wrapper's own classes (`mt-2`, the focus ring, `p-0 m-0`) went with the wrapper, and each section's own padding is what was visible anyway. **Confirmed it bites:** renaming the settings page's accent heading to `accent-label-renamed` and leaving `aria-labelledby="accent-label"` behind fails **exactly 1** surface — `settings` — with `[dangling-label] points at #accent-label, which is not in the page`. Reverted, `md5sum` verified. Three contract cases came with it: a control whose label points at nothing *while still being named* (the case that shows why the name audit cannot catch this one — `unnamedControls` is empty and the reference is broken), a reference naming one real element and one that is gone (only the missing id is reported, by name), and a resolving reference beside an **empty** one, which must stay silent or the rule would be inventing a second question.
- **The description half came next, and it is the label rule with worse consequences.** `dangling-description` scans every `[aria-describedby]` and asks whether each id it names exists — the same existence test and the same `isRendered` skip as `dangling-label`, for the same reason: a description that is `hidden` is still handed to a reader when it is named directly. What differs is what breaks. A label that does not resolve *falls through* to `aria-label` and the element's own contents, so the control still says something; `aria-describedby` is the only way to give a hint at all, so a reference to an id nothing renders means the hint is **never read** — and because the field renders, is named and looks complete, nothing on the page suggests anything is missing. The app renders no `aria-describedby` today (`grep` finds zero), so the rule is green across all 17 surfaces on arrival — which is the expected result rather than a non-event: it means nothing here points a hint at a description that is not there. **Confirmed it bites on a real component:** giving `ThemeChoiceGroup`'s radiogroup an `aria-describedby="theme-hint-gone"` — a hint pointing at a description nobody renders — fails **exactly the two surfaces that render it** (`settings` and `the nav, with the mobile panel opened`), each with `[dangling-description] describes itself with #theme-hint-gone, which is not in the page`, while the name audit stays satisfied (the group is still named; only the reference is broken). Reverted, `md5sum` verified. Four contract cases came with it: a hint pointing at nothing *on a control that is otherwise fine* (the silent-goes-unread case, asserting `unnamedControls` is empty **and** one violation), a reference naming one real element and one gone (only `#gone` reported), a resolving reference beside an **empty** one (which must stay silent), and a **`hidden`** description that must still count as rendered. **And then the target check was not the whole rule, so a second half was added: the hint must be hung on something that can carry one.** `misplaced-description` reports `aria-describedby` on an element that is neither a control nor anything with a role of its own — a bare `<div>`/`<span>`, whose `generic` role does not support a description at all, so the attribute is written, the target can be there in full, and no reader is ever given it. It is reported *before* the target question and on its own (`continue`): a hint no reader can receive is the root cause, and where it points does not arise. The rule deliberately stops at **a control *or* anything with a role** rather than demanding a control, because a described `region`, `radiogroup` or `group` is correct ARIA and flagging it would be the audit objecting to a decision the standard endorses — the same reasoning that exempts the `listbox` from the name half. **Confirmed it bites on a real component, and in isolation:** giving `ThemeChoiceGroup`'s role-less wrapper `<div>` an `aria-describedby={labelId}` that points at the group's *existing* heading fails **exactly the two surfaces that render it** (`settings` and `the nav, with the mobile panel opened`) with `[misplaced-description] carries a hint, but is not a control and has no role that supports a description, so no reader is ever given it` — and **no `dangling-description`**, because the target exists, which is what proves the two halves are separate. Reverted, `md5sum` verified. Four more contract cases came with it: a hint on a role-less wrapper *whose target exists* (isolating the misplacement), the same wrapper *also* pointing at nothing (one violation, the root cause, not two), a hint on a `role="region"` container (correct ARIA, silent), and a hint on a control (where it belongs).
- **The references all resolve against ids, so the ids themselves are checked too.** `duplicate-id` is the substrate rule those three reference rules sit on: an `id` is a promise a document makes **once**, and two elements sharing one make every `getElementById` — and therefore every `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby` and `aria-controls` that targets it — ambiguous, with the parser handing back the first claimant and the other element silently unreachable. It is the one failure that breaks all three reference rules *at once*, which is why it is a `stateViolations` rule rather than a separate pass. Two deliberate differences from the rules above: it is reported **once per duplicated id, not once per element** (named, so a failure points at the id; a count in the message says how many claim it), and it is **not filtered by `isRendered`** — a hidden duplicate still answers `getElementById`, so it breaks a reference exactly as well as a visible one. An empty `id` is skipped, because nothing resolves to it and two of them make nothing ambiguous. The app's ids are all static-and-unique-per-page (Radix generates its own; the pickers use `useId`), so the rule is **green across all 17 surfaces** on arrival. **Confirmed it bites, and in isolation:** renaming the settings page's bio textarea `id="bio"` to `id="display-name"` — a copy-paste collision with the display-name input above it — fails **exactly the two surfaces that render that page** (`settings` and `the settings page, with the profile-visibility select opened`) with `[duplicate-id] "display-name" is used by 2 elements, so every reference to it is ambiguous`, and **no `dangling-label` and no nameless control** (the textarea borrows the display-name label's text, so it is still named). Reverted, `md5sum` verified. Four contract cases came with it: two elements sharing one id, one id claimed by three (the count), a `hidden` duplicate (still reported), and distinct ids beside two empty ones (silent).
- **And the labels' own `for`, which is what decides whether a field has a label at all.** `dangling-field` scans `label[for]` and asks whether the id it names is in the page — the same existence test as every reference rule above. It is the field-level twin of the name audit's oldest case (`<label>Color</label><input type="color">`, a label rendered *beside* a control): the words are right there and look attached, but `for` points at an id nothing renders, so the label is wired to nothing. Reported even when the label **wraps** its control and so still names it, for the same reason `dangling-label` fires on a control that still announces something — the reference is what quietly stopped working. Existence is the whole test: a pointing at a `hidden` field counts. The app's 20 `htmlFor`s all resolve, so the rule is green on arrival. **Confirmed it bites:** renaming the settings page's `<Label htmlFor="visibility">` to `htmlFor="visibility-gone"` fails **exactly 1** surface — `settings` — with `[dangling-field] names #visibility-gone, which is not in the page, so the field it labels has no label`, and **no nameless control**: the Radix `SelectTrigger` is a `combobox` that still takes its name from its content ("Everyone on LinkMe+"), so only the reference broke, which is the isolation this rule wants. Reverted, `md5sum` verified. Five contract cases came with it (missing target, resolving target, empty `for` beside a wrapping label, a hidden target, and a wrapping label with a broken `for`).
- **The one surface the `for` mutation *did not* fail is worth stating, because the reason is a real behaviour rather than a gap.** `the settings page, with the profile-visibility select opened` renders the same broken label and stays green: Radix's `Select` is **modal**, so while it is open it sets `aria-hidden="true"` on the rest of the page (measured in that surface: the label's ancestor `div` is hidden, and 3 of `document.body`'s children carry the attribute), which means `isRendered(label)` is false and the rule correctly leaves it alone — the same reason no rule reports the controls behind an open dialog. So the expected failure count is **1**, and the second surface is green for a reason, not by accident.
- **What the state rules found on their first run:** the notification panel's **`Mark all as read`** and **`Close notifications`** buttons, both icon-only and both nameless — invisible to every earlier audit because the panel is only mounted while open. They are `IconButton`s now, and the surface that opens the bell is what keeps them named. Two tests also hold the line the state rules cannot: `the app's disclosures` asserts the bell's and the menu button's own `aria-expanded`/`aria-controls` directly, since a disclosure rewritten to own nothing at all has no `aria-controls` for a rule to find.
- **`src/test/a11y.test.ts`** (60 tests) is the contract test for the helper, written against hand-made markup so each case settles one rule: what has *no* name (an icon-only button, a `Label` sitting **beside** an unattached input — the trap the cover studio fell in, an empty `menuitemradio`), what *has* one (visible text, `sr-only` text, `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby` pointing elsewhere, an image's `alt` inside the control, an attached label either by `for=` or by wrapping, a placeholder, `title`), and what is not there to be named (`hidden`, `aria-hidden`, a hidden input). Its state cases are the other half, one rule at a time: a silent choice in a `group`, in a `radiogroup`, in a `tablist` and in a `listbox` (with the stated version of each), a choice group with no name, a `radiogroup` whose options are not buttons, a menu's `menuitemradio` group, a `tablist` that states neither half (which asserts both rules land, in order), a listbox that is deliberately unnamed because the combobox that owns it carries the name, a named listbox whose options are still silent, a control that owns a region and reports nothing, one that claims a region that is not in the page, one that names a region nothing renders (and the same reference resolving to a panel that is merely `hidden`, which must stay silent), a control whose `aria-labelledby` points at nothing while its own text still names it, a reference naming one real element and one gone, a resolving label beside an empty one, a hint pointing at a description nothing renders (on a control that is otherwise fine), a description reference naming one real element and one gone, a resolving description beside an empty one, a `hidden` description that must still count as rendered, a hint hung on a role-less wrapper (reported as misplaced while its target exists, and reported once — as the root cause — when the target is missing too), a hint on a container that carries a role of its own (correct ARIA, so silent), a hint on a control (where it belongs), two elements sharing one id (reported once, by name), one id claimed by three elements (the message counts them), a duplicated id that is `hidden` (which must still be reported, since `isRendered` is deliberately *not* applied to this rule), ids that are distinct and ids that are empty (which must stay silent), a label whose `for` names a field that is not there (reported by name), a label whose `for` resolves, a label with an empty `for` beside a wrapping one (both silent), a label pointing at a *hidden* field (still a field), a label that wraps its control but still carries a broken `for` (reported anyway), and a tab that correctly says `aria-selected` instead. Without it a green audit would mean only "the helper found nothing", which is not the same claim as "there is nothing to find".
- **The environment is a stub in setup, never in subject.** `fetch` answers the endpoints with canned payloads so the *populated* states are what get audited, and the modules that reach for a session are replaced (`next/navigation`, `@/components/auth-provider`, `@/lib/auth-client`, the Supabase browser client, the notifications provider). What is asserted is only what the components themselves render. **One trap worth keeping in mind:** every mocked value is created once and handed back unchanged, because a mock that builds a fresh object per call hands a component a new `user` on every render and an effect keyed on `[user]` never settles — the first version did that and the communities page hung until the test timed out. That is a real class of bug the app could have too (a provider that does not memoise the value it puts in context).
- **Two jsdom gaps, stated rather than hidden.** No CSS is computed, so `isRendered` reads `display:none` off the class list: a bare `hidden` with no breakpoint that brings it back counts as unrendered (`hidden md:flex` is audited; the composer's `className="hidden"` file input is not). And `src/test/setup.ts` now shims the browser globals a mounted page asks for, all behind a `typeof window !== "undefined"` guard so the node tests can never be handed them — `IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT`, `ResizeObserver` (jsdom has none, and Radix measures a tooltip trigger with one), `Element.prototype.scrollIntoView` and `window.matchMedia` (jsdom lays nothing out, and the messages page scrolls its list and the cover studio honours reduced motion), and `HTMLCanvasElement.prototype.getContext` pinned to `null` so jsdom's "Not implemented" log stops polluting the one output that is read closely.
- **What it found, on its first run — five unnamed controls.** The listing card's **save** button (`aria-label={liked ? "Remove from saved" : "Save listing"}` now) and the messages page's **send** button in the conversation header, which was icon-only *and* had no handler at all — a dead control that was also nameless, so it is gone rather than named, naming having only made it look functional. The composer's own Send took `aria-label={`Send message to ${selectedConversation.name}`}`. And **three cover-studio fields had labels that named nothing**: the background hex colour, the subtitle and the duration. In each case the `Label` was rendered *beside* the input; a label names a control only through `htmlFor`/`id` or by wrapping it, so what looked labelled was unnamed. All three are associated now (`cover-background-color`, `cover-subtitle`, `cover-duration`) — which is the trap `a11y.test.ts` names in `a field whose label sits beside it but is not attached`. **The fourth `Label` on that page, `Profile photo (required)`, is left as it is and is not a defect:** it sits above a styled control (an `<img>` preview and a `Change` button that carries its own text), and whatever file input it belongs to is hidden, so nothing reachable is unnamed.
- **The audit was then checked against Chromium's own accessibility tree** — an independent judge, since a helper that agrees with itself proves nothing. On `/messages` the nameless `button` is absent from Chromium's tree (`textbox "Search conversations…"` and no bare button); on `/marketplace`, clicking a card's save control flips exactly that one to `Remove from saved` while its sibling still reads `Save listing`. **And on `/feed` the whole page agrees, control for control**: the nav's `link "Search"`, `button "Notifications"`, the account menu, and every post card's controls all carry names — including the video's own controls, which the audit does not own. **One near-miss worth keeping:** the account menu trigger has no `aria-label` at all; its name is the avatar's `alt`, which Chromium reports as `button "Theo Wu"`. A hand-rolled name check that skips `img alt` (or `sr-only` text) reports it as a defect and is wrong — which is exactly why the audit implements the content rules rather than reading attributes, and why `a11y.test.ts` pins `an image's alt text inside the control` as *named*.
- **It bites when it should.** With the audit in place, reintroducing a nameless control in the nav fails the nav surface; the unnamed-field and unnamed-menu-item contracts fail in `a11y.test.ts`. Two mutations were run against the *fixed* code to confirm the audit guards its own repairs: putting the three cover-studio labels back to unattached form fails the cover-studio surface, and removing the listing card's `aria-label` fails the marketplace surface. One honest note on the fix that **isn't** guarded: the cover studio's *textarea* is named by its placeholder, so a mutation removing its `Label` does not fail — the spec accepts a placeholder as a name, which is why the audit does too.
- **What it cannot reach.** Hover cannot be driven in jsdom, so a control that is only named while hovered is out of scope (nothing here is). The audit covers the surfaces it mounts; a page that needs a fetch mock to render and isn't in the list is unaudited, and adding it is one call. And it judges *names*, not *roles* or order — the audience picker's radio semantics, the `aria-current` markers and the `aria-pressed` chips are pinned by their own tests, not here.

## The media module: what was deleted and why

- `src/components/ui/media.tsx` exported four things and only one was used. **Deleted: `MediaGallery`, `MediaVideo`, `MediaAvatar`** — there were no references to any of them anywhere in the repo, and `MediaGallery` was not "unwired but wanted": **this app has no multi-media UI for it to serve.** A post has one image (`post-card.tsx` takes `image` + `mediaType`), the composer attaches one image with its own named remove button, and the profile cover shows one. `MediaVideo` was reachable only from `MediaGallery`, and `MediaAvatar` duplicated the Radix `ui/avatar.tsx` that the whole app actually uses. Deleting the grid is also how its unnamed `×` remove button was dealt with — a component with no callers does not need its button named, it needs to not be there to be reached for later.
- **What is left is `MediaImage`, and it was carrying two bugs.** One: its default fallback was `/images/placeholder.png`, and **this project serves no static assets at all — there is no `public/` directory** — so a cover that failed to load swapped itself for a second image that also failed, and made a second request to find that out. The fallback is now opt-in with no default: with none, the browser shows the `alt`, which at least says what is missing. Two: it copied `src` into state on mount (`useState(src)`), so a caller that changed the image kept seeing the old one. It now records *which source failed* and derives the rest, which fixes the swap and keeps the anti-loop guard (the fallback failing must not start a cycle).
- **The stale-source bug was reachable, not theoretical.** `cover-edit-dialog.tsx` saves a `coverUrl` and `profile/page.tsx` swaps that prop on the same component instance (`coverConfig` goes back to `null`), so replacing one photo cover with another left the old picture on screen until a reload. **It was fixed without a live reproduction on purpose**: exercising it by hand means changing the viewer's real cover, which uploads to R2 and cannot be undone cleanly. The reachability is from the code path; the behaviour is pinned by a test that re-renders with a new `src`.
- **Nothing currently exercises `MediaImage` in the browser**: no seeded member has a photo cover, so every profile renders the default gradient. What was verified live is that the pages that could use it still render — gradient covers, avatars and post images all load, no console errors. Its success path is deliberately unchanged (`<img src alt className loading onError>`), so what the tests cover is the two changed behaviours.

## Feed/notification dev behaviours

- In development the initial-load effect re-runs when Vite/react-refresh remounts the page. That refetch pulls page 1, which injects any held post and dismisses the "N new posts" pill without a click. This is a dev-server/HMR artifact, not the subscription: in a built app the effect only re-runs on an auth change or a real navigation.

## Timestamp columns and JS dates

- `posts.created_at` (and its siblings) are `timestamp without time zone` holding UTC wall-clock values. postgres.js writes a `Date` parameter as UTC but reads that column back as *local* time, so a `Date` round-trip shifts by the machine's UTC offset. Do not compare a JS `Date` against these columns: select the key as text (`to_char(created_at, 'YYYY-MM-DD"T"HH24:MI:SS.US')`) and cast it back with `::timestamp`, as the posts API cursor does in `src/lib/cursor-pagination.ts`.
- `posts` has no index on `created_at`; deep feed paging sorts the table. Add a `(created_at DESC, id DESC)` index if the feed grows.
- `notifications` has an index on `(user_id, created_at desc)` from migration `0004`; the inbox read and the unread count both use it.

## Tests

- `npm test` runs vitest — **482 tests in 49 files** as this is written, and treat the number as a property of the checkout at that moment rather than of the last edit: it moved twice during the Page passes because other work landed in the same tree (see the note in the `followers`-subject section). The numbers this runbook quotes per pass are each pass's own contribution; the per-pass `npx tsc --noEmit` counts below (51, 52, 54) are historical readings, and the **current** baseline is **0 errors** after the `@types/node` pass — see **Zero type errors, and a real lint gate** at the end of this file. Both numbers are what to check a change against. It could not start at all until this was fixed: `vitest.config.ts` asked for `environment: "miniflare"`, which comes from `vitest-environment-miniflare` — not a dependency — so vitest exited with `MISSING DEPENDENCY` before collecting anything. It now uses `environment: "node"`; switch it back if that package or `@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers` is added.
- **The config sets `esbuild: { jsx: "automatic" }`** and it is load-bearing. `tsconfig.json` keeps `jsx: "preserve"` for Next, so without this every component test fails with `React is not defined` before it asserts anything. `@vitejs/plugin-react` is installed but did *not* fix it here; the esbuild option did.
- `src/test/setup.ts` is the setup file: it sets fake `process.env` values (`DATABASE_URL`, `AUTH_SECRET`, the R2 pair) and, behind a `typeof window !== "undefined"` guard, the browser globals a mounted page needs — see the jsdom bullet below. `npm run typecheck` still reports `src/test/setup.ts` and `vitest.config.ts` themselves — they are real program files, not fixtures — but both now typecheck cleanly, because `@types/node` supplies the `process`/`Buffer`/`fs` globals they reach for; see **Zero type errors, and a real lint gate** at the end of this file for how the count went from **51 to 0**. **`npm run lint` runs ESLint now**: it is `eslint .` rather than `next lint`, backed by `eslint`, `eslint-config-next` and `eslint.config.mjs` (Next's eslintrc-style shareable configs bridged through `FlatCompat`), and it reports **0 errors and 0 warnings** (the last backlog of warnings was cleared in a later pass — see **Zero type errors, and a real lint gate** at the end of this file).
