- **`npm run mutation:coverage` is a gate now rather than only a test file: it runs the load-bearingness check under its isolating config, reads Vitest's report, and answers the same `--json` contract `mutation-guards.mjs` answers — `gate`, `checked`, `survivors` — so a coverage gate that stopped being load-bearing is reported the way a route guard that survived its sweep is, and no consumer needs to know which check produced it.** What was missing above was not the check but the thing that makes it fail a *build*: `.freebuff/mutation-coverage.mjs` spawns `vitest run --config vitest.mutation.config.ts --reporter=json --outputFile=…`, maps that report back, and closes with the sweep's exit codes — 0 when every gate was caught, 1 when a case survived its weakening, 2 when the run could not be read at all (no report, or Vitest could not be spawned), which still writes the report with the reason in the survivor's `detail`, because a broken run is a survivor and never silence. Every case that did not pass is a survivor, grouped by what it means: `survived` — the gate's own test file ran, asserted, and did not notice the weakening, which is the finding this exists for — and `broken` — a drifted anchor, a mapped test file that would not load, or a case that was skipped, all of which mean the gate is *unchecked*, which is how a gate disappears without anyone lowering a number. `checked` counts the cases that ran, so a run that quietly stopped collecting reads as a survivor rather than as a clean pass. `MUTATION_COVERAGE_VITEST` points the launcher at another Vitest entry, which is how the new `src/test/mutation-coverage.test.ts` (**6 tests**) drives the mapping against a stub instead of paying for five nested runs: the passing case pins the flags the isolation depends on, one test proves a `survived` survivor and a `broken` one are told apart (and that a file which would not load is one of them), and three prove a skipped case, an empty run and a crash are each a survivor rather than a pass. In `.freebuff/ci.mjs` it is the new stage 6, `mutation-coverage`, with the guard sweep as stage 7: the two are the pair that edits the working tree — one file at a time, each restored as its check ends — so they run last and nothing else may touch the tree in that window; the stage's `inputs` are the coverage scripts, the check, the test files the mutations must fail and both configs, and `vitest.mutation.config.ts` joined `GLOBAL_FORCE` so a change to it turns the change-based skip off entirely. The nightly job already runs the whole gate (`npm run --silent ci -- --json --skip=preflight`), so the new stage is in the nightly by construction and `nightly-report.mjs` publishes it unchanged — the summary table row, the per-survivor bullets, and the `::error file=…` annotations. `ci.yml` also runs `npm run mutation:coverage` as an ordinary step in the test job, because editing a gate script or one of its tests is exactly what moves a pin and that edit arrives in a pull request; the five single-file Vitest runs cost **25s**, against the minutes-long route sweep the nightly owns alone. Verified by making the wiring fail on purpose: replacing the floor mutation's `<=` with a *semantically neutral* rewrite (`if ((pct < threshold))`) — a real source change that weakens nothing — made the floor case survive, and both halves said so (`npm run mutation:coverage` → `[1/5] SURVIVED …`, `SURVIVED WEAKENING (1)`, `1 survivor(s): 1 gate(s) no longer load-bearing`, exit 1; `node .freebuff/ci.mjs --only=mutation-coverage` → `FAIL  coverage gate mutation — 5 checked, 1 survivor(s)`, a `SURVIVED WEAKENING` detail, and an `annotations` entry naming `src/test/coverage-mutation.test.ts`, exit 1); reverted, `npm run mutation:coverage` is 5/5 again, `src/test/ci-runner.test.ts` is **82 passed / 1 skipped** with the new stage's four tests (pass, survived-versus-broken, a crash, and the real launcher read through the runner against a stub Vitest) plus a `--changed-only` case proving a `.freebuff/coverage-floor.mjs` change keeps only `lint` and `mutation-coverage`; `npx tsc --noEmit` is 0, `npm run lint:ci` is clean, and every touched file is LF.

- **A killed `mutation:coverage` can no longer leave a gate script weakened: the check holds a lock while a script is mutated and the launcher restores from it before it runs — the crash safety the guard sweep has had since an interrupted sweep left a route fail-open.** A `finally` only runs if the process gets to run it, and a SIGKILL, a closed terminal or a power cut runs no handler at all; a weakened gate left on disk is the one outcome worse than the check it was mutating (`<=` in `coverage-floor.mjs` refuses a file sitting exactly on its floor, an unanchored glob in `coverage-scopes.mjs` hands a threshold files it was never meant to hold). The lock's **file name and shape are owned by a new module, `.freebuff/mutation-coverage-lock.mjs`**, which the check imports for `writeLock`/`clearLock` and the launcher imports for `recoverInterruptedRun` — the same arrangement that keeps `.freebuff/collect-budget-soft.mjs` and its sidecar from drifting, and it is separate rather than the launcher's own exports for a reason the run found the hard way: the check first imported the launcher, whose top-level CLI code then ran *inside the vitest worker* and exited it (`the check file failed to load — process.exit unexpectedly called with "1"`, the launcher's `broken` survivor classification catching it exactly as designed). The lock is written atomically (`tmp` + rename) before the script is overwritten, carries `pid`, `startedAt` and the script's `path`, `kind`, `where`, `original` and both hashes, and is cleared once the script is back. Recovery has the sweep's three cases and no more: a script still matching the mutation is restored from the lock's copy, one already whole just has its lock cleared, and one matching neither was edited by someone else in the window and is left alone with the lock in place, because the lock's copy is older than that edit. A lock whose `pid` is still running means another run holds the tree, so the launcher refuses to start (`REFUSING TO START`, exit 3) rather than fighting it for the same file, and `--recover` is that recovery on its own, for putting a tree back without paying for the check. `src/test/mutation-coverage.test.ts` grew from **6 tests to 11** with the recovery, driven through the real launcher's `--recover` against a lock written by hand (a kill being the one thing a test cannot stage) — restore and clear the lock; clear a stale lock whose script is already whole; refuse to clobber a script edited since, keeping the lock; stand down with exit 3 while a live pid holds it; and one that proves recovery runs on the ordinary path too, a stubbed run healing a temp script on the way in and still reporting its own outcome. The lock names a temp file in those tests, because recovery keys on the path the lock carries, so no live `.freebuff/coverage-*.mjs` is ever at risk. Verified against real scripts by reconstructing exactly what a SIGKILL leaves — `coverage-floor.mjs` rewritten to `if (pct <= threshold)`, then `coverage-scopes.mjs` unanchored, each with a hand-written lock — where the next `npm run mutation:coverage` printed `RESTORED .freebuff/coverage-floor.mjs from an interrupted coverage mutation check (gate: src/test/coverage-floor.test.ts).` on entry, ran **5/5 caught**, and left each script **byte-identical to its original** (`cmp`), the lock cleared; and watching a live run shows the lock appearing mid-case with `kind=gate where=src/test/coverage-floor.test.ts` and both hashes, gone when the run ends. The stage's `inputs` gained `.freebuff/mutation-coverage*.mjs`, so a change to the lock module keeps its check (proven: `CI_CHANGED_FILES=.freebuff/mutation-coverage-lock.mjs` → `would run 2 stage(s): lint, mutation-coverage`). `src/test/ci-runner.test.ts` and `src/test/mutation-coverage.test.ts` together are **101 passed / 1 skipped**; `npm run lint:ci` is clean; the one `npx tsc --noEmit` error is not from this pass — another session's in-flight edit added `CI_CACHE_FILE` to the env literal in `ci-runner.test.ts`'s unreadable-diff test and left `delete env.CI_CHANGED_FILES` untypable (`error TS2339` at line 2052), which is left for them to fix; every file this pass touched is LF.

- **The two tree-editing checks now hold one lock, written by one module: `.freebuff/mutation-lock.mjs`.** The sweep had its own copy of the crash-safety machinery (atomic write, live-pid refusal, stale-lock recovery, temp cleanup) inline, and the coverage check had just grown a second copy of the same thing — the kind of duplication where a fix lands in one and not the other, and the whole point of both is that it must not be missed. The module owns the file and its shape, exports `LOCK_FILE`, `LOCK_PATH`, `writeLock({ check, path, kind, where, original, mutated })`, `clearLock()` and `recoverInterruptedRun()`, and hashes the two contents itself so a caller passes source rather than hashes; the sweep imports it for all four (its writeLock calls now read `writeLock({ check: "guard sweep", path: route, kind, where, original, mutated })`), and the check imports it for `writeLock`/`clearLock` with `check: "coverage mutation check"`. It is **one lock file for both — `.freebuff/.mutation-lock.json`, replacing `.mutation-sweep-lock.json` and the day-old `.mutation-coverage-lock.json` — because the lock means "this working tree is being edited right now", which is a property of the tree rather than of the check holding it.** That is not decoration: with the coverage check mid-case, `node .freebuff/mutation-guards.mjs --list` now prints `REFUSING TO START: another tree-editing check (coverage mutation check, pid 47516, started …) holds .freebuff/.mutation-lock.json.` and exits 3, where before the two checks would have rewritten different files at the same time. The lock also records `check`, so a recovery message can name whose run left it (`RESTORED src/app/api/admin/moderate/route.ts from an interrupted guard sweep (guard: src/app/api/admin/moderate/route.ts:29 …)`). One thing the unification forced: **the lock path had to become a test seam (`MUTATION_LOCK_FILE`)** — the two crash-safety suites now point the lock at a temp file of their own, and without that they clobbered each other, because they run in parallel workers and shared one file (three failures the first run: one suite's `afterEach` deleting the other's lock, one suite's live `pid` making the other refuse, one restore attributed to the wrong reader). The seam is also the safer arrangement for the repo: a test must never hold the lock a real run reads, which is exactly what both suites did before. Verified through the real scripts, not only the suites: a slice of the real sweep on the shared lock (`--file=admin --limit=2 --no-fail-open`) still catches both mutations and leaves no lock; reconstructing a killed sweep on a live route — `admin/moderate/route.ts` left `if (false)` with a hand-written lock — the next `--list` run printed `RESTORED …` on entry and left the route **byte-identical** (`cmp`), lock cleared; the coverage equivalent still heals the same way; and the two crash-safety suites together are **15 passed** (4 sweep + 11 check) in parallel. Full suite **133 files, 1644 passed / 1 skipped**, `npx tsc --noEmit` 0, `npm run lint:ci` clean, every touched file LF.
- **A weakened gate script that a killed run left behind is now visible on the run page, and the cache can no longer pretend it was checked.** The recovery itself existed a pass earlier; what was missing is that it was only ever said in the child's stderr, inside a stage that *passed* — the one case a CI run has nowhere to put. So `.freebuff/mutation-lock.mjs` now returns what it did (`{ action, path, check, kind, where, message }`) instead of only printing it, the launcher and the guard sweep carry it into their `--json` payload as `recovered`, and `.freebuff/ci.mjs` maps it through one `recoveryDetails()`/`recoveredNote()` pair shared by both mutation stages: the note rides the stage's own summary (`— 1 recovered lock`) and the event becomes a `WARN RECOVERED` detail *first* in the block, because it is the older event and the one a reader can act on. `nightly-report.mjs` publishes it as the summary-table row's note, its own `### Warnings` entry, and a `::warning file=…,title=<stage>::` annotation, since a warning on a stage that passed is neither a failure nor something a check mark can carry. `src/test/ci-runner.test.ts` and `src/test/nightly-report.test.ts` gained the cases for both halves of a recovery (one file put back, one somebody else had edited and the lock left for a human). Verified against a real kill: weakening `.freebuff/coverage-propose.mjs` (`cell.pct > cell.basePct` → `>=`) behind a hand-written lock, the stage printed `PASS  coverage gate mutation — 5 coverage gate(s) checked, no survivors — 1 recovered lock` with `WARN RECOVERED  .freebuff/coverage-propose.mjs  RESTORED … from an interrupted coverage mutation check (gate: src/test/coverage-propose.test.ts).`, the nightly report rendered the row and the `### Warnings` entry and emitted the `::warning file=.freebuff/coverage-propose.mjs,title=coverage gate mutation::` annotation, and the script came back byte-identical to its original (sha1) with the lock cleared. That run exposed a second thing: **the result cache could answer a tree-editing stage from a pass recorded against debris, leaving the weakened script and its lock on disk while reporting the gate checked — worse than the silence this pass set out to fix.** The key is taken before the stage runs, deliberately (a pass speaks for the inputs it started with), so a run that *heals* a kill records the debris key; and the check applies the same mutation every time, so the next identical kill hashes the same. Reproduced on real files: with the poisoned entry on record, re-seeding the same kill made `--explain-cache` say `reuse — inputs unchanged since a passing run` and the run print `REUSE coverage gate mutation — 5 coverage gate(s) checked, no survivors — 1 recovered lock (inputs unchanged since a passing run)` over a weakened `coverage-propose.mjs` and a live lock — a stale `1 recovered lock` claimed while the lock sat there. Fixed by marking both tree-editing stages `editsTree: true` (the guard sweep had the same exposure; it is the other thing that restores a file an interrupted run left mutated) and having `decideStage` always run them, with the reason in the explanation: `run — its run edits the tree, which a recorded pass cannot vouch for`. Re-run under the fix, the same kill runs, heals, counts a pass rather than a reuse, and clears its lock; two new `src/test/ci-runner.test.ts` cases pin it (a marker proves both stages run twice with a pass already on record, and the explanation reports a run with a matching entry), and both fail when the flag is deleted, so the guard is load-bearing rather than decorative. One drive-by in the same feature: the explanation's `newest input` was `Math.min` of the inputs' mtimes — the newest *label* on the oldest *file*, which hid a gate script it had just rewritten behind one untouched for hours (it read `6h ago` seconds after the write); now `Math.max`, and the same line reads `1m ago`. Verified: `src/test/ci-runner.test.ts` **108 passed / 1 skipped**, `src/test/mutation-coverage.test.ts` and `src/test/nightly-report.test.ts` green with it (135 passed together), `npm run mutation:coverage` **5/5 caught**, full suite **133 files, 1661 passed / 1 skipped**, `npx tsc --noEmit` 0, `npm run lint:ci` clean, every touched file LF, and no probe cache, report or lock left behind.
- **A killed run's lock is now healed by the run itself, before any stage measures the tree, so `--skip`, `--only` and `--changed-only` can no longer leave a weakened gate script or a fail-open route behind — and the reuse hole is gone for good.** The recovery existed but only ever ran inside a stage: the check that owns the lock heals it when *that check* runs, which is exactly what the run can decide not to do, and a `finally` in a killed process runs nothing at all. So `.freebuff/ci.mjs` now heals ahead of its stages — `recovery = existsSync(LOCK_PATH) ? recoverInterruptedRun({ mode: "report" }) : null`, before the loop that runs them — which also fixes a hole nobody had named: the mutation stages are *last*, so every stage that ran before the healer measured the weakened script (or the fail-open route) as the real thing. The heal is unconditional on selection, so it covers the four ways a stage does not run (excluded, unselected, fed by nothing that changed, stopped short by the failure budget) and the diagnostic exits still do not touch the tree. `recoverInterruptedRun` grew a `mode` because the two callers want different things from a lock it cannot deal with: a check is about to rewrite the file, so a live holder must stop it (`exit`, the default — 3 for a live pid, 2 for a restore that did not verify), while the runner only read the tree and wants the state described, so `report` answers `held` and `failed` as events and never exits mid-report. The recovery is attributed rather than merely announced: each tree-editing stage's `editsTree` now carries the `check` name its lock records, so the run knows which stage a lock belongs to, attaches the `WARN RECOVERED` detail to that stage's own row (and its summary's `— 1 recovered lock`) when that stage runs — the outcome the earlier pass delivered, now sourced from the run's single heal — and otherwise reports it in its own voice, `── interrupted run recovery (in place of coverage gate mutation) ──`, carries it in the `--json` payload as a top-level `recovered` array with the `mark` a report reads, and turns it into a `::warning file=…,title=…::` annotation. `nightly-report.mjs` lists it under the same **Warnings** heading as a stage's own warnings, named for the stage it stood in for, with its own note line — a healed tree is a warning on a green run, never a failure. The cases live in **`src/test/ci-runner-tree-editing.test.ts`** — nine of them, and the file is a finding rather than a preference. `ci-runner.test.ts` is the suite's longest, ~110 `spawnSync` calls deep, and adding runs of the real runner to it pushed its Vitest worker past the keepalive twice over: first `[vitest-worker]: Timeout calling "onTaskUpdate"` with **every test in it passing** and the command still exiting 1, then — with that first set moved out and two more cases left behind — a real `Test timed out in 5000ms` on a spawn that had simply queued too long behind the rest of the file. So every case this chain added to that file left it: the runner's file is back to **109 passed / 1 skipped**, the new file is **9 passed**, and each half was confirmed by filtering: the runner's file with our blocks removed exits 0, and with them moved out the whole suite ran green in its tests — **135 files, 1680 passed / 1 skipped** — where the run before the move had failed. The new file carries a `seedLock`/`seedKill` pair that writes a lock in the module's own shape against a temp file, and its `runCi` points `CI_CACHE_FILE` at a throwaway; `ci-runner.test.ts` also keeps every spawn off the project's own lock via a default `MUTATION_LOCK_FILE`, because a test must never hold — or heal — the lock a real run reads. Two of the nine are the cache policy this all rests on (a tree-editing stage is never answered from a recorded pass, and `--explain-cache` says why), which moved here from the runner's file for the same reason. The rest: `--skip` excludes the owner and the tree is still put back; `--changed-only` leaves it unchanged and the payload carries `recovered[0]` marked `WARN RECOVERED` with the annotation to match; the owning stage's row carries it without the run narrating it twice; a failure that stops the run short of the stage still heals; and a lock with a live pid is described (`WARN LOCK HELD`) with the file and the lock left exactly as they were — plus `src/test/nightly-report.test.ts` rendering the run-level entry. Two of the nine drive the whole chain rather than one end of it: the *real* runner writes the payload and the *real* `nightly-report.mjs` CLI renders it, so the `— 1 recovered lock` summary, the table row that repeats it, the `### Warnings` bullet, the note line and the `::warning` (and never a `::error`) are asserted against what the two scripts actually produce, instead of against a fixture kept in step by hand — once with the owning stage running, and once with it `--skip`ped, where the bullet has to read `(in place of coverage gate mutation, which did not run)` and the excluded disclaimer has to survive beside it. Every one of the nine is load-bearing: nulling the heal fails all five recovery cases, and nulling only the run-level report fails the four that need it while the stage-row case still passes; dropping the summary note fails the stage-row case and the run-page case that reads its row, dropping the payload's top-level `recovered` fails the payload case and the run-page case, and emptying the report's run-level rendering fails the run-page case and the renderer's — each seam broken on its own, which is how the two reporting paths were told apart from the two scripts that carry them. Verified against a real kill, not only stubs: `coverage-propose.mjs` weakened to `cell.pct >= cell.basePct` behind a hand-written lock, `node .freebuff/ci.mjs --only=lint,mutation-coverage --skip=mutation-coverage` printed `── interrupted run recovery (in place of coverage gate mutation) ──` and `WARN RECOVERED  .freebuff/coverage-propose.mjs  RESTORED …`, left the script **byte-identical** to its original (sha1 `f4d8b6a3cb2b`) with the lock cleared, and exited 0; the same kill under `--changed-only --only=mutation-coverage --json` produced `unchanged: ['mutation-coverage']`, `recovered[0].mark = WARN RECOVERED`, `recovered[0].stage = mutation-coverage`, one warning annotation, and a nightly summary reading `Lock(s) an interrupted run left behind, dealt with in place of a stage that did not run: 1 healed.` with the bullet `**WARN RECOVERED** (in place of coverage gate mutation, which did not run)` — and with the owner selected instead, the row keeps its `PASS  coverage gate mutation — 5 coverage gate(s) checked, no survivors — 1 recovered lock` while the real check still catches all five weakenings. The two diagnostic exits are deliberately outside this: `--dry-run` and `--explain-cache` promise to run nothing and to write nothing, so they report rather than heal, and a tree is put back by the next real run. `npx tsc --noEmit` 0, `npm run lint:ci` clean, `npm run mutation:coverage` 5/5, full suite **135 files, 1680 passed / 1 skipped** — green in its tests in *every* run, and the runner's own file green twice on its own (**109 passed / 1 skipped**, no stall). One thing this pass did **not** fix, and should be recorded rather than glossed: the suite's *exit code* is still a coin flip on this box. Vitest intermittently reports `[vitest-worker]: Timeout calling "onTaskUpdate"` with every test passing and the command exiting 1 — 5 of the ~10 full-suite runs today, both before and after this work, and on two runs of the *same* tree minutes apart, which makes it load rather than content: the workers run ~135 files of synchronous `spawnSync` work while other sessions use this machine. What this pass fixed is the half that was real — a `Test timed out in 5000ms` on a spawn queued behind `ci-runner.test.ts`'s other 110, which is why the cases moved out. Every touched file LF, runbook Contents up to date, and no probe cache, report or lock left behind.
- **The result cache now records the tree a pass *leaves* rather than only the one it was handed, and the stages it may answer for are stated in one place — and checked.** The key was always taken before a stage ran, deliberately: the mutation stages rewrite source as they work, so the inputs a pass speaks for are the ones the run started with. That is right for a check and wrong for a stage that edits what it reads, which is exactly the pair the recovery above made common; an entry keyed to the tree a pass started from is an entry a *later* run can be answered with over a tree that pass never produced. So each turn of the loop now reads the same globs twice — immediately before the pass and immediately after it — and the entry holds both: `hash`, the tree the pass left, is what a later run is compared against, and `startedHash` is the tree it started from, kept so a reader can see the two differ. The second reading needed a seam of its own: each file's digest is memoized for the life of the run (one read however many stages name it), so asking for a key again would hand back the pre-pass value — `rereadStageKey` drops the memo first, which is why the code can claim to record what a pass left at all. The key the *run decided* against is a third reading, taken up front and before any healing, and it is deliberately not what is recorded: a healing run therefore re-runs rather than reuses, the safe direction. `CACHE_VERSION` went 1 → 2, because the same field name means something else now — demonstrated on the real tree: with the v1 file on disk `--explain-cache` answered `run — no recorded pass for these inputs`, the next run wrote a v2 entry, and the run after that answered `reuse — inputs unchanged since a passing run` against the left-behind digest. For every stage the cache answers for the two readings are the same file contents, so the distinction is inert today and will not be tomorrow: it covers a check that restores a killed run's lock — which edits the very files its own key covers — and a stage that rewrites its inputs, a formatter say, which would otherwise be reused against a tree its pass never produced. **And the policy is now written down and machine-checked, not implied by three comments in three places:** the header's cache section says in one breath that the cache may answer for every stage that does not edit the working tree, that `editsTree` (whose value is the `check` name its lock carries) is the one place a stage says it may not be, and what the two recorded digests mean — and a test drives it: with both stages on record, `--explain-cache --json` answers `reuse` for `preflight` and `run — its run edits the tree, which a recorded pass cannot vouch for` for `mutation-coverage`, with `reused: ["preflight"]` in the payload. Three cases were added to `src/test/ci-runner-tree-editing.test.ts` (**12 passed**): the shape (both digests recorded, equal for a pass that changed nothing it reads), which field governs (a hand-edited entry with a junk `hash` re-runs while one with a junk `startedHash` still reuses, the marker proving the stage did not run), and the policy above. Each has teeth: making `startedHash` the governing field fails the governance case, dropping `startedHash` from the entry fails the shape case, and taking `editsTree` off the coverage stage fails 9 of the 12 — the whole recovery feature depends on that value, which is the point of the property. `npx tsc --noEmit` 0, `npm run lint:ci` clean, `src/test/ci-runner.test.ts` still 109 passed / 1 skipped, full suite **135 files, 1685 passed / 1 skipped** (exit code again the keepalive flake above, the fourth sighting today), every touched file LF, and no probe cache or lock left behind.
- **A drift alarm on the coverage gates, so a script weakened by hand — not by a run, and with no lock behind it — fails the build instead of passing every test it was written to pass.** The three things already watching the gates each answer a different question: `src/test/coverage-*.test.ts` pins what a script *does*, `npm run mutation:coverage` proves those tests still notice a weakening, and `.freebuff/mutation-lock.mjs` puts a script back when a killed run left it edited. None of them reads the script itself, which leaves a hole: a floor lowered a point, a threshold moved in `coverage-thresholds.mjs`, or a comparison loosened in a way that keeps the mutation check's anchor intact passes every test and leaves no lock, because no run ever *opened* one. The obvious check — `git diff HEAD` — is unavailable here (this checkout has no commits), so "committed" is recorded *content*: `.freebuff/gate-hashes.mjs` holds one **sha1** per gate script, generated by `npm run gates:pin` and compared by `npm run gates:drift`, the shape the runbook's pinned Contents and the collect-budget baselines already use. It pins **every `.freebuff/coverage-*.mjs`, all seven** — floor, floor-rules, headroom, report, propose, scopes and thresholds — and not only the five that run, because the *numbers* a gate enforces live in `coverage-thresholds.mjs` and `coverage-floor-rules.mjs`: pinning the scripts alone would leave the backstop free to drop from 85 to 60 with every script byte-identical. The watch rule (`dir`, `pattern`) and the algorithm are recorded *in* the manifest, so widening or narrowing the set is a reviewed line rather than a constant buried in the script. Three findings, all a failure: `changed` (a pinned script's hash is not the recorded one — the weakened gate this exists for), `unpinned` (a watched script nobody pinned, exactly as unguarded as a weakened one), and `gone` (a pinned script renamed or deleted, so a gate cannot disappear quietly); a **missing or malformed manifest is not drift but exit 2**, the alarm being unable to run at all, so "the check could not answer" can never read as "the gates are fine". `--write` re-pins, and repairs an unreadable manifest rather than refusing, because re-pinning is exactly what the alarm asks for; `renderManifest` is exported so the test can compare the committed file to it **byte for byte**, which catches a hand-edit that keeps the hashes but changes the watch rule. `GATE_HASHES_FILE` is the test seam. In `.freebuff/ci.mjs` it is the new **stage 6, `drift`**, placed *before* the two tree-editing stages: read-only and instant, so unlike them it is cacheable, and going first means a script weakened outside the lock — the one case the pre-stage heal cannot reach — is named as drift rather than surfacing second-hand as a mutation check that can no longer find its anchor. `CI_DRIFT_SCRIPT` is the stage seam, and every stage-list assertion after it moved one place in `ci-runner.test.ts` (`have:` lists, the `--dry-run` selections, the `--skip`-empties-the-run case, the `--max-failures` length and the dry-run JSON arrays); a `.freebuff/coverage-floor.mjs` change under `--changed-only` now keeps **three** stages (`lint, drift, mutation-coverage`) rather than two, which is the alarm doing its job. `ci.yml` runs `npm run gates:drift` as an ordinary step in the **Test** job — between the collect-budget summary and the load-bearing check, with the numbers-and-pin-versus-tests split written into both comments — so the same alarm fires on a pull request and not only at night. `src/test/gate-drift.test.ts` is **12 tests**: the pass, each finding and all three at once (ordered changed/unpinned/gone), both ways it cannot answer (no manifest, an unparseable one), the re-pin guidance in the human report, `--write` recording a tree and a check then agreeing, `--write` repairing an unreadable manifest, the manifest excluding *itself* from the pin even when the watch rule matches it, and — the ratchet — the committed manifest against the real scripts, byte-compared to `renderManifest`, with the payload's `changed`/`unpinned`/`gone` arrays pinned beside the rich `findings`. **Verified load-bearing, not merely present:** appending a line to `.freebuff/coverage-scopes.mjs` made the committed-manifest test fail (`expected 1 to be 0`) and the CLI report `CHANGED  .freebuff/coverage-scopes.mjs` with exit 1; restored, the file's sha1 is `07f3ec2575c1` again and `node .freebuff/gate-drift.mjs` prints `7 coverage gate script(s) pinned in .freebuff/gate-hashes.mjs, all match.` `npm run mutation:coverage` is **5/5 caught** with the new files in the tree, `npx tsc --noEmit` is 0, `npm run lint:ci` is clean, every touched file is LF, and no probe cache or lock is left behind.

Its exit codes are the contract that the steps' `continue-on-error: true` turns into a red step rather than a red job: `0` when the comment was posted *or* when there was nothing to post and the run page says so, `2` for an invocation it will not act on (an unknown flag, a flag with no value, a missing `--producer`, and `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`/`PR` unset — without which the API path would be a well-formed request to `repos//issues/`, exactly the opaque failure that step would then swallow), `1` for a `gh` that could not be started at all — the runner failing rather than an invocation it refused — and `gh`'s own status when it ran and refused; **every non-zero exit is announced on the run page as well as on stderr**, because a red `continue-on-error` step in an otherwise green job is one line in a log nobody opens, which left a reviewer reading the page with the job's presence and none of its outcome. A refusal and a miss are deliberately **two different notes**: a post `gh` rejected was answered with `was not written, or was empty` by the older, sillier version of the failure path, which is the wrong diagnosis and sends the reader looking for a file that was there all along. The failure note (`## <label> — ❌ the comment was not posted`) names the command it ran, `gh`'s exit status, and — the part a failure does not say by itself, and the one a reader has to act on — what the pull request shows *now*, which differs by verb: a failed `PATCH` leaves the comment the marker found **untouched**, so the previous run's summary stands there reading as this run's until somebody notices the date on it, while a failed `POST` leaves no comment at all. The one case `gh` says nothing about has its own wording, because there is no status to report: a `gh` that could not be started carries the reason the spawn gave (`which could not be started (spawn gh ENOENT)`) and exits **1**, which is deliberately not the `2` that means this refused to act — here it acted and could not. Two deliberate decisions the tests pin: the **marker is a flag, not something read out of the body** — a marker derived from the text would move with the text, so a reordered first line would post a second comment instead of updating the one already there; and a **failing listing falls back to `POST`** with a warning naming why, because a transient failure should cost a duplicate comment before it costs the comment itself — and since a second sticky comment was the one outcome left for a reviewer to meet with no explanation at all, the run page carries it too: `## <label> — ⚠️ the previous comment could not be looked up` names the listing that failed and its exit status in the same clause, says a new comment was posted rather than the one the marker would have found, and that a marked comment already on the pull request means the page now shows two of them — marked ⚠️ rather than ❌, because nothing was lost and nothing failed. It is written **after** the fallback post lands, and that ordering is the substance rather than an implementation detail: a lookup that failed *and* a post that failed leave no duplicate to explain, so that case gets the failure note alone — asserted, not assumed. - **A run that never posted a pull-request comment cannot finish green any more: each comment step's verdict is read back from its outcome and turned into a red job.** The three comment steps in `ci.yml` are `continue-on-error: true` on purpose — a comment that could not be posted must not take the drift check, the coverage-mutation check or the two artifact uploads with it — and the price of that choice is that a failed comment step left the job **green**: the run-page note the pass above added (`❌ nothing to post`, `❌ the comment was not posted`) made the loss visible on a page that a green check sends nobody to read, which is visibility without consequence. The mechanism is the poster's exit status, whose contract this pass narrowed to the one question the job can act on — *is the comment on the pull request?*: `0` when it is; `1` when it is not and the script knows why (nothing to post, or a `gh` that could not be started); `gh`'s own status when it ran and refused; `2` for an invocation it refused to act on at all, which is a broken workflow rather than an unposted comment. A missing body therefore moved from `0` to `1` — the note stays exactly as it was and the exit code is what makes it count — and that is not a detail: Actions has no other way to ask a step whether it posted, so the status *is* the interface the gate reads. **`.freebuff/comment-gate.mjs` is the new piece**, called once per job with the steps as `<label>=<outcome>` (`"Collect-budget summary comment=${{ steps.comment-summary.outcome }}"`), read from `steps.<id>.outcome` — what the step *did*, not `conclusion`, which is what `continue-on-error` let the job make of it. It holds the one judgment of the pass: `success` and `skipped` pass, `failure` and `cancelled` fail the job. That pair is the whole reason it takes a list rather than a count — `skipped` is a step that was never *owed* a comment (a fork's pull request, whose token cannot comment; a push with no pull request; a proposal the proposer did not earn — every one of them an `if:` decision), while `failure` is a comment this run did owe, so reading one as the other would either fail every fork or pass every loss. Three invocations are refused rather than assumed: no entries at all, an entry that is not `<label>=<outcome>`, and an outcome word Actions cannot produce — the last being the one that matters, because a word this did not recognize would otherwise read as a pass, the single failure mode a gate must not have. Failing writes a `## Comments — ❌ a comment this run owed was not posted` block on the run page naming each label and why, plus one `::error` annotation per step, so the checks list and the page agree; passing writes nothing at all. **The labels are the steps' own** — the `--label` each passed to the poster — so the page carries one name for a loss rather than two notes about it under two headings, and that tie is a test rather than a convention. Wiring: the three comment steps gained `id:`s, and each of the two jobs that has comment steps now *ends* with `Fail when a comment this run owed was not posted` (`if: always()`, because a step failing without `continue-on-error` — the drift check is one — otherwise takes the rest of the job with it and the verdict would never be reported; and no `continue-on-error` of its own, since a gate that fails quietly is worse than none). The apply job deliberately has none, and the asymmetry is pinned rather than left to be rediscovered: its reply step is the last thing that job does and is *not* `continue-on-error`, so a poster exiting non-zero — a blank reply, or a `gh` that refused — already fails the job, and there is nothing after it to protect. `src/test/comment-gate.test.ts` is new, **14 tests**, following `pr-comment.test.ts`'s shape (the real script, spawned, `GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` pointed at a file the test reads back): the pass side — all posted, posted beside skipped, nothing owed — asserts exit **0**, the count it reports and that the run page stays *empty*; the fail side — a failure, two failures named in the order they were given, a cancellation with wording of its own — asserts exit **1**, the annotation, the page block, and that the step which *did* post is not named in it; the five refusals cover no entries, no outcome, no label, an unknown word and a word in the wrong case; and the pure pieces (`parseEntries`, splitting at the *last* `=` so a label may contain one; `unposted`; `gateAnnouncement`) keep the verdict and the wording reachable without a process. `src/test/collect-budget.test.ts` grew **4** to **123**: every step that calls the poster has an `id` and a `--label`, asserted by name so a rename fails here; each is named in a gate under that same label; the number of gate entries equals the number of poster call sites, counted rather than listed so a fourth comment step cannot pass by being outside a list a test keeps by hand; every gate is `if: always()` with no `continue-on-error` and appears after the step it judges; and the apply job has no gate *and* no `continue-on-error` on its reply. Those four read the workflow through a step-block split on `      - ` at the steps' indentation — the one fact about the layout they rely on, and one a reformat would break loudly rather than by quietly letting a step out of the check, the workflows being pinned by content anyway. `src/test/pr-comment.test.ts` is **28**, its three skip cases and its blank-reply case now asserting the status the gate reads, with the contract stated in its header. **Verified live, not only in fixtures:** the `test` job's gate step was extracted from the YAML and run under `bash` with the two expressions substituted — `success`/`skipped` exits **0** and writes no run page at all, and `success`/`failure` exits **1** with the `::error` line, the log line, and a page block naming `Coverage-proposal comment` and nothing else; the gate itself was run over all four outcome words and all five refusals in the shell; both workflows parse as YAML with the new step last in each job; `npx tsc --noEmit` 0; `npm run lint` reports **0 errors and 0 warnings in the files this pass touched**, the 2 warnings it reports at all being `mutation-guards.mjs`, which a concurrent session is editing; and the full suite is **146 files, 1908 passed / 1 skipped** with no failures at all — the one failure it reported before the re-pin being the manifest-matches-the-tree case that the re-pin answers. The hashes this pass moved are `pr-comment.mjs` `fae3b1eb → 466d4c5a`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml` `9762ce91 → dc3a5e2b`, `.github/workflows/collect-apply.yml` `7abc0c61 → daf4b2bd` and the new `comment-gate.mjs` `20aad7df`, each recomputed from the file rather than read back. **The pin went 35 → 36 files, and a targeted `--write` could not have done it:** that command refuses a path the manifest does not pin, which is the right refusal — a gate nobody pinned is exactly what the alarm exists to find — so a new gate file needs the whole-tree `npm run gates:pin`, the one command that can also bless a file nobody reviewed. It was therefore run only once the drift check named *this pass's four files and nothing else* (`changed` + `unpinned` = `pr-comment.mjs`, `ci.yml`, `collect-apply.yml`, the new `comment-gate.mjs`): a concurrent session's `.freebuff/gate-drift.mjs` and `.freebuff/mutation-guards.mjs` had been drifting in and out of the tree all pass, and were left to that session rather than absorbed — it pinned them itself before this one ran, which is why the whole-tree pin was safe at that moment and would not have been half an hour earlier. The watch rule went `^(ci|gate-drift|redact|nightly-report|pr-comment)\.mjs$` → `^(ci|comment-gate|gate-drift|redact|nightly-report|pr-comment)\.mjs$`, with `RULES` in `src/test/gate-drift.test.ts` moving with it; `npm run gates:drift` read `36 gate file(s) … all match.` afterwards, and the manifest's own two lines were checked against hashes recomputed by hand rather than read back out of the file they were written into.

- **The comment body is now scrubbed before it is posted, so a summary or a proposal that names a secret cannot reach a pull request — and the redactor learned the two shapes a secret has when it is text rather than a file name.** Until this pass the poster published the body *unread*: `--body` handed `gh` the renderer's path and `gh` opened it itself (`-F body=@path`), so the one artifact of the four `.freebuff/redact.mjs` serves — and the one with the widest audience, a pull request rather than an artifact or a log — was the only one the vocabulary was never applied to. Both sources are read here now, scrubbed, and sent as the raw field `-f body=…`, which is not a preference but a consequence: `gh` doing the reading is exactly the read the scrub has to happen before, so the `-F` shape is now *unreachable* rather than merely unused, and the earlier `-f`-versus-`-F` distinction between text and a file collapses into the shape that can be redacted. A body that had to be changed says so: a `⚠️ the comment was redacted before posting` note on the run page with **how many** substitutions and never which — naming them would publish the thing just hidden — written after the post lands, like the duplicate note, plus a line on stderr for the log reader. The run's artifact keeps the body as the renderer wrote it, and the comment is the published form of it: the two are allowed to differ in exactly that direction, and a reader seeing `<redacted>` in a comment now has a page that explains it rather than a renderer that looks like it lost a name. **The vocabulary itself grew a second half, because this is the first writer here that publishes prose rather than paths.** A secret in text has no file name to match, so `redact.mjs` gained the two shapes it has there — the userinfo of a URL that carries credentials (`postgresql://builder:hunter2@db.internal:5432/app` → `postgresql://<redacted>@db.internal:5432/app`, keeping the scheme and host so a reader can see *what* was redacted) and a private key written out between its `BEGIN`/`END` markers, whole or pasted truncated. Values are applied before names, because the name pass reads its way through the same text and would otherwise leave a URL's host looking like a token it had matched; the near-misses are left exactly as they were (`ssh://git@github.com/org/repo`, `https://example.com:8080/guide`, `mailto:`, a bare `127.0.0.1:5432`), since a scrubber that hides ordinary text teaches its readers to distrust the marker. What is deliberately *not* there is a table of provider prefixes (`ghp_`, `sk-`, `AKIA…`): such a list is stale the day it is written and a reader who sees it starts trusting it for the keys it does not name, so the module keeps one certain rule rather than a hopeful table. `redactText` became `redact(text).text`, with `redact` returning `{ text, redactions }` — one implementation and two views, because the poster has to *say* how much it hid while the three publishing callers (`ci.mjs`, `gate-drift.mjs`, `nightly-report.mjs`) go on reading a string; both are idempotent, since nothing in the vocabulary matches the marker it writes. The other three writers gain the value rules for free, which is the point of one definition: a stage detail or a drift diff that quotes a connection string is now scrubbed in the same breath. `src/test/redact.test.ts` is new, **10 tests**, and it pins the *vocabulary* where it lives — until now the rules were only ever proved through their writers, so `ci-runner.test.ts`, `gate-drift.test.ts` and `nightly-report.test.ts` would all have gone on passing if one had been dropped: the name rules in prose and with a `:line` suffix, `redactInputs` collapsing a run of them to one marker, the URL and key shapes, the four near-misses above, the count across both vocabularies, `redactText === redact().text`, and idempotence. `src/test/pr-comment.test.ts` is **33** (+5): a `.env.production` in a slowest-collects table is posted as `<redacted>` with a note saying `1 substitution` and the name absent from the page as well; a credentials URL and a key are scrubbed with `2 substitutions`; the apply job's composed `--text` reply goes through the same scrub rather than being the one body that bypasses it; the marker survives the scrub, pinned because losing it would not fail — it would post a fresh comment on every push; and ordinary URLs get no note at all, since a page that announced a redaction that did not happen sends a reader looking for a loss that is not there. The re-pin was targeted for once, and named **both** files in one command — `--write a b` puts both in the set it is allowed to move, so neither counts as drift the pin did not cause: `pr-comment.mjs` `466d4c5a → b3e84e80` and `redact.mjs` `9d9cffcb → 850a1233`, each recomputed by hand, with `36 gate file(s) … all match.` afterwards.

- **The poster can now be rehearsed: `--dry-run` walks the whole path — parse, read, scrub, payload — and stops before the first `gh` call, printing the payload it would send and the run-page notes it would publish, and changing nothing.** The script is executable and heavily tested, but the only way to *see* what a comment step would post was to post it — the tests can reach the posting path only by spawning the script with a stub `gh`, so a person editing a step, or the poster itself, had no dry form at all. The flag is a switch rather than a valued option (`--dry-run=true` is a setting nothing reads, so it is **refused** like an unknown flag) and it changes three things, each deliberately: it exits **0**, because a rehearsal that posted nothing has lost nothing and must not read as a lost comment to `.freebuff/comment-gate.mjs`; it leaves `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` **byte-untouched**, because a run-page line is exactly the side effect a rehearsal exists to avoid; and it prints where a real run would write. **The notes take the same path either way.** A new `pageWriter(args)` returns `onRunPage` for a real run and a stdout printer for a dry run, and every note in `main` now goes through the `page` it returns — so the branch that decides *what* to say, and the wording it says it in, is one body of code with two sinks rather than two renderings kept in step by hand; the printed form is prefixed `pr-comment: dry run — the run page would say:` so a reader can tell a rehearsal's note from a real one. **What it honestly cannot rehearse is the verb, and it says so rather than guessing:** whether the comment would be created or updated is the marker lookup's answer, and the lookup *is* a `gh` call, so the rehearsal prints both commands (`-X POST repos/o/r/issues/7/comments`, `-X PATCH repos/o/r/issues/comments/<id>`) and stops — the alternative was to show `POST` alone and be wrong silently half the time. The empty-body branch is part of the path too, so a dry run of a missing body prints the ❌ note a real run would write **and** a line saying that run would exit 1 with the gate reading it as a lost comment, while itself exiting 0. `src/test/pr-comment.test.ts` grew **33 → 39** (six standing cases, plus the switch and the refusal inside two tables that already had cases): a body naming `.env.production` prints the payload with `<redacted>` and the ⚠️ note with `1 substitution`, with **no** `gh` invocation logged and an empty run page; the printed payload is compared against the argv the *real* posting hands `gh` (`sent[5]`), so the two cannot drift; both verbs are asserted with no listing made; a missing body prints the ❌ note and exits 0; and a rehearsal still **refuses** an invocation the real run refuses (`PR=""` → exit 2, no `gh`), because a dry run that accepted what the real run rejects would rehearse a different path. **Verified live, not only in fixtures:** the poster was run with `--dry-run` under `bash` against a body naming `.env.production` — it printed the payload line (`-f body=…`, with the body's `.env.production` collapsed to `<redacted>`) and the ⚠️ note, wrote no run page, and exited 0 — and the missing-body and `--dry-run=true` paths were run the same way. `npx tsc --noEmit` 0 and `npm run lint:ci` clean. The re-pin was targeted and named one file — `pr-comment.mjs` `b3e84e80 → e2c87d4d`, recomputed by hand — because a concurrent session's `.freebuff/mutation-guards.mjs` was drifting through the whole pass and was left to it; `npm run gates:drift` reported that one file and nothing else, which is why the pass's first full-suite run had a single red — `gate-drift.test.ts`'s committed-manifest case, naming exactly that file (it was rewritten again mid-run, so the run's own drift watch reported it) and nothing this pass touched — and the re-run, once that session had pinned it, was green: **148 files, 1937 passed / 1 skipped**, with `src/test/pr-comment.test.ts` at **39/39** alone. The known `[vitest-worker]: Timeout calling "onTaskUpdate"` unhandled error still appears with every test passing, which earlier passes here have recorded as this box's load rather than content.
- **The poster now files a record of what it redacted, beside the body it scrubbed and inside the artifact's reach, so the posted comment and the raw text can be compared substitution by substitution.** The redaction note on the run page deliberately counts and never names — the names are what it just hid — and that left the two ends of a redaction on separate surfaces with nothing joining them: the comment shows `<redacted>` and no value, the artifact holds the value and no marker, and a reviewer had to eyeball a diff to learn which span the two differ by, or whether a difference was a redaction at all. `redact()` now returns a **record** of each substitution beside its count — the rule that fired, the exact span it replaced and what it wrote there, in the order applied — and the poster writes it as JSON to `<body>.redactions.json` next to the body it read (`collect-gates.md` → `collect-gates.redactions.json`), which is exactly where the artifact upload already reaches: the `coverage-report` artifact gained the two records for the bodies it carries and `collect-budget-proposal` gained the one for its body, so the pair ships together or not at all. **It is deliberately not on the pull request or the run page.** The note there keeps counting and gains a single line — `` What was replaced is recorded in `<body>.redactions.json`, beside that body in the run's artifact `` — so the doctrine that the wide surfaces never name a secret stays intact while the reader is handed the map; the record carries the hidden text because the artifact beside it already does, and a record that hid the value from *both* places would make the comparison it exists for impossible. A `--text` reply (the apply job) gets no record, for the reason written into the poster: there is no body file in any artifact to compare it against, so a record there would put a secret in the checkout rather than in an artifact. **The vocabulary learned to name its rules**, because a record saying only “something was hidden here” would leave its reader guessing which rule fired: `url-credentials`, `private-key` and `private-key-header` are distinct on purpose (a whole key reads differently from a paste that lost its end), the token pass records `secret-name`, and `redactions` is now `substitutions.length` — one number, so the count and the record cannot disagree. The three other writers that only want the text (`ci.mjs`, `gate-drift.mjs`, `nightly-report.mjs`) are untouched, still reading `redactText` or `.text`. **The record's path is derived rather than flagged** — `recordPathFor(body)`, exported and unit-pinned, with an extensionless body keeping its whole name and a dot-file keeping its dot — so a step cannot point the record somewhere nothing uploads: `src/test/collect-budget.test.ts` ties each body in the workflow to its record through `artifactFor`, which finds the `upload-artifact` step naming the body and requires that same step to name the record. It is written **after the post lands**, with the other notes that describe a comment really there, and a write that fails does not fail the step — the comment is already on the pull request, so the failure goes to stderr and the note simply omits the path rather than promising a file that is not there. `*.redactions.json` joined `.gitignore`. The re-pin was targeted and named all three files in one command — `redact.mjs` `850a1233 → 57da8734`, `pr-comment.mjs` `e2c87d4d → bed41ab3` and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` `dc3a5e2b → e437070d`, each recomputed by hand.
- **The poster now also warns when a body carries a run that looks like a generated key and no rule claims it — and deliberately does not hide it.** The vocabulary is a set of rules that are *certain*, and that certainty is what makes collapsing a match safe; a body can also carry a shape that is merely *suspicious*, and the old answer there was a choice between two bad ones — redact it, and teach the reader that `<redacted>` sometimes means nothing (the thing the module's own near-miss list exists to prevent), or say nothing, and let a key-shaped run onto a pull request unremarked. The third answer is a warning, and it is the opposite of a redaction in every respect: `redact.mjs` gained `suspectTokens(text)`, which returns the runs it *thinks* may be keys and changes nothing, and the poster puts `## <label> — ⚠️ the body carries a run that may be a secret` on the run page with the runs **named** — because the comment is already carrying them, so a note that withheld them would hide the thing it is about, exactly where the redaction note withholds a value it *removed* and so names nothing. It is a ⚠️ and the exit code stays 0: a suspect is a question for a person, and the status still answers only whether the comment arrived. The scan runs on the text that would be **posted** rather than on the file, so a run a rule already took is gone and only the survivors are named; nothing is recorded (no substitution happened, so no `proposal.redactions.json`), the dry run prints the warning in full because a note is all a rehearsal can show, and a body with both something hidden and something uncertain gets **both** notes under one heading name. **The rule is four conditions and each exclusion is the design**, since a warning that fires on the shapes these reports are made of is a warning its reader learns to ignore: a run must be at least 24 characters (`SUSPECT_MIN_LENGTH`, below which an identifier and a key overlap), must carry **both cases and a digit** (so hex — git hashes, the drift alarm's sha1s, npm digests — plus UUIDs and all-lowercase blobs stay quiet; this is the one deliberate blind spot, a hex secret and a commit id being the same shape), must have its **digits through the letters rather than gathered at the end**, and must measure at least 4 bits per character (`SUSPECT_MIN_ENTROPY`, Shannon). The third condition is the one that earns its keep, and it was found by measuring rather than guessed: long identifiers carrying a year measure 4.0-4.3 bits — at or *above* the entropy floor, so entropy alone cannot separate them from a key — while a generated key interleaves its digits (`ghpA1b2C3d4…`) and a word with a year on it does not (`CollectBudgetProposal2026`); the fourth rejects a run that merely has the right punctuation, such as the repeated-word placeholder `AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE` (3.7 bits). What it still cannot do is the honest limit of the whole idea: a base64 blob of ordinary words and a base64 API key are the same shape, and both are flagged — which is *why* it warns instead of redacting, since the cost is one look rather than a reader who stops trusting the marker. Tests: `src/test/redact.test.ts` **14 → 18** (a key-shaped run returned with its text unchanged; the shapes a report is made of left quiet, ten of them named one by one; the digit-position boundary asserted as a pair that differs only in where the digit sits; and the marker the rules write not being a suspect), `src/test/pr-comment.test.ts` **45 → 50** (the warning on the run page with the token *in* the posted body and no record; digests and identifiers silent; the cap naming five and counting the rest; the note in a dry run; and both notes together on one body). **Verified live, not only in fixtures:** the real poster was run under `bash` with `--dry-run` over a body naming `.env.production`, a `sklive…` key and a `Zm9v…` blob — the payload kept the two runs unredacted, both ⚠️ notes printed, the digest `9f86d081…` and the identifier `CollectBudgetProposal2026` were not flagged, and it exited 0. `npx tsc --noEmit` 0 and `npm run lint:ci` clean. The re-pin was targeted at the two files that moved — `redact.mjs` `57da8734 → 89614866` and `pr-comment.mjs` `bed41ab3 → 9f42bcd7`, each recomputed by hand, with `npm run gates:drift` reading `36 gate file(s) … all match.` afterwards. Read from the other side: with those two files excluded the rest of the suite is **146 files / 1793 passed**, `gate-drift.test.ts` alone is **46/47** with only the manifest case red, and the two files this pass changed are green together at **68/68**.
- **The watch rules have one declaration now — `DEFAULT_WATCHES` in `.freebuff/gate-drift.mjs` — and the manifest records it instead of being a second copy any part of the alarm can follow.** Three hand-kept copies of the same eight rules existed: the script's constant, the rendered `watches` in `.freebuff/gate-hashes.mjs`, and a byte-for-byte `RULES` array in `src/test/gate-drift.test.ts`. The pass that widened the rule to reach `.freebuff/comment-gate.mjs` and `.freebuff/pr-comment.mjs` moved the manifest and the test's copy and left the constant naming the old `^(ci|gate-drift|redact|nightly-report|pr-comment)\.mjs$`, and nothing compared them. The cost was not cosmetic: `readManifest` adopts `loaded.watches` — that is how a fixture manifest can name its own throwaway tree — so the rules a run scans by came from the file rather than from the script. A widening of the constant would therefore have been silently reverted by the next `npm run gates:pin`, and a hand-widening of the manifest silently kept, with the test's `toEqual(RULES)` failing either way as though the pinner had done something wrong. So the test's copy is gone — it imports `DEFAULT_WATCHES`, which is what makes the default, the record and what `--write` renders one list — and `readManifest` now refuses *its own* manifest when the rules it records are not the declaration, as a `problem`: exit 2, naming the one command that re-renders them, and because `--write` repairs a `problem` by rendering the declaration rather than the record, `npm run gates:pin` converges from both directions. The `GATE_HASHES_FILE` seam is the one honest exception, stated in the code rather than left to be rediscovered: the seam exists to point the alarm at a *different* pin — a temp tree with a rule that names it — so a substituted manifest is taken rules and all, which is what keeps the forty-odd fixture cases in the same file meaningful. **Verified:** `src/test/gate-drift.test.ts` is **47 cases** — the new one clears the seam and reads the committed manifest (no problem, rules equal to `DEFAULT_WATCHES`), then a manifest recording a different but well-formed rule set (refused, with `watches` still the declaration, so the repair writes the declared list) — and the manifest's own `Generated — do not edit by hand` header moved with the doc updates, was regenerated by the targeted `--write`, and compares byte-for-byte to `renderManifest` (`true`, checked by hand as well as by the byte-equality case). `npx tsc --noEmit` 0, `npm run lint:ci` clean, `npm run mutation:coverage` **5/5 caught**, runbook Contents up to date (60 sections), every touched file LF, and the full suite **148 files, 1937 passed / 1 skipped** with a clean exit (the usual `Timeouts calling "onTaskUpdate"` unhandled error appears, with every test passing). The re-pin was targeted — `--write .freebuff/gate-drift.mjs` (`46a3d34f → 6ea9772b`) — because no gate file was added and the whole-tree command would have blessed a concurrent session's `.freebuff/mutation-guards.mjs`, which drifted in and out of the tree all pass and was left to it; `npm run gates:drift` reads `36 gate file(s) … all match.`

- **Nothing server-only can reach a client bundle any more, and the check that says so is a walk of the real module graph rather than a list of files.** `NEXT_PUBLIC_` is the whole contract: the bundler inlines exactly those names into code that ships to a browser, and every other environment name belongs to the server. A module that reads one of the others is wrong twice over — the client cannot have the value (`undefined`, or a throw, because there is no `process` in a browser to read `env` off), and if the value *were* inlined it would be published to every visitor — so the two symptoms are refused together rather than told apart. The reason this had to be a graph question is that the answer is not a filename: `src/lib/r2.ts` reads `R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and the rest today and publishes nothing only because no client boundary reaches it, and **one `import { upload } from "@/lib/r2"` in a component is the entire difference**. So `src/test/client-env.test.ts` (new, **27 tests**) starts at every `"use client"` directive (86 of them), follows imports, dynamic imports **and** re-exports (an `export { upload } from "@/lib/r2"` puts that module in the bundle with no local name to notice, which is why the walk reads both halves of an edge), and asks each of the 109 modules it reaches for environment reads it may not carry. **The limb that matters most is the alias, because that is how this repo reads a secret**: `const runtimeEnv = (globalThis as { process?: { env?: Record<string, string | undefined> } }).process?.env ?? {}` appears in `lib/r2.ts` and `lib/db/index.ts` precisely because a Worker has no `process` at all, so a detector that only knew the spelling `process.env.NAME` would be blind to the way this repo actually reads a credential and green forever. `serverEnvReads` therefore reads `process.env.NAME`, `process.env["NAME"]`, the optional-chained `?.["NAME"]`, `import.meta.env.NAME`, a destructured pattern (`const { DATABASE_URL } = process.env`), and members off a module-scope alias of the environment object — transitive, since an alias of an alias is still the environment. `NODE_ENV` is allowed by name and the allowance is pinned by a case, because the bundler substitutes it rather than the server owning it, and an allowance nothing pins is how a guard rots. **The other direction of the same promise is a detector too**: a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` name carrying a credential word is a secret published by whoever typed the prefix — `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` being exactly the mistake a Supabase app makes — so `publicSecretNames` reads identifier, string and template tokens (never comments, which is what lets the rule be documented in prose that names a bad example) and flags any name whose underscored remainder contains a **whole segment** from the vocabulary. `KEY` is deliberately absent: `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` is Supabase's browser-side key and public by design, and flagging it would teach a reader to ignore this guard; the escape hatch for an api key that really is publishable is to name it what it is (a publishable, public or client key), which is one word of edit that makes the claim reviewable. And the same half is a **ratchet**: the declared public vocabulary is written down in the test as exactly `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY` and `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`, so publishing a third value is an edit to that list — a line in a diff a reviewer reads — rather than a prefix typed in a component. **The build configs are the third limb, because the module graph is only one way a value reaches a bundle and the config is the faster one** (nothing has to import anything; the bundler is told to substitute). `define` is Vite's substitution table and is read for the wholesale shape (`define: { "process.env": … }` republishes the environment in every bundle, in any spelling of the key), for a value that reads a non-public name (`define: { URL: JSON.stringify(process.env.DATABASE_URL) }` bakes one in), and `env` is Next's own client-facing list and is read the same way — a value that reads a server name, a value published under a credential name (`env: { R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: "…" }`), or a shorthand entry with no value expression at all. An alias is followed here too, which is the shape `next.config.mjs` sits one line away from today: it already does `const publicUrl = process.env.R2_PUBLIC_URL`, so `env: { PUBLIC_URL: publicUrl }` would publish that value and the guard names the name behind the alias rather than the alias. **Four controls, because a clean run is the one thing that cannot show a check was vacuous**: the tree really is read (`readModuleSources`, **188 modules**) and the walk reaches far more than its roots (109 > 86, which is the edges being followed rather than the directives listed); `src/lib/r2.ts` **is** in the set and the detector **does** report `R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` for it, so the rule is known to fire on this repo's own code and would fire the moment that module entered the graph; a read planted in a module a boundary *imports* fails the sweep in every spelling (direct, bracketed, alias, destructured, `import.meta`) with the planted module named; and the same planted read with nothing reaching it is **not** a leak, which is the control's control and the difference between this guard and a grep over the tree. A server value planted into the real `next.config.mjs` fails the config check at the real file's own line number. **New plumbing, each piece replacing a hand-rolled half:** `source-scan.ts` gained `stringLiteral` and `importSpecifiers` — the other half of `reExportSpecifiers`, since an edge read in one direction is half an edge — and `module-index.ts` gained `readModuleSources()`, every app module keyed `src`-relative and read from disk, with tests left out deliberately (no bundler places a test file in a bundle, and reading `src/test/setup.ts`'s own `process.env` would report the suite's scaffolding as if it shipped) and sharing the one module cache so a resolution the walk makes costs nothing. Tests: `src/test/client-env.test.ts` **27** (new), `src/test/source-scan.test.ts` **45** (+6, one per import spelling plus the `from`-inside-the-clause trap that a first-match walk gets wrong), `src/test/module-index.test.ts` **22** (+3, the tree, the exclusions and the cache), and the three detectors are registered in `CONVENTION_GUARDS` with `EXPECTED_GUARDS` — so the meta-test drives them and the sweep must weaken them. **The sweep grew 13 entries for them — three whole-detector neuters and ten limb strikes, one per decision the meta-test's single fixture cannot separate** (the alias, the bracket, the destructuring, `import.meta`, the boundary directive, the vocabulary word, the segment boundary, the config value, the published credential name, the wholesale key), taking the scoped family from 22 to **35 strikes, 25 of them limbs, every one caught and none with an ambiguous anchor**. One of those anchors was *pre-existing* and had to move: `if (tokens[at]?.text === "?") at += 1;` stopped naming a single decision once the client-env walkers stepped over optional chains too, and the sweep said so in its own words (`anchor found 3 time(s), expected exactly 1; skipped`) rather than quietly dropping the beat-seam limb — the anchor now carries the line below it. Two honest limits: the audit reads **60 of 74 decisions un-struck** (up from 43 of 55, informational — no baseline file is committed here, and the ratchet only bites when one is, which is why the limb strikes above were added rather than assumed), and a credential spelled with lowercase letters would not look like an environment name to the alias branch, which this repo's vocabulary never is. **Verified:** the full suite is **149 files, 2002 passed / 1 skipped**, `npx tsc --noEmit` 0, `npm run lint:ci` clean (`module` as a loop variable is a Next lint error, fixed), `node .freebuff/collect-gates.mjs` exits 0 with the tightest file at 7% of its collect budget, `npm run gates:drift` reads `36 gate file(s) … all match.`, runbook Contents up to date (60 sections), and the usual `[vitest-worker]: Timeout calling "onTaskUpdate"` unhandled error appears with every test passing. - **A save that would leave a pinned gate script unreadable is now refused before it lands: `.freebuff/whole-write.mjs` reads the text *about to be written* and, for a pinned script, writes nothing unless it balances — and the four writers that rewrite a pinned script in place save through it.** The truncation the passes above keep naming (`.freebuff/preview-preflight.mjs`, cut mid-template at its line 970) is the case this closes from the other end: the parse guard in the runner and the tail pin in `src/test/preview-preflight.test.ts` both read a file that is *already* broken, and neither can stop the write that breaks it. `saveWholeScript(path, text)` is a stub for `writeFileSync` that refuses a pinned script whose text leaves a delimiter, a string, a template, a block comment, or nothing at all behind, and `assertWholeScript(text, label)` is the same refusal without the write. The pin is `f45b2c93` (targeted `--write`, the alarm left reading `43 … all match`), and the sweep the truncation had been blocking is finally proven on the real source: **28 of 28 caught, every branch by a test that names it**, `report/register-sentence` last, caught by the tail pin — `npx vitest run src/test/preview-preflight.test.ts src/test/mutation-preflight.test.ts` is **38 passed**, `node .freebuff/whole-write.mjs --check` reads 38 scripts whole.

- **The sweep's strike counts are held against the tables they count now — in the header line and in the `--json` payload both — so a count that drifts from its list fails a case instead of reading plausibly.** A family's size reaches a reader twice, the header a plain run prints and the `self`/`convention`/`limb`/`runner`/`lock`/`ratchet` fields the payload carries, and both are written as `<TABLE>.length` in the sweep's own source; nothing else held either number to the list behind it, because the Pass 9 vocabulary case checks that a count *field exists* per family, never that its value is that family's length. So a count changed to a literal, or pointed at a sibling's table, reads correctly until the table grows past it — the silent drift this closes. **The length of each table is read from the sweep, not restated:** `--anchors --json` enumerates every self-mutation with the family `strikeKind` gives it, one row to a strike, so the rows counted by kind *are* the family lengths (`self 10, convention 10, limb 25, runner 5, lock 2, ratchet 1` — 53 today). The **header** is the line a plain `--list` run prints, the header being emitted before `--list` exits so nothing is struck; the **payload** is the object the refusal writes before its first strike, read over a scratch strike root with one anchor rotted through `MUTATION_STRIKE_ROOT` — its counts come from the same `jsonPayload` a full run uses, so the values are the full run's without a strike (`checked: 0` asserted), which is the only cheap way to read the counts rather than just the field names, since the `--file` that makes a probe cheap is exactly what zeroes the tables being counted. - **The vocabulary the sweep refuses over is readable on its own now: `--vocabulary` lists every declared family beside the exact strikes that stamp it, and marks each hole, so a disagreement is inspectable before it becomes a refusal.** The refusal above names a hole only when a run would otherwise strike; this is the same question asked in report-only form, and the one place a hole is *readable* rather than merely named — a word no entry stamps is printed as a family with `0 strike(s)` under it, and a kind no word declares is printed under its own `NO DECLARED WORD` heading instead of being folded into a neighbour's, which is exactly what a count-only report would hide. - **The CI runner's survivor marks and count words are now held to the vocabularies the three sweeps declare, source against source: a mark or count word renamed in `.freebuff/ci.mjs` alone reds a case.** The mutation stage's per-kind `group`/`noun` maps and the two other mutation stages' `group` maps were held only by runtime literals read off a stub survivor — the stub cannot know the sweep's declared set, so a kind dropped from a stage map passed every case and fell through to the runner's `SURVIVED (<kind>)` / `unclassified` fallbacks, and a mark reworded drifted from the sweep's own report with nothing to say so.
